name: Propaedeutics of Internal Medicine
description: Complete study manual · 14 practical class topics

topics.title: The tasks of the propaedeutics of internal medicine. The order of patient examination. The case history outline. History taking

goals.text: To introduce the student to the content of the propaedeutics of internal medicine, the order of the clinical examination of the patient and the outline for keeping the case history (medical record); to teach the student to collect the complaints, the history of present illness (anamnesis morbi) and the life history (anamnesis vitae) from the patient independently.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the concepts of propaedeutics, semiotics, symptom, syndrome and diagnosis;
the main (physical) and additional methods of the clinical examination of the patient;
the structure of the case history and what is written in each section;
the principles of dividing complaints into main and additional groups;
the plan of the anamnesis morbi and the anamnesis vitae;
the principles of medical deontology and medical confidentiality.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: start the conversation with the patient correctly, introduce himself or herself and obtain consent;
use open and closed questions appropriately;
analyze each complaint in detail according to a plan;
record the collected information in the case history competently.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The main tasks of propaedeutics: to teach a systematic and complete examination of the patient; to teach how to detect and interpret symptoms and syndromes; to teach how to make a syndromic (provisional) diagnosis; to teach how to keep the case history correctly; to instill medical ethics and deontology.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: It is a mistake to base a diagnosis on a single sign. For example, ascites is not specific to liver cirrhosis: it also occurs in heart failure, nephrotic syndrome and tumors of the peritoneum. The combination of all the signs must always be analyzed.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The basic rules of communicating with the patient: introduce yourself, address the patient by name and obtain consent for the examination; sit face to face with the patient, with your eyes at the same level, in a relaxed position; listen to the patient without interrupting and show your attention by nodding; hide your negative emotions and stay calm even if you detect a serious sign; keep medical confidentiality: information about the patient is used only for treatment.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Leading (suggestive) questions push the patient toward a wrong answer and lead to diagnostic error. The conversation should begin with open questions and then move on to closed questions for clarification (the “funnel” technique).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The order of the examination is always the same: **history taking → general inspection → inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation of the organ systems → additional investigations**. The systems are usually examined in the following order: the respiratory, cardiovascular, digestive, urinary, endocrine, musculoskeletal and nervous systems.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The four methods of physical examination — **“IPPA”**: **I**nspection, **P**alpation, **P**ercussion, **A**uscultation. Never change the order: first we look, then we touch, then we tap, and last of all we listen.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The case history is a legal document. Every entry made in it is confirmed with the date, time and signature; corrections are made only in the established manner. Giving information about the patient to third parties without his or her consent is a breach of medical confidentiality.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: In English-language textbooks (Macleod’s), the analysis of pain is remembered as **SOCRATES**: **S**ite, **O**nset, **C**haracter, **R**adiation, **A**ssociations (accompanying symptoms), **T**ime course, **E**xacerbating/relieving factors, **S**everity.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The smoking index (**“pack-years”**) = number of cigarettes smoked per day × years of smoking / 20. When the index exceeds 10 pack-years, the risk of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) rises considerably.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The review of systems is not a “formality”. For example, in a young woman who complains only of joint pain, questioning may reveal a facial rash and hair loss, pointing to systemic lupus erythematosus; in a patient admitted with a respiratory disease, the discovery of nocturia and edema may lead to heart or kidney disease.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: When working with a patient, the student: introduces himself or herself as a student and obtains the patient’s consent; does not give the patient independent information about the diagnosis or prognosis — this is the task of the attending physician; does not share information about the patient (photos, case history) on social media; respects the patient’s decision if he or she refuses.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Protection against errors is the question **“What else could it be?”** After every diagnosis, list at least two alternative diseases and look for the signs that rule them out or confirm them.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Every additional investigation is ordered **to answer a clinical question**. Ordering many tests “just in case” exhausts the patient, increases costs and, because of incidental findings (“incidentalomas”), may lead to unnecessary invasive procedures. A correctly collected history and a meticulous physical examination reduce the number of investigations needed.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The **“3A” rule** of a good history: **A**ttend (do not interrupt the patient), **A**nalyze (each complaint according to the plan), **A**ffirm (repeat back what you heard and get the patient’s confirmation).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In the case history, write not the patient’s own expressions (“my insides burn”, “my heart is being squeezed”) but their medical interpretation; however, do not arbitrarily exaggerate or play down the patient’s words. For example, “my heart is being squeezed” may not be written down as “angina pectoris” without clarifying what it means.

sections.title: 1. The propaedeutics of internal medicine: the subject, its aim and tasks

blocks.text: **Propaedeutics** (Greek propaideuo — “to teach beforehand, to introduce into a science”) is the introductory stage of the clinical disciplines. The propaedeutics of internal medicine teaches the future physician the methods of examining the patient, how to detect and interpret the signs of disease and make a syndromic diagnosis, as well as medical ethics and deontology. This knowledge is needed not only in the senior years but throughout the physician’s whole career.
The discipline has three main parts:

items: **Diagnostic technique** — the methods of history taking, inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation of the patient, as well as laboratory and instrumental investigations.
**Semiotics (semiology)** — the study of the signs of disease (symptoms), their mechanism of origin and diagnostic significance.
**Diagnostic methodology** — clinical reasoning, combining the signs into syndromes and the rules for formulating the diagnosis.

parts.text: The main tasks of propaedeutics:

items: to teach a systematic and complete examination of the patient;
to teach how to detect and interpret symptoms and syndromes;
to teach how to make a syndromic (provisional) diagnosis;
to teach how to keep the case history correctly;
to instill medical ethics and deontology.

blocks.text: The concepts of health and disease
According to the Constitution of the World Health Organization (WHO), **health** is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.

**Disease** is a complex general response of the organism to the action of harmful factors, in which structural, functional and metabolic changes and a breakdown of adaptive processes are observed and the capacity for work is limited. The causes of disease are mechanical, physical, chemical, biological, psychological and hereditary (genetic) factors.

sections.title: 2. The concepts of symptom, syndrome and diagnosis

blocks.text: A **symptom (sign)** is a single manifestation of disease. Symptoms are classified according to several principles.

blocks.title: Table 1.1. Classification of symptoms
head: Basis of classification
Type
Example
rows: Pain, nausea, a sensation of shortness of breath
A diastolic murmur and the “quail rhythm” — in mitral stenosis

blocks.text: A **syndrome** is a combination of symptoms that share a common pathogenesis. For example, the syndrome of lung tissue consolidation: a dull note on percussion, increased vocal fremitus and bronchial breathing. One syndrome may occur in several diseases (consolidation — pneumonia, pulmonary infarction, tumor).
A **diagnosis** is the physician’s brief and precise conclusion about the patient’s disease. The process of making a diagnosis proceeds in the following sequence.

blocks.title: Table 1.2. Stages of making a diagnosis
head: Stage
Content
rows: Collecting data: history taking, physical examination, additional investigations
Analysis of the signs (assessing the significance of each sign)
Combining the signs into syndromes according to their pathogenetic connection (synthesis)

blocks.text: Types of diagnosis

items: **Primary (provisional)** — made after the first examination of the patient.
**Clinical (main)** — made after clinical, laboratory and instrumental investigations, usually within three days.
**Final** — made before the patient is discharged from hospital (or after death).

blocks.text: The structure of the clinical diagnosis: **the main disease**, **complications of the main disease**, **a competing disease**, **a background disease** (for example, diabetes mellitus) and **concomitant diseases**. A complete diagnosis includes anatomical (morphological), functional, pathogenetic and etiological components.

parts.text: An example of a complete clinical diagnosis: “Rheumatic heart disease: mitral stenosis (moderate). Complication: atrial fibrillation, permanent form. Chronic heart failure stage IIA, NYHA functional class III.” Here the morphology (the defect), function (the failure), complication (the arrhythmia) and etiology (rheumatic) are reflected in a single conclusion.

blocks.text: Methods of clinical reasoning

items: **Induction** — moving from particular signs to a general conclusion: the signs are collected and combined into syndromes, and then a conclusion about the disease is drawn.

**Deduction** — from general knowledge to the particular: the physician looks in the patient for the other signs characteristic of the disease he or she suspects and confirms or rejects the hypothesis.
**Diagnosis ex juvantibus** — if treatment directed against the suspected disease is effective, the diagnosis is considered confirmed.

parts.text: It is a mistake to base a diagnosis on a single sign. For example, ascites is not specific to liver cirrhosis: it also occurs in heart failure, nephrotic syndrome and tumors of the peritoneum. The combination of all the signs must always be analyzed.

sections.title: 3. Medical deontology and communication with the patient

blocks.text: **Medical deontology** (Greek deon — duty, logos — study) is the study of the physician’s professional duty and conduct. **Medical ethics** is a broader concept covering the relationships of the health worker with the patient, his or her relatives, colleagues and society.

Great contributions to the history of deontology were made by Hippocrates (“Do no harm” — primum non nocere), Avicenna (Ibn Sina) (“A physician should have the eyes of a falcon, the hands of a maiden, the wisdom of a serpent and the heart of a lion”) and, later, the Declaration of Geneva (1948), the International Code of Medical Ethics (1949) and the Declaration of Helsinki (1964).

parts.text: The basic rules of communicating with the patient:

items: introduce yourself, address the patient by name and obtain consent for the examination;
sit face to face with the patient, with your eyes at the same level, in a relaxed position;
listen to the patient without interrupting and show your attention by nodding;
hide your negative emotions and stay calm even if you detect a serious sign;
keep medical confidentiality: information about the patient is used only for treatment.

blocks.label: Figure 1.1
blocks.caption: The position of the physician and the patient during the conversation (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 1)

blocks.text: Types of questions

blocks.title: Table 1.3. Questions used in history taking
head: Type of question
Purpose
Example
rows: “What is bothering you?”, “How did your illness begin?”
“Does a cough bother you at night?”
Checking that the patient’s meaning has been understood correctly
“So the pain appears when you climb stairs, is that right?”
“The pain spreads to your left arm, right?”

parts.text: Leading (suggestive) questions push the patient toward a wrong answer and lead to diagnostic error. The conversation should begin with open questions and then move on to closed questions for clarification (the “funnel” technique).

sections.title: 4. Methods and order of the clinical examination of the patient

blocks.text: The examination of the patient is divided into **main (physical)** and **additional (laboratory and instrumental)** methods.

blocks.title: Table 1.4. Methods of examining the patient
head: Group
Method
Latin name
What is determined
rows: Complaints, history of the illness and of the patient’s life
General condition, skin, body build, shape of the organs
Condition of the organs, pain, vibration, pulsation
Borders of the organs, density and air content of the tissues
Breathing, heart sounds, murmurs, intestinal peristalsis
Analysis of blood, urine, sputum and aspirates
X-ray, ECG, US, endoscopy, spirometry, CT, MRI

parts.text: The order of the examination is always the same: **history taking → general inspection → inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation of the organ systems → additional investigations**. The systems are usually examined in the following order: the respiratory, cardiovascular, digestive, urinary, endocrine, musculoskeletal and nervous systems.

blocks.text: In the opinion of experienced clinicians, history taking provides about half of the information needed for the diagnosis, the physical examination about 30 percent and laboratory and instrumental investigations about 20 percent. For example, the diagnosis of angina pectoris can in many cases be made from the characteristics of the pain.

parts.text: The four methods of physical examination — **“IPPA”**: **I**nspection, **P**alpation, **P**ercussion, **A**uscultation. Never change the order: first we look, then we touch, then we tap, and last of all we listen.

sections.title: 5. Outline of the case history (medical record)

blocks.text: The case history is the main medical and legal document in which all the information about the patient is recorded. The student’s educational case history is written according to the same outline.

blocks.title: Table 1.5. Structure of the case history
head: Section
Content
rows: Full name, age, sex, nationality, occupation, place of work, address, date of admission, referred by whom
Main and additional complaints, each in detail
When and how the disease began, its course, treatment, the latest deterioration
Growth and development, living conditions, occupation, harmful habits, past illnesses, allergy, heredity
General inspection and objective examination by systems
Detailed information on the main affected organ
The syndromes identified and the conclusion based on them

parts.text: The case history is a legal document. Every entry made in it is confirmed with the date, time and signature; corrections are made only in the established manner. Giving information about the patient to third parties without his or her consent is a breach of medical confidentiality.

sections.title: 6. History taking (interrogatio)

blocks.text: Although history taking seems simple, it is the most complex and the most valuable method of examination. It consists of the following parts: passport data → complaints → history of present illness → life history.
6.1. Passport data

The patient’s age, sex, occupation and place of residence are important for the diagnosis. For example, dyspeptic symptoms that appear for the first time in old age raise suspicion of a tumor, whereas in a young person they are most often associated with a functional disorder. The occupation helps to suspect occupational diseases (pneumoconiosis, intoxication).
6.2. The patient’s complaints (querelae)
Complaints are divided into two groups:

items: **Main (leading) complaints** — the signs that made the patient seek medical help and that are characteristic of the main affected organ (for example, cough and sputum, pain in the heart region).
**Additional (general) complaints** — general weakness, easy fatigability, fever, sweating, loss of appetite, sleep disturbance, change in body weight.

blocks.text: Once the main complaints have been established, the **review of systems** is carried out: all the systems are briefly asked about (respiratory, circulatory, digestive, urinary, nervous, endocrine and musculoskeletal systems and the sense organs) to detect the signs that the patient has forgotten or not paid attention to.
Each complaint, especially pain, is analyzed in detail according to the following plan.

blocks.title: Table 1.6. Plan for analyzing pain (a complaint)
head: Feature
Question to ask
Example (angina pectoris)
rows: When and after what did it begin?
What kind of pain is it?
To the left arm, shoulder blade, lower jaw

parts.text: In English-language textbooks (Macleod’s), the analysis of pain is remembered as **SOCRATES**: **S**ite, **O**nset, **C**haracter, **R**adiation, **A**ssociations (accompanying symptoms), **T**ime course, **E**xacerbating/relieving factors, **S**everity.

blocks.text: 6.3. History of present illness (anamnesis morbi)
The history of present illness reflects the course of the disease from its onset to the present day. It answers the following questions:

items: When, where and under what circumstances did the patient fall ill?
How did the disease begin — suddenly (acutely) or gradually?
In the patient’s opinion, what caused the disease (chilling, physical or emotional strain, dietary errors, infection, occupational factors)?
What were the first signs?
When and where was medical help first provided, and with what result?
How has the disease progressed: the dynamics of the symptoms, periods of exacerbation and remission and their duration?
What investigations were carried out and with what results (outpatient card, discharge summaries, ECG, X-ray films)?
What treatment did the patient receive, and how effective was it?
What caused the latest deterioration, and what led to the present hospital admission?

blocks.text: 6.4. Life history (anamnesis vitae)
The life history is the patient’s medical biography. It helps to identify the factors predisposing to disease and the risk factors.

blocks.title: Table 1.7. Plan of the life history
head: Section
What is determined
rows: Place of birth, which child in the family, growth and development in childhood, education
Housing, family status, regularity and quality of meals, physical activity
Since when the patient has worked, occupation, working conditions, occupational hazards (dust, chemicals, noise, vibration), military service
Smoking (from what age, how many a day), alcohol, drugs
In chronological order from childhood: infections, tuberculosis, hepatitis, sexually transmitted diseases, injuries, operations, blood transfusions
Reactions to drugs, foods and household allergens: urticaria, angioedema (Quincke’s edema), anaphylactic shock
Arterial hypertension, IHD, diabetes mellitus, tumors, tuberculosis and mental illness in close relatives
Age at menarche, regularity of menstruation, pregnancies, deliveries, abortions, menopause
Contact with an infectious patient, travel, contact with animals, injections
Disability group, duration of temporary incapacity for work

parts.text: The smoking index (**“pack-years”**) = number of cigarettes smoked per day × years of smoking / 20. When the index exceeds 10 pack-years, the risk of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) rises considerably.

The key to the diagnosis often lies in the life history: frequent tonsillitis and joint pain in childhood raise suspicion of rheumatic heart disease; mining — of silicosis; prolonged fever after a tooth extraction — of infective endocarditis; frequent injections — of hepatitis and endocarditis.

sections.title: 7. A brief history of the development of internal medicine and propaedeutics

blocks.text: The methods of examining the patient have taken shape over thousands of years. Knowing their history helps to understand the meaning of each method more deeply.

blocks.title: Table 1.8. Important milestones in the history of internal medicine
head: Period
Scientist
Contribution
rows: Made observation and questioning of the patient the basis of medicine; described direct auscultation (with the ear placed on the chest), the “Hippocratic face”, “Hippocratic fingers” and the “succussion splash” of fluid and air in the pleural cavity
Study of the pulse, anatomical and physiological observations
“The Canon of Medicine”: more than 10 types of pulse, inspection of urine and stool, systematization of the signs of disease; precepts on medical ethics
Discovered the method of percussion (“Inventum novum”)
Introduced percussion widely into practice and developed the semiotics of heart disease
Invented the stethoscope and created indirect auscultation and the nomenclature of breath sounds
Developed the physical basis of percussion and auscultation
Russian clinical schools: Botkin — viewing disease as a disease of the whole organism, and clinical reasoning; Zakharyin — raised history taking to the level of an art
Method of measuring blood pressure (Korotkov sounds, 1905)
Deep sliding methodical palpation of the abdominal organs; among the first to describe the clinical picture of myocardial infarction (1909)
Discovery of X-rays — the beginning of the era of imaging the internal organs

blocks.text: The formation of the clinical school of internal medicine in Uzbekistan is linked to the founding of the medical faculty of Turkestan (later Central Asian) State University in the 1920s. The Tashkent school of therapy was founded by Professor A.N. Kryukov; later, many Uzbek clinicians emerged and developed the schools of propaedeutics, cardiology, pulmonology and gastroenterology in the republic.

parts.text: History shows that every physical method was “high technology” in its time. Even though CT and MRI exist today, the stethoscope and percussion remain the only examination methods that are used at every patient’s bedside, are free and safe and can be applied anywhere.

sections.title: 8. Review of systems

blocks.text: The review of systems (anamnesis per systemae, review of systems) is carried out to detect the signs that the patient has not mentioned. It is performed after the main complaints and the history of present illness, with short, precise questions. Concomitant diseases are often discovered at this stage.

blocks.title: Table 1.9. Plan of the review of systems
head: System
Main signs to ask about
rows: Weakness, easy fatigability, fever, chills, night sweats, change in body weight (over what period, how many kg), appetite, thirst
Rash, itching, change in color, changes in the hair and nails, enlargement of the lymph nodes
Cough, sputum, hemoptysis, dyspnea, choking attacks, chest pain, snoring and pauses in breathing during sleep
Pain in the heart region, palpitations and skipped beats, dyspnea, orthopnea, nocturnal choking attacks, edema, syncope, leg pain on walking
Appetite, difficulty swallowing, heartburn, belching, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, bowel movements (frequency, character, admixture of blood), jaundice
Frequency of urination and pain on urination, nighttime urination (nocturia), color and amount of urine, low back pain, edema
Thirst, polyuria, intolerance of heat or cold, sweating, change in weight, enlargement of the neck
Joint pain, swelling, morning stiffness and its duration, muscle pain, low back pain
Headache, dizziness, syncope, seizures, sensory and motor disturbances, sleep, mood, anxiety
Bleeding, bruising, bleeding gums, frequent infections
Decreased vision, double vision, tinnitus, decreased hearing

parts.text: The review of systems is not a “formality”. For example, in a young woman who complains only of joint pain, questioning may reveal a facial rash and hair loss, pointing to systemic lupus erythematosus; in a patient admitted with a respiratory disease, the discovery of nocturia and edema may lead to heart or kidney disease.

sections.title: 9. Special situations in analyzing complaints

blocks.text: 9.1. Features related to age, sex and occupation
The same complaint is interpreted differently in different patients:

items: **Age:** chest pain in a 20-year-old man is most often due to a musculoskeletal or pleural cause, whereas in a 60-year-old male smoker it is due to angina pectoris; constipation or weight loss appearing for the first time in the elderly raises suspicion of a tumor.
**Sex:** in women, angina pectoris often runs an atypical course (weakness, dyspnea, nausea); iron deficiency anemia, thyroid diseases and systemic lupus erythematosus are more common in women.

**Occupation:** silicosis in miners and stonecutters; byssinosis and the effects of pesticides in cotton growing; diseases of the vocal apparatus in teachers and singers; low back pain, hemorrhoids and ischemic heart disease in drivers; viral hepatitis and tuberculosis in health workers.

blocks.text: 9.2. Pain rating scales
Because the intensity of pain is subjective, expressing it in numbers makes it easier to follow its dynamics.

blocks.title: Table 1.10. Pain rating scales
head: Scale
Content
rows: 0 — no pain, 10 — the worst pain imaginable; 1–3 — mild, 4–6 — moderate, 7–10 — severe
The patient marks the intensity of pain on a 10 cm line
Pictures of faces for children and patients who cannot speak

blocks.text: 9.3. The patient’s “words” and medical terms
Patients express their sensations in everyday expressions. The student must interpret them correctly.

blocks.title: Table 1.11. Patients’ expressions and their possible meaning
head: Patient’s expression
What needs clarifying
Possible medical meaning
rows: Is it pain or anxiety? Is it related to exertion?
Is it fast beating or skipped beats?
When, on what exertion? Does it get worse when lying down?
Behind the sternum or in the epigastrium? Is it related to food?
How often are the bowels opened?
Do the surroundings spin, or does the vision go dark?
Has the blood pressure been measured?

sections.title: 10. Modern principles of medical ethics

blocks.text: Modern medical ethics (biomedical ethics) rests on four basic principles (T. Beauchamp and J. Childress):

blocks.title: Table 1.12. The basic principles of biomedical ethics
head: Principle
Content
Example in practice
rows: No intervention should cause more harm than benefit
Choosing the most effective, evidence-based treatment
The patient has the right to make decisions about his or her own health
Informed consent, respecting the right to refuse treatment
Equal and impartial treatment of all patients
Equal care regardless of nationality, religion or social status

blocks.text: **Informed consent** is voluntary consent obtained after the purpose, benefits, risks and alternatives of an investigation or treatment have been explained to the patient in understandable language. Before invasive procedures (puncture, endoscopy, surgery) it is documented in writing.

parts.text: When working with a patient, the student:

items: introduces himself or herself as a student and obtains the patient’s consent;
does not give the patient independent information about the diagnosis or prognosis — this is the task of the attending physician;
does not share information about the patient (photos, case history) on social media;
respects the patient’s decision if he or she refuses.

blocks.text: A modern model of the consultation
According to the **Calgary–Cambridge model**, widely used in international practice, the consultation consists of the following stages:

items: **Initiating the session** — introductions, identifying the reason for the patient’s visit, agreeing on the plan of the conversation.
**Gathering information** — moving from open to closed questions, identifying the patient’s ideas, concerns and expectations.
**Physical examination.**
**Explanation and planning** — explaining the findings in understandable language and making decisions together with the patient.
**Closing the session** — summarizing, explaining the next steps and what to do if “red flag” symptoms appear.

sections.title: 11. Typical errors in clinical reasoning

blocks.text: Most diagnostic errors arise not from a lack of knowledge but from errors in reasoning.

blocks.title: Table 1.13. Cognitive errors in clinical reasoning
head: Error
Content
Example
rows: Clinging to the first impression and ignoring new information
A patient who came with a cough is labeled “bronchitis”, and the hemoptysis and weight loss found later are ignored
Stopping the search once a diagnosis has been made
Anemia is found, but its cause (intestinal bleeding) is not sought
Looking only for signs that confirm one’s own hypothesis
Thinking of angina pectoris and failing to hear the signs of pericarditis (a friction rub)
Recalling only the most recently seen or vivid cases
Regarding any fever as influenza during an influenza epidemic
Not taking seriously the complaints of a patient with a mental illness or alcoholism
Missing a head injury in an intoxicated patient

parts.text: Protection against errors is the question **“What else could it be?”** After every diagnosis, list at least two alternative diseases and look for the signs that rule them out or confirm them.

sections.title: 12. General semiotics: common general signs

blocks.text: Some signs are not specific to a single organ but occur in many diseases. Although they are “nonspecific”, they are often the first and only manifestation of the disease.

blocks.title: Table 1.14. General signs and their main causes

Main causes
What to clarify during history taking
rows: Anemia, hypothyroidism, diabetes mellitus, heart failure, chronic infections, tumors, depression
Since when, in the morning or in the evening, does it pass after rest
Tumors, thyrotoxicosis, diabetes mellitus, tuberculosis, HIV, malabsorption, depression
Is the appetite preserved (in thyrotoxicosis and diabetes the appetite is good)
Tuberculosis, lymphomas, chronic infections, infective endocarditis, menopause
Does it force the patient to change the nightshirt
Type, duration, with or without chills
Cholestasis, chronic kidney disease, Hodgkin lymphoma (lymphogranulomatosis), erythremia (after bathing), allergy
Diabetes mellitus, diabetes insipidus, hypercalcemia, diuretics
How much fluid the patient drinks a day, whether he or she gets up at night

parts.text: **“B symptoms”** — fever (above 38 °C), night sweats and loss of more than 10 % of body weight in 6 months — are important prognostic signs in lymphomas. The presence of all three signs together always requires a thorough investigation.

blocks.text: 12.1. Pathophysiological types of pain

blocks.title: Table 1.15. Types of pain
head: Type
Source
Features
Example
rows: Skin, muscles, bones, parietal pleura and peritoneum
Well localized, sharp, worse on movement

blocks.text: **Zakharyin–Head zones** — pain and increased sensitivity (hyperesthesia) in certain areas of the skin in diseases of the internal organs. For example, for the heart — the left shoulder girdle, the inner surface of the left arm and the region of the left shoulder blade (segments CIII–CIV and ThI–ThV); for the liver and gallbladder — the right hypochondrium and the region of the right shoulder blade.

sections.title: 13. An overview of laboratory and instrumental methods of investigation

blocks.text: Besides the physical methods, the discipline of propaedeutics also studies the purpose and capabilities of the main additional investigations.

blocks.title: Table 1.16. The main additional methods of investigation
head: Method
Principle
Diagnostic capabilities
rows: Glucose, bilirubin, enzymes, creatinine, lipids, electrolytes
Disorders of the liver, kidneys, heart and metabolism
Diseases of the kidneys and urinary tract, diabetes
Different absorption of X-rays by the tissues
Lungs, cardiac shadow, bones, intestinal obstruction
Liver, gallbladder, kidneys, thyroid gland, heart (echocardiography), pleural fluid
Recording the electrical activity of the heart
Viewing hollow organs with an optical instrument
Gastrointestinal tract, bronchi; taking a biopsy
Measuring the function of an organ

parts.text: Every additional investigation is ordered **to answer a clinical question**. Ordering many tests “just in case” exhausts the patient, increases costs and, because of incidental findings (“incidentalomas”), may lead to unnecessary invasive procedures. A correctly collected history and a meticulous physical examination reduce the number of investigations needed.

sections.title: 14. Medical records and legal responsibility

blocks.text: The case history (the medical record of the inpatient) and the outpatient card are **legal documents** that confirm the patient’s rights, the physician’s work and the quality of medical care. The following requirements apply to them:

items: entries are made **on time**, accurately and legibly, with the date and time indicated and with a signature;
the results of investigations, the treatment prescribed and the patient’s consent (or refusal) are recorded;
corrections are made in the established manner (without erasing the old entry: it is crossed out, dated and signed);
information about the patient is **medical confidentiality** and is not given to third parties except in cases established by law.

blocks.text: The Law of the Republic of Uzbekistan “On the Protection of the Health of Citizens” establishes the patient’s rights — respectful treatment, receiving information about his or her health, giving consent to medical intervention or refusing it, and the preservation of medical confidentiality.

sections.title: 15. Special situations in history taking

blocks.title: Table 1.17. History taking in difficult situations
head: Situation
Recommendations
rows: Information is obtained from relatives, ambulance staff and documents; the vital functions are assessed first
Speak slowly, clearly and loudly; take impaired hearing and vision into account; find out whether the patient takes many medicines (polypharmacy); if memory is impaired, talk to the relatives
Through an interpreter (a professional rather than a relative wherever possible); short, simple questions
Allow more time, acknowledge the patient’s feelings, use open questions
Stay calm, keep a safe distance, stand on the side of the door, do not raise your voice
With the parents; adolescents are also questioned alone for part of the interview
Begin with an explanation (“We ask all patients these questions”), do not judge

parts.text: The **“3A” rule** of a good history: **A**ttend (do not interrupt the patient), **A**nalyze (each complaint according to the plan), **A**ffirm (repeat back what you heard and get the patient’s confirmation).

sections.title: 16. Clinical part

blocks.text: Algorithm of independent history taking
From the moment the student enters the patient’s ward, he or she follows this order:

items: Cleans the hands and checks the gown and mask (if necessary).
Greets the patient and introduces himself or herself: “Hello, I am a 3rd-year student ..., may I ask you about your illness?”
Establishes the patient’s passport data.
Asks an open question: “What is bothering you?” — and listens to the patient without interrupting for 1–2 minutes.
Identifies the main complaints and asks about each in detail according to the plan.
Identifies the additional (general) complaints, then carries out a brief review of systems.
Collects the history of present illness in chronological order.
Collects the life history according to the plan.
Briefly repeats what he or she has heard and gets the patient’s confirmation: “Have I understood you correctly?”
Thanks the patient and explains the next stage — the objective examination.

blocks.text: Sample case history entry

**Complaints:** cough, production of up to 50 ml of mucopurulent sputum a day, a rise in body temperature to 38.5 °C, stabbing pain in the right side of the chest on deep inspiration. Additional complaints: general weakness, sweating, loss of appetite.

**History of present illness:** considers himself ill for 5 days. The illness began suddenly after chilling, with chills and a rise in temperature to 39 °C. The next day a cough and right-sided pain were added. He took paracetamol at home without effect. Because his condition worsened, he was admitted to hospital by ambulance.

**Life history:** 45 years old, the third child in the family; his growth and development kept pace with his peers. A driver; working conditions involve cold and dampness. Has smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 25 years (smoking index 25 pack-years). Denies tuberculosis, hepatitis and venereal diseases. No drug allergy. His father had arterial hypertension.

parts.text: In the case history, write not the patient’s own expressions (“my insides burn”, “my heart is being squeezed”) but their medical interpretation; however, do not arbitrarily exaggerate or play down the patient’s words. For example, “my heart is being squeezed” may not be written down as “angina pectoris” without clarifying what it means.

skills.title: Skill: detailed analysis of the patient’s complaint

items: Seat the patient comfortably and sit face to face with him or her.
Ask an open question: “What is bothering you?”
For each complaint, ask according to the plan: site, onset, character, radiation, duration, exacerbating and relieving factors, severity, associated symptoms.
Divide the complaints into main and additional groups.
Carry out a brief review of systems.
Briefly repeat the information obtained to the patient and get confirmation.
Record the result in the case history in medical terms.

skills.title: Skill: collecting the life history

items: Begin with the biography (place of birth, growth, education).
Establish the living and dietary conditions.
Ask about the occupational history and occupational hazards.
Identify harmful habits and calculate the smoking index.
Ask about past illnesses, operations and blood transfusions in chronological order.
Establish the allergy history, especially drug allergy.
Collect the family and epidemiological history and, in women, the gynecological history.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 58-year-old man presented saying “my heart is being squeezed”. The student immediately asked, “The pain spreads to your left arm, right?”, the patient answered “yes”, and the student wrote “angina pectoris” in the case history.
cases.ask: What mistakes did the student make? How should the complaint have been analyzed?
cases.answer: The student asked a leading question and wrote a diagnosis without clarifying the patient’s words. The correct way is to start with an open question (“Describe the squeezing”) and to analyze the pain according to the plan: site, onset (on exertion?), character, radiation, duration, the effect of nitroglycerin and rest, associated symptoms. The complaint is written in the case history in medical terms after the analysis, and the diagnosis is made only after all the information has been collected.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 35-year-old woman complains of palpitations and dyspnea. From the life history: in childhood she often had tonsillitis, and at the age of 14 she had “migrating” pain in the knee and ankle joints and was treated in hospital.
cases.ask: Which information in the life history is important? Which disease can be considered?
cases.answer: Recurrent tonsillitis in childhood and migrating polyarthritis are characteristic of acute rheumatic fever. The present palpitations and dyspnea give grounds to think of rheumatic heart disease (most often mitral stenosis) and its complications (atrial fibrillation, heart failure). This example shows how important it is to collect the life history in full.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: After a patient was admitted to hospital, penicillin injections were prescribed. After the first injection the patient developed dizziness, flushing of the skin and a sharp fall in blood pressure. It later turned out that the patient had wanted to say that he had previously “come out in a rash” from penicillin, but nobody had asked.
cases.ask: Which stage of history taking was missed? What are the consequences of such an error?
cases.answer: The allergy history was not collected. As a result, the patient developed drug anaphylaxis (anaphylactic shock), a life-threatening condition. Every patient must be asked about reactions to drugs, foods and other allergens, and the result is recorded separately on the first page of the case history.

topics.title: General inspection of the patient: general condition, consciousness, position, body build. Inspection of the head, face and neck

goals.text: To teach the student the rules of performing the general inspection, how to assess the patient’s general condition, consciousness, position and constitutional type, and the diagnostic signs detected on inspection of the head, face, eyes, oral cavity and neck.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the conditions and order of performing the general inspection;
the grades of the general condition and their criteria;
the quantitative and qualitative types of impaired consciousness and the Glasgow Coma Scale;
the active, passive and forced positions of the patient and their causes;
the signs of the constitutional types (normosthenic, hypersthenic, asthenic);
the facial appearances characteristic of diseases (facies);
the eye signs of thyrotoxicosis and the changes in the tongue and neck.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: perform the general inspection according to a set plan;
assess consciousness and calculate the score on the Glasgow scale;
determine the epigastric angle and establish the constitutional type;
inspect the face, eyes, tongue and neck and record the result in the case history.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Conditions of the inspection: the room should be warm (so that the patient does not get chilled) and quiet; the light should be **natural, diffuse daylight**: jaundice and pallor are poorly seen in artificial (electric) light; the light should fall from the side: protrusions and depressions on the body surface and pulsation are then well seen; the patient’s body is uncovered step by step, and the parts not being examined are kept covered; the symmetrical parts of the body are always compared.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The total GCS score ranges from 3 to 15: **15** — clear consciousness; **13–14** — obtundation; **9–12** — sopor (stupor); **8 or less** — coma (the airway needs protecting).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Coma by the odor of the breath: **“Acetone — Ammonia — Alcohol — Liver”**. Acetone — diabetic coma, ammonia (urine) — uremic coma, alcohol — alcoholic coma, sweetish-musty “liver odor” (fetor hepaticus) — hepatic coma.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In lung abscess and bronchiectasis, the patient lies on the affected side, because on turning onto the healthy side, pus flows through the draining bronchus into the trachea and increases the cough and sputum production. However, this very feature is used in treatment: for **postural drainage**, the patient is placed in the position in which the sputum drains out.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The epigastric angle — **“Hyper — Wide, Asthenic — Narrow”**: in the HYPERsthenic type the angle is wide (>90°), in the ASTHENIC type it is narrow (<90°), and in the normosthenic type it is a right angle (90°).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: When assessing distension of the neck veins, the patient lies at an angle of 45°. If the upper level of the internal jugular venous pulsation is **more than 3 cm above** the sternal angle, the central venous pressure is considered raised.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Normally, the venous pulsation rises no higher than **3 cm above** the sternal angle (CVP up to 8 cm H2O). At 4 cm or more the CVP is raised: right ventricular failure, tricuspid regurgitation, cardiac tamponade, constrictive pericarditis, hypervolemia. If the neck veins are full with the patient sitting upright, the CVP is markedly raised.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Sudden confusion and restlessness in an elderly patient are often not “old age” but a sign of **pneumonia, urinary tract infection, hypoglycemia, dehydration or an adverse drug effect**. In such a situation the cause must be actively sought.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Inspection of the hands is **“a mirror that tells a great deal”**: the nails (clubbing, koilonychia, Terry’s nails), the palms (erythema, pallor, Dupuytren’s contracture), the fingers (Osler’s nodes, Heberden’s and Bouchard’s nodes, rheumatoid deformities), tremor (thyrotoxicosis, asterixis), temperature and moisture. That is why it is convenient to begin the objective examination by taking the patient’s hand and counting the pulse.

sections.title: 1. Rules for performing the general inspection

blocks.text: However advanced laboratory and instrumental methods become, the general inspection (inspectio) remains one of the main methods of examination. An experienced physician often draws an important conclusion at the very first sight of the patient: a patient with heart failure sitting in the orthopnea position, a thyrotoxic patient with protruding eyes, and so on.

parts.text: Conditions of the inspection:

items: the room should be warm (so that the patient does not get chilled) and quiet;
the light should be **natural, diffuse daylight**: jaundice and pallor are poorly seen in artificial (electric) light;
the light should fall from the side: protrusions and depressions on the body surface and pulsation are then well seen;
the patient’s body is uncovered step by step, and the parts not being examined are kept covered;
the symmetrical parts of the body are always compared.

blocks.text: The inspection is performed according to a plan: first the **general inspection** (general condition, consciousness, position, habitus — body build, posture and gait), then the **inspection of the body regions** (head, face, neck, trunk, limbs), and then the skin, subcutaneous fat, lymph nodes, muscles and joints are assessed.

sections.title: 2. Assessment of the general condition

blocks.text: The general condition is assessed according to the patient’s consciousness and position, the degree of impairment of organ function and the presence of a threat to life.

blocks.title: Table 2.1. Grades of the general condition
head: Grade
Criteria
Examples
rows: Consciousness clear, position active, the function of the vital organs almost unimpaired
Mild diseases, the period of remission
Consciousness clear or slightly clouded, position active or forced, organ function markedly impaired, but no immediate threat to life
Heart failure IIA, moderately severe pneumonia
Consciousness often impaired (obtundation, sopor), position often passive or forced, the function of the vital organs sharply impaired
Lobar pneumonia at its height, status asthmaticus
Coma, profound impairment of the vital functions (respiration, circulation), urgent resuscitation measures needed

sections.title: 3. Assessment of consciousness

blocks.text: Consciousness may be **clear** (the patient answers questions quickly and correctly and is oriented in time, place and person) or **impaired**. Impairments are divided into **quantitative** (depression of consciousness) and **qualitative** (change in the content of consciousness) types.

blocks.title: Table 2.2. Degrees of depression of consciousness
head: Grade
Definition
Signs
rows: The patient answers questions with delay and briefly, is drowsy and indifferent to the surroundings
The patient responds only briefly to a loud voice or a painful stimulus and then “falls asleep” again
Makes defensive movements only in response to a strong painful stimulus, does not answer questions, reflexes preserved
No response to any stimulus, reflexes depressed or absent, vital functions impaired

blocks.text: **Qualitative disturbances** of consciousness: delirium — disorientation in time and place, hallucinations, agitation (alcohol withdrawal, severe infections, high fever); hallucinations and illusions; amentia.

parts.text: English-language textbooks (Bates, Macleod) use the **AVPU** scale for rapid assessment of consciousness: **A**lert; **V**oice — responds to voice; **P**ain — responds only to pain; **U**nresponsive — no response. The **Glasgow Coma Scale** (GCS) is used for detailed assessment.

blocks.title: Table 2.3. The Glasgow Coma Scale
head: Parameter
Response
Score

parts.text: The total GCS score ranges from 3 to 15: **15** — clear consciousness; **13–14** — obtundation; **9–12** — sopor (stupor); **8 or less** — coma (the airway needs protecting).

blocks.text: Types of coma and their distinguishing signs

blocks.title: Table 2.4. Common comas
head: Coma
Main cause
Distinguishing signs
rows: Dry skin, odor of acetone on the breath, Kussmaul breathing, soft eyeballs
Moist skin, profuse sweating, seizures, rapid onset
Skin pale gray, dry, scratch marks, odor of ammonia on the breath, Kussmaul breathing
Jaundice, “liver” (sweetish-musty) odor from the mouth, “spider angiomas”
Cyanotic face, dilated pupils, odor of alcohol on the breath
Flushed face, deep and noisy breathing, hemiparesis
Tonic-clonic seizures, bitten tongue, involuntary passage of urine and stool

parts.text: Coma by the odor of the breath: **“Acetone — Ammonia — Alcohol — Liver”**. Acetone — diabetic coma, ammonia (urine) — uremic coma, alcohol — alcoholic coma, sweetish-musty “liver odor” (fetor hepaticus) — hepatic coma.

sections.title: 4. The patient’s position

blocks.text: The patient’s position may be of three kinds: **active**, **passive** and **forced**.

items: **Active position** — the patient can assume any position he or she wishes and moves freely (mild diseases).
**Passive position** — the patient cannot change the position independently; the head and limbs hang down (coma, extreme weakness, spinal cord injury).
**Forced position** — a position the patient assumes himself or herself to relieve his or her condition (to lessen pain, dyspnea or cough).

blocks.label: Figure 2.1
blocks.caption: Forced position of the patient: sitting leaning forward (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 1)

blocks.title: Table 2.5. Forced positions and their diagnostic significance
head: Forced position
In which disease
Mechanism
rows: Part of the blood pools in the leg veins, and congestion in the pulmonary circulation decreases
Sitting leaning forward with the hands propped on a table or the edge of the bed
Attack of bronchial asthma, exacerbation of COPD
The shoulder girdle is fixed and the accessory respiratory muscles come into play
Dry and exudative pleurisy, lung abscess, bronchiectasis
Movement of the pleural layers decreases and the pain lessens; the healthy lung takes part freely in breathing; pus does not flow into the bronchus, so the cough does not increase
Lying on the affected side increases the pain
The fluid shifts downward and the pressure on the base of the heart and the great vessels decreases
Lying motionless on the back with the legs bent
Movement of the peritoneum and its pain decrease
Lying on the side with the head thrown back and the legs drawn up to the abdomen (the “pointing dog” position)
Attack of angina pectoris, acute ischemia, intermittent claudication
When movement stops, the oxygen demand of the myocardium (muscle) decreases
Restless tossing from side to side
The pain is very severe; no comfortable position can be found

parts.text: In lung abscess and bronchiectasis, the patient lies on the affected side, because on turning onto the healthy side, pus flows through the draining bronchus into the trachea and increases the cough and sputum production. However, this very feature is used in treatment: for **postural drainage**, the patient is placed in the position in which the sputum drains out.

sections.title: 5. Body build (constitution)

blocks.text: **Constitution** is the combination of the morphological and functional features of the organism shaped by heredity and the environment. According to the classification of M.V. Chernorutsky, three types are distinguished. The main distinguishing parameter is the **epigastric angle** (the angle between the costal arches, determined by placing the palms along the arches).

blocks.label: Figure 2.2
blocks.caption: Normosthenic type (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 2)

blocks.label: Figure 2.3
blocks.caption: Hypersthenic type (same source)

blocks.label: Figure 2.4
blocks.caption: Asthenic type (same source)

blocks.title: Table 2.6. Constitutional types
head: Feature
Normosthenic
Hypersthenic
Asthenic
rows: Height average or short, trunk broad
Broad and short, large anteroposterior diameter

Position of the diaphragm and heart
Arterial hypertension, atherosclerosis, IHD, obesity, diabetes mellitus, gallstone disease

parts.text: The epigastric angle — **“Hyper — Wide, Asthenic — Narrow”**: in the HYPERsthenic type the angle is wide (>90°), in the ASTHENIC type it is narrow (<90°), and in the normosthenic type it is a right angle (90°).

sections.title: 6. Inspection of the head

blocks.text: The shape and size of the head are assessed. **Macrocephaly** (enlargement of the head) is seen in hydrocephalus, and **microcephaly** in developmental delay. In acromegaly, the skull bones, lower jaw, nose and ears enlarge. Rhythmic **nodding** of the head in time with the heartbeat — **de Musset’s sign** — is characteristic of aortic regurgitation. Head tremor is seen in Parkinson’s disease.

sections.title: 7. Inspection of the face

blocks.text: The facial expression (facies) often provides important information for the diagnosis.

blocks.label: Figure 2.5

sections.title: 8. Inspection of the eyes, nose, mouth and tongue

blocks.text: Eyes and eyelids

items: **Eyelid edema** — kidney diseases, hypothyroidism, allergic edema (angioedema).
**Xanthelasmas** — yellowish flat patches on the eyelids (lipid metabolism disorders, atherosclerosis, cholestasis).
**Yellowing of the sclerae** — the earliest sign of jaundice.
**Pallor of the conjunctiva** — anemia.
**Pupils**: constriction (miosis) — morphine poisoning, uremia, intracerebral hemorrhage; dilation (mydriasis) — atropine poisoning, coma, agony; anisocoria — neurological damage.
**Horner’s triad** (ptosis, miosis, enophthalmos) — damage to the cervical sympathetic fibers, including a tumor of the lung apex (Pancoast tumor).

blocks.title: Table 2.8. Eye signs in thyrotoxicosis
head: Feature
Content
rows: On looking down, the upper eyelid lags behind the eyeball, and a strip of sclera is visible above the iris
Inability to converge the eyes on a near object (weakness of convergence)
Widening of the palpebral fissure, sclera visible above the iris
On looking up, the upper eyelid rises ahead of the eyeball

blocks.text: Nose

Movement of the nasal alae during inspiration (“flaring” of the nostrils) is a sign of severe respiratory failure and lobar pneumonia. A saddle nose — congenital syphilis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Cyanosis of the tip of the nose — heart failure.
Oral cavity and tongue

The color of the lips (pallor — anemia, cyanosis — heart and respiratory failure), cracks at the corners of the mouth (**angular stomatitis** — iron and vitamin B2 deficiency), herpetic eruptions (lobar pneumonia, influenza), bleeding of the gums and the state of the teeth are assessed.

blocks.label: Figure 2.8
blocks.caption: Inspection of the tongue: from left to right — normal, in peptic ulcer disease, in scarlet fever, in severe intoxication (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 7)

blocks.title: Table 2.9. Diagnostic significance of changes in the tongue
head: Appearance of the tongue
Disease or condition
rows: Moist, pink, papillae distinct, no coating
Dry, covered with a brown coating
Smooth, shiny, red (“lacquered tongue”, Hunter’s glossitis)
Enlarged (macroglossia), with tooth marks at the edges

sections.title: 9. Inspection of the neck

blocks.text: On inspection of the neck, attention is paid to the following:

items: **Shape and symmetry** — enlargement of the thyroid gland (goiter), enlargement of the lymph nodes, tumors.
**Neck veins** — distension and pulsation (right ventricular failure, tricuspid regurgitation, pericarditis).
**Strong pulsation of the carotid arteries** — the “carotid dance” (aortic regurgitation).
**Use of the accessory muscles** — tensing of the sternocleidomastoid muscles during breathing (bronchial asthma, COPD).
**“Stokes’ collar”** — edema of the neck, face and shoulder girdle with dilated veins (compression of the superior vena cava, tumors of the clavicular region).

parts.text: To assess the thyroid gland on inspection, the patient is asked to swallow a sip of water: during swallowing the gland rises together with the larynx. If a swelling in the neck moves with swallowing, it belongs to the thyroid gland; a lymph node, by contrast, hardly moves on swallowing.

When assessing distension of the neck veins, the patient lies at an angle of 45°. If the upper level of the internal jugular venous pulsation is **more than 3 cm above** the sternal angle, the central venous pressure is considered raised.

sections.title: 10. Additional methods of assessing the constitution

blocks.text: In addition to the epigastric angle, anthropometric indices are used to determine the constitutional type.

blocks.title: Table 2.10. Indices for assessing the constitution
head: Index
Calculation
Interpretation
rows: Less than 10 — hypersthenic; 10–30 — normosthenic; more than 30 — asthenic
Ratio of chest circumference to height
50–55 — normosthenic; more than 55 — hypersthenic; less than 50 — asthenic
Ratio of limb length to trunk length
Normally about 1.0; more than 1.05 — Marfan syndrome suspected

parts.text: Tall stature, long thin limbs and fingers (**arachnodactyly**), chest deformity, dislocation of the lens and joint hypermobility are signs of **Marfan syndrome**. Such a patient has a high risk of aortic root dilation, aortic dissection and aortic regurgitation, so echocardiography is necessary.

sections.title: 11. Posture, gait and movements

blocks.text: The patient’s posture and gait are observed from the moment he or she enters the room.

blocks.title: Table 2.11. Types of gait
head: Type of gait
Signs
Cause
rows: The paralyzed leg is held straight and brought forward in a semicircle from the side; the arm is flexed
Trunk bent forward, small shuffling steps, no arm swing, difficulty stopping
The trunk sways from side to side
The leg is lifted high, the foot drops
The time of weight bearing on the painful leg is shortened
Joint and bone diseases, intermittent claudication

blocks.text: **Involuntary movements:** hand tremor — fine and rapid in thyrotoxicosis; “pill-rolling” at rest in Parkinson’s disease; in alcoholism; in liver failure, a **“flapping tremor”** (asterixis — a wing-beating movement of the hands when the arms are stretched forward); seizures; chorea (ARF, Huntington’s disease).

blocks.label: Figure 2.9
blocks.caption: Face characteristic of acromegaly: enlarged lower jaw, nose and lips (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 7)

head: Feature
Content
Diagnostic significance

Yellowing under the tongue and of the gums

blocks.text: Detailed inspection of the eyes

blocks.label: Figure 2.10
blocks.caption: Horner’s triad: on the right, drooping of the eyelid (ptosis), constriction of the pupil (miosis) and retraction of the eyeball (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 5)

items: **Pupillary reaction to light:** normally the pupils are equal and constrict briskly to light (direct and consensual reaction). Absence of the reaction — deep coma, severe brain damage, atropine poisoning.
**Argyll Robertson sign** — no pupillary reaction to light, but the reaction to convergence is preserved (neurosyphilis, diabetes mellitus).
**Conjunctival petechiae** (Lukin–Libman sign) — infective endocarditis.
**Bluish sclerae** — iron deficiency, osteogenesis imperfecta.

**A gray ring at the edge of the cornea** (arcus senilis) — if it appears before the age of 50, a sign of hypercholesterolemia; the **Kayser–Fleischer ring** (brownish-green) — Wilson’s disease (Wilson–Konovalov disease).
**Exophthalmos** — if it is unilateral, an orbital tumor must also be excluded.

sections.title: 13. Inspection of the neck: assessment of the central venous pressure

blocks.text: The filling of the neck veins reflects the pressure in the right atrium (the central venous pressure — CVP). Its assessment is important in detecting heart failure and pericarditis and in judging fluid balance.

**Method:** the patient lies at an angle of 45° with the head turned slightly to the left. The highest point of pulsation of the right internal jugular vein is identified. The vertical distance from it to the **sternal angle** (angle of Louis) is measured. Because the sternal angle lies about 5 cm above the right atrium, CVP ≈ the measured distance + 5 cm.

parts.text: Normally, the venous pulsation rises no higher than **3 cm above** the sternal angle (CVP up to 8 cm H2O). At 4 cm or more the CVP is raised: right ventricular failure, tricuspid regurgitation, cardiac tamponade, constrictive pericarditis, hypervolemia. If the neck veins are full with the patient sitting upright, the CVP is markedly raised.

sections.title: 19. Algorithm for performing the general inspection “from head to toe”

items: **First impression (as the patient enters the room or in bed):** general condition, consciousness, position, facial expression, breathing, color, body build, gait.
**Vital signs:** pulse, BP, respiratory rate, body temperature, SpO2, pain score.
**Anthropometry:** height, weight, BMI, waist circumference.
**Head:** shape, hair, scalp.
**Face:** expression, symmetry, color, edema, rashes.
**Eyes:** eyelids, conjunctiva, sclerae, pupils, position of the eyeballs.
**Nose and ears.**
**Oral cavity:** lips, gums, teeth, tongue, palate, tonsils, odor.
**Neck:** shape, thyroid gland, lymph nodes, veins, arterial pulsation, position of the trachea.
**Hands:** palms, fingers, nails, joints, tremor, skin.
**Trunk:** skin, chest, breasts, abdomen (followed by the systematic examination).
**Legs:** edema, veins, skin, nails, joints, peripheral pulses.

parts.text: Inspection of the hands is **“a mirror that tells a great deal”**: the nails (clubbing, koilonychia, Terry’s nails), the palms (erythema, pallor, Dupuytren’s contracture), the fingers (Osler’s nodes, Heberden’s and Bouchard’s nodes, rheumatoid deformities), tremor (thyrotoxicosis, asterixis), temperature and moisture. That is why it is convenient to begin the objective examination by taking the patient’s hand and counting the pulse.

sections.title: 20. Clinical part

blocks.text: Sample case history entry

**General condition** moderately severe. Consciousness clear (GCS 15), oriented in time and place. Position forced — sitting with the legs lowered (orthopnea). Body build hypersthenic, epigastric angle 100°. The face is puffy, the lips and tip of the nose are cyanotic (acrocyanosis). The sclerae are not subicteric, the conjunctivae pink. The tongue is moist, covered with a white coating. The neck is symmetrical, the thyroid gland is not visible, and the neck veins are distended and pulsate even in the upright position.
**Conclusion:** orthopnea, acrocyanosis and distended neck veins raise suspicion of heart failure with congestion in the systemic and pulmonary circulations.

skills.title: Skill: determining the epigastric angle and establishing the constitutional type

items: Undress the patient to the waist with him or her standing.
Place the palms of both hands along the costal arches so that the tips of the thumbs touch the xiphoid process.
Assess the angle between the thumbs: 90° — normosthenic, more than 90° — hypersthenic, less than 90° — asthenic.
Assess the additional signs: the shape of the chest, the length of the neck and limbs, muscular development.
Write the conclusion in the case history.

skills.title: Skill: assessing consciousness with the Glasgow Coma Scale

items: Address the patient by name and observe eye opening (4–1 points).
Ask simple questions: “What is your name? Where are you now? What month is it?” (5–1 points).
Give a command: “Raise your hand.” If it is not obeyed, apply a painful stimulus (pressure on the sternum, nail-bed pressure) and assess the response (6–1 points).
Add up the points and record the result, for example: “GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5)”.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 24-year-old man was brought to the emergency department unconscious. His skin is dry, the eyeballs are soft, his breathing is deep and noisy, and an odor of acetone is noticeable in the room. His relatives said that he had been on insulin for 5 years and that in the last few days he had had influenza, was not eating and had therefore stopped his insulin injections.
cases.ask: Which level of consciousness and which type of coma can be considered? What is this type of breathing called?
cases.answer: Coma. The clinical signs (dry skin, soft eyeballs, odor of acetone, development after stopping insulin and against the background of an infection) are characteristic of ketoacidotic diabetic coma. Deep, noisy, slow breathing is Kussmaul breathing; it serves to compensate for metabolic acidosis.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 62-year-old woman is sitting on the bed in the ward with her legs lowered, propping herself on the edge of the bed with her hands. When an attempt is made to lay her down, her dyspnea increases. There are bluish-red patches on her cheeks, and her lips and the tip of her nose are cyanotic.
cases.ask: Assess the patient’s position and facial appearance. Which disease can be considered?
cases.answer: Forced position — orthopnea; facial appearance — facies mitralis. These signs are characteristic of mitral stenosis and of heart failure with congestion in the pulmonary circulation. In the orthopnea position, part of the blood pools in the leg veins, congestion in the lungs decreases and the dyspnea is relieved.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 30-year-old woman complains of palpitations, sweating, hand tremor and weight loss. On inspection: her eyes are protruding and shining, the upper eyelid lags behind on looking down, and she blinks infrequently. On the anterior surface of the neck there is a visible swelling that rises on swallowing.
cases.ask: What signs have been found? Which disease are they characteristic of?
cases.answer: Exophthalmos, Graefe’s sign (lagging of the eyelid on looking down), Stellwag’s sign (infrequent blinking) and enlargement of the thyroid gland (a swelling that moves on swallowing) have been found. Together with the complaints, these are characteristic of diffuse toxic goiter (Graves’ disease). The facial appearance is facies Basedowica.

topics.title: General inspection: skin, subcutaneous fat, muscles, bones, joints. Fever. Anthropometry. Palpation. Palpation of the lymph nodes and thyroid gland

goals.text: To teach the student to inspect the skin, subcutaneous fat, muscles, bones and joints, to measure body temperature and assess the types of fever, to determine the anthropometric parameters and to examine the lymph nodes and thyroid gland by palpation.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the changes in skin color (pallor, cyanosis, jaundice, hyperpigmentation) and their causes;
the primary and secondary elements of skin rashes;
the types of edema and the difference between cardiac and renal edema;
the normal values of body temperature and the grades and types of fever;
the normal values of the body mass index and waist circumference;
the types of palpation, the groups of lymph nodes and the criteria for assessing them;
the grades of thyroid enlargement (WHO).

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine skin turgor, moisture and edema;
measure body temperature in the axilla and fill in the temperature chart;
measure height, weight and waist circumference and calculate the body mass index;
palpate the peripheral lymph nodes and the thyroid gland.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: In central cyanosis the skin is **warm**, and the tongue and lips are also blue; in peripheral cyanosis the skin is **cold**, the tongue is usually pink, and the blueness is found in the parts of the body farthest from the heart (acral). Cyanosis becomes visible when the amount of reduced hemoglobin in the blood exceeds **50 g/l**; for this reason it appears late in severe anemia.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Distinguishing jaundice: in **true jaundice** the sclerae, the palate and the mucosa under the tongue also turn yellow; in **false jaundice** (from eating carrots, carotene, taking quinacrine) only the palms and soles turn yellow, while the sclerae remain white. Assess jaundice only in daylight.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The causes of clubbing — **“LHL”**: **L**ungs (suppurative diseases, cancer), **H**eart (“blue” congenital defects, infective endocarditis), **L**iver (cirrhosis) and inflammatory bowel diseases.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Normal temperature: in the axilla **36.4–36.8 °C** (36.3–36.9 °C in the textbook); in the mouth **0.3–0.5 °C** higher than in the axilla; in the rectum **0.5–1.0 °C** higher. In a healthy person the daily fluctuation does not exceed **1 °C**: the lowest temperature is between 3 and 6 in the morning, and the highest between 17 and 21 h in the evening.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **“Continuous — Lobar”**: in lobar pneumonia the fever is continuous (continua) and ends with a crisis. **“Hectic — Pus”**: a hectic fever always makes one think of a suppurative process (abscess, sepsis).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: BMI misjudges fat tissue in athletes with strongly developed muscles and in patients with edema. That is why the waist circumference must always be measured together with the BMI: abdominal obesity may be present even with a normal BMI.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: General rules of palpation: the physician’s hands should be **warm**, the nails short and the movements **gentle**; the examination begins in a painless area, and the painful area is palpated last; the patient should be in a comfortable position with the muscles relaxed; symmetrical areas are always compared.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Older textbooks (the classification of O.V. Nikolaev) distinguished **grades 0–V** of goiter. Present-day practice uses the simplified **grade 0–II** classification recommended by the WHO, and the gland volume is determined precisely by US (normal up to 18 ml in women and 25 ml in men).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The three large groups of fever of unknown origin — **“INC”**: **I**nfection, **N**eoplasm (tumor), **C**onnective tissue (rheumatic) diseases.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: If a lymph node is **larger than 2 cm**, **hard**, **fixed**, located **in the supraclavicular region**, or remains enlarged for **more than 4 weeks** and the patient is older than 40, there is a strong indication for biopsy. It is a mistake to keep observing such a node as “inflammation”.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: A BMI below 18.5 kg/m^2^ and marked weight loss over a short period are signs of **protein-energy malnutrition**. Malnutrition occurs in 20–40 percent of hospital patients, and it increases the risk of infectious complications, slow wound healing and death.

sections.title: 1. Inspection of the skin

blocks.text: The skin is regarded as a “mirror” reflecting the state of the whole organism. On inspection of the skin, its **color**, **moisture**, **turgor (elasticity)**, **rashes**, **vascular changes**, **scars**, **edema** and the state of the hair and nails are assessed.
1.1. Skin color

blocks.title: Table 3.1. Changes in skin color
head: Change
Mechanism
Causes
rows: Decreased hemoglobin or constriction of the skin vessels
Anemia, blood loss, shock, aortic regurgitation, glomerulonephritis
Dilation of the skin vessels, increased red cells

Lung diseases (respiratory failure), “blue” congenital heart defects
Slowing of blood flow, increased extraction of oxygen by the tissues
Heart failure (lips, tip of the nose, earlobes, fingertips)

parts.text: In central cyanosis the skin is **warm**, and the tongue and lips are also blue; in peripheral cyanosis the skin is **cold**, the tongue is usually pink, and the blueness is found in the parts of the body farthest from the heart (acral). Cyanosis becomes visible when the amount of reduced hemoglobin in the blood exceeds **50 g/l**; for this reason it appears late in severe anemia.

Distinguishing jaundice: in **true jaundice** the sclerae, the palate and the mucosa under the tongue also turn yellow; in **false jaundice** (from eating carrots, carotene, taking quinacrine) only the palms and soles turn yellow, while the sclerae remain white. Assess jaundice only in daylight.

blocks.text: 1.2. Skin moisture and turgor

Skin moisture increases in the fall of a high fever (crisis), thyrotoxicosis, hypoglycemia and tuberculosis (night sweats). Dry skin — dehydration, hypothyroidism, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease.

**Skin turgor** is determined by picking up a fold of skin on the back of the hand or on the chest between the thumb and index finger and releasing it: normally the fold smooths out at once; in dehydration, old age and cachexia it smooths out slowly.
1.3. Skin rashes

In which condition

A larger (over 1 cm) area of redness
