blocks.text: 1.4. Vascular changes in the skin and other signs

items: **“Spider angiomas”** (telangiectasias) — on the face, neck, chest and shoulders; **liver palms** (palmar erythema) — redness of the thenar and hypothenar eminences. Both are signs of liver cirrhosis.
**White and pink lines (striae)** — obesity, pregnancy; **broad purple-red striae** — Cushing’s syndrome.
**Subcutaneous nodules** — rheumatic (acute rheumatic fever), rheumatoid and gouty nodules (tophi).
**Osler’s nodes** — painful pea-sized nodules on the fingertips; **Janeway lesions** — painless hemorrhagic spots on the palms and soles (infective endocarditis).

blocks.text: 1.5. Nails and hair

blocks.label: Figure 3.1
blocks.caption: Changes in the nails: A — “watch-glass” nails; B — Terry’s nails (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 11)

items: **Clubbing** (Hippocratic fingers) — bulbous enlargement of the terminal phalanges of the fingers with nails convex like a “watch glass”. It occurs in chronic hypoxia and suppurative lung diseases (bronchiectasis, lung abscess, lung cancer), in “blue” congenital heart defects, infective endocarditis and liver cirrhosis.
**Koilonychia** (spoon-shaped nails) — iron deficiency anemia.
**Terry’s nails** (whitening of the nail plate with a pink band at the tip) — liver cirrhosis, chronic kidney disease.
**Hair loss (alopecia)** — SLE, hypothyroidism, iron deficiency; male-pattern hair growth in women (hirsutism) — hyperandrogenism.

parts.text: The causes of clubbing — **“LHL”**: **L**ungs (suppurative diseases, cancer), **H**eart (“blue” congenital defects, infective endocarditis), **L**iver (cirrhosis) and inflammatory bowel diseases.

sections.title: 2. Edema

blocks.text: **Edema** is an excess accumulation of fluid in the interstitial spaces. If a pit remains after pressing with a finger for 5–10 seconds, the presence of edema is confirmed (it is usually tested on the anterior surface of the lower leg, around the ankle and over the sacrum). Edema of the whole body is **anasarca**; accumulation of fluid in the body cavities is ascites, hydrothorax, hydropericardium.

blocks.title: Table 3.3. Differences between cardiac and renal edema
head: Feature
Cardiac edema
Renal edema
rows: First in the legs (in ambulatory patients); in bedridden patients over the sacrum and lower back
First on the face, especially the eyelids
Spreads rapidly, to the whole body
Dyspnea, acrocyanosis, liver enlargement, distended neck veins

sections.title: 3. Subcutaneous fat, muscles, bones and joints

blocks.text: The development of the **subcutaneous fat** is assessed by the thickness of a skinfold (next to the umbilicus, below the shoulder blade, on the back of the upper arm). Normally the skinfold is 1–2 cm thick. Decreased fat tissue is weight loss, and its sharp decrease is **cachexia** (tumors, tuberculosis, thyrotoxicosis, severe chronic diseases). Excess accumulation is obesity: uniform (alimentary), in the abdominal region (“apple” type, metabolic syndrome), on the thighs and buttocks (“pear” type).

The **muscular system** is assessed on inspection by the degree of development, symmetry, atrophy and hypertrophy, tone and strength. Muscle atrophy is seen in damage to the nervous system, prolonged immobility and cachexia.

blocks.label: Figure 3.2
blocks.caption: Muscle atrophy (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 14)

blocks.label: Figure 3.3
blocks.caption: Varicose veins of the leg (same source, Fig. 15)

blocks.text: The **bones** are assessed on inspection for deformity, thickening and pain: the “rosary” and bowed legs after rickets, enlargement of the bones in acromegaly, pain on tapping the bones in myeloma and leukemias.

On inspection of the **joints**, their shape (swelling, deformity, defiguration), the color and temperature of the overlying skin, the range of movement and pain are assessed. Acute rheumatic fever is characterized by “migrating” inflammation of the large joints (knee, ankle, elbow), and rheumatoid arthritis by symmetrical involvement and deformity of the small joints of the hands and feet.
On inspection of the **limbs**, varicose veins, trophic ulcers, edema, tremor and contractures are detected.

sections.title: 4. Body temperature and fever

blocks.text: 4.1. Measuring body temperature

Body temperature is measured with mercury thermometers (used less often today for safety reasons), electronic (digital) and infrared (ear, forehead) thermometers. The main method is **measurement in the axilla**: the axilla is wiped dry, the tip of the thermometer is placed in the center of the axillary fossa and the arm is pressed against the chest; with a mercury thermometer the measurement takes **10 minutes**. The temperature is measured at least twice a day (in the morning at 7–8 a.m. and in the evening at 17–19 h) and recorded on the **temperature chart**.

blocks.label: Figure 3.4
blocks.caption: Normal values of body temperature at various sites (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 23)

parts.text: Normal temperature: in the axilla **36.4–36.8 °C** (36.3–36.9 °C in the textbook); in the mouth **0.3–0.5 °C** higher than in the axilla; in the rectum **0.5–1.0 °C** higher. In a healthy person the daily fluctuation does not exceed **1 °C**: the lowest temperature is between 3 and 6 in the morning, and the highest between 17 and 21 h in the evening.

blocks.text: 4.2. Fever (febris) and its grades

**Fever** is a rise in body temperature resulting from an upward shift of the “set point” of the thermoregulatory center in the hypothalamus under the action of pyrogens. It must be distinguished from **hyperthermia**: in hyperthermia (heatstroke) the thermoregulatory center has failed and heat loss is insufficient.

blocks.label: Figure 3.5
blocks.caption: Grades of fever: 1 — low-grade; 2 — moderate; 3 — high; 4 — hyperpyretic; 5 — extremely high (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 24)

blocks.title: Table 3.4. Grades of fever (axillary)
head: Grade
Temperature

blocks.text: Stages of fever:

items: **Stage of rising temperature** (stadium incrementi) — heat production exceeds heat loss: chills, shivering, pale and cold skin (“goose flesh”).
**Stage of high temperature** (stadium fastigii) — heat production and heat loss are balanced at a high level: a feeling of heat, flushed and hot skin, headache, tachycardia.

**Stage of falling temperature** (stadium decrementi) — heat loss predominates, with profuse sweating. If the temperature falls sharply within a few hours, it is a **crisis** (risk of vascular insufficiency — collapse); if it falls gradually over several days, it is **lysis**.

parts.text: For every 1 °C rise in temperature, the heart rate increases by about **8–10 beats** per minute. If the temperature is high but the pulse is relatively slow (**relative bradycardia**), typhoid fever, brucellosis and legionellosis should be considered. In lobar pneumonia, collapse may develop during the critical fall: the patient sweats, turns pale and the blood pressure falls.

parts.text: **“Continuous — Lobar”**: in lobar pneumonia the fever is continuous (continua) and ends with a crisis. **“Hectic — Pus”**: a hectic fever always makes one think of a suppurative process (abscess, sepsis).

sections.title: 5. Anthropometry

blocks.text: **Anthropometry** is the measurement of the body’s dimensions (height, weight, chest and waist circumference). Height is measured in the morning, without shoes, with a stadiometer; weight is measured on an empty stomach, in light clothing.
**Body mass index** (BMI, Quetelet index) = weight (kg) / height^2^ (m^2^).

blocks.title: Table 3.6. Classification by body mass index (WHO)
head: BMI, kg/m^2^
Interpretation

blocks.text: The **waist circumference** is measured at the level midway between the lower edge of the costal arch and the iliac crest. The criterion of abdominal (visceral) obesity: **more than 94 cm** in men and **more than 80 cm** in women (for Europid populations, IDF); the level of a further increased cardiometabolic risk is more than 102 cm in men and 88 cm in women. A waist-to-hip ratio greater than 0.9 in men and 0.85 in women is also regarded as abdominal obesity.

parts.text: BMI misjudges fat tissue in athletes with strongly developed muscles and in patients with edema. That is why the waist circumference must always be measured together with the BMI: abdominal obesity may be present even with a normal BMI.

sections.title: 6. Palpation as a method of objective examination

blocks.text: **Palpation** is a method of examination based on the tactile sensitivity of the palm and fingers. It is used to determine the location, size, shape, consistency, surface, mobility and tenderness of organs, as well as pulsation and vibration.

blocks.title: Table 3.7. Types of palpation
head: Type
Content
Application
rows: Palpation with light pressure of the whole palm, comparing symmetrical areas
Skin temperature and moisture, muscle tension, tender areas, the abdominal wall
Palpation with deeper pressure of the fingers
With two hands, holding the organ from two sides
Detecting the liver and spleen in ascites
Keeping the palm placed over the organ
Chest vibration (vocal fremitus), the cardiac impulse

parts.text: General rules of palpation: the physician’s hands should be **warm**, the nails short and the movements **gentle**; the examination begins in a painless area, and the painful area is palpated last; the patient should be in a comfortable position with the muscles relaxed; symmetrical areas are always compared.

sections.title: 7. Palpation of the peripheral lymph nodes

blocks.text: Normally the peripheral lymph nodes are not palpable, or in some groups (inguinal, axillary) they are found up to **1 cm** in diameter, soft-elastic, painless, mobile, and not adherent to each other or to the skin.

blocks.label: Figure 3.8
blocks.caption: Palpation of the cervical lymph nodes (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 13)

blocks.text: **Order of palpation** (from above downward, symmetrically on both sides at the same time): occipital → postauricular → preauricular → submandibular → submental → anterior and posterior triangles of the neck → supraclavicular and infraclavicular → axillary → cubital → inguinal → popliteal.

blocks.title: Table 3.8. Criteria for assessing the lymph nodes
head: Criterion
Normal
Pathology and possible cause
rows: Stony hard — tumor metastasis; firm-elastic — lymphoma
Fixed to the surrounding tissues — metastasis, tuberculosis

parts.text: **Virchow’s node** — an enlarged hard node in the left supraclavicular fossa — is the classic sign of metastasis of gastric (and other abdominal) cancer. The right supraclavicular nodes most often enlarge in tumors of the lung and esophagus.

sections.title: 8. Palpation of the thyroid gland

blocks.text: The thyroid gland is located on the anterior surface of the neck, below the thyroid cartilage of the larynx, and consists of two lobes and the isthmus connecting them. Normally a lobe is no larger than the terminal phalanx of the patient’s thumb.

**Method of palpation (from in front of the patient):** the patient sits or stands with the head bent slightly forward. Standing opposite the patient, the physician places the thumbs of both hands below the thyroid cartilage at the inner edge of the sternocleidomastoid muscles. The patient is asked to swallow a sip of water: during swallowing the gland slides upward under the fingers, and its lobes and isthmus are palpated.
**Method of palpation (from behind the patient):** the physician stands behind the patient, places fingers 2–4 of both hands over the gland and palpates the lobes during swallowing.

The following are assessed: size, consistency (soft, firm, hard), surface (smooth, uneven), the presence of nodules, tenderness, mobility. A systolic bruit heard on auscultation over the gland indicates the increased blood flow of diffuse toxic goiter.

blocks.title: Table 3.9. Grades of goiter (WHO, 2001)
head: Grade
Definition
rows: No goiter: the lobes are smaller than the terminal phalanx of the thumb of the person examined
The goiter is palpable but not visible with the neck in the normal position
The goiter is visible with the neck in the normal position

parts.text: Older textbooks (the classification of O.V. Nikolaev) distinguished **grades 0–V** of goiter. Present-day practice uses the simplified **grade 0–II** classification recommended by the WHO, and the gland volume is determined precisely by US (normal up to 18 ml in women and 25 ml in men).

sections.title: 9. Additional aspects of the skin examination

blocks.text: 9.1. Technique of assessing skin turgor and moisture

blocks.label: Figure 3.9
blocks.caption: Picking up a skinfold (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 9)

blocks.label: Figure 3.10
blocks.caption: Observing the smoothing out of the fold (same source, Fig. 9)

blocks.text: A skinfold is picked up with the thumb and index finger on the back of the hand or on the skin of the chest or abdomen and released. If the fold persists for more than 2 seconds, turgor is reduced (dehydration, old age, cachexia). Skin moisture is assessed with the back of the hand: dry, normally moist, moist, wet (profuse sweating).
9.2. Additional types of skin rashes

blocks.text: Other changes of the nails: **Beau’s lines** (transverse grooves — a temporary arrest of nail growth after a severe illness), **leukonychia** (white spots), **onycholysis** (separation of the nail plate — thyrotoxicosis, psoriasis), **splinter hemorrhages** under the nail (infective endocarditis), **nail pitting** (the “thimble” sign — psoriasis).

sections.title: 10. Pathogenetic types of edema

blocks.text: Edema is the accumulation of fluid in the interstitial spaces and develops as a result of a disturbance in the balance of the Starling forces: the hydrostatic pressure in the capillaries drives fluid out, and the plasma oncotic pressure (mainly albumin) retains it inside the vessel.

blocks.title: Table 3.11. Pathogenetic types of edema
head: Type
Mechanism
Examples
rows: Heart failure, venous thrombosis, varicose veins
Nephrotic syndrome, liver cirrhosis, starvation (“hunger edema”), enteropathies
After removal of lymph nodes, filariasis, tumors; firm, does not pit
Hypothyroidism (myxedema — firm, does not pit), hyperaldosteronism, glucocorticoids

parts.text: Unilateral leg edema with pain and redness may be a sign of deep vein thrombosis; because of the risk of **pulmonary embolism**, this condition requires urgent Doppler ultrasound. Bilateral symmetrical edema is most often linked with a systemic cause (heart, kidneys, liver, hypoalbuminemia).

sections.title: 11. Examination of the muscles and joints

blocks.text: **Muscle strength** is assessed on a 0–5 point scale.

blocks.title: Table 3.12. Scale for assessing muscle strength (MRC)
head: Score
Definition
rows: A flicker of contraction is felt, no movement
Movement with gravity eliminated (in the horizontal plane)
Movement against gravity, but not against resistance
Movement against resistance, strength slightly reduced

blocks.text: The sequence of **examining the joints**: inspection (shape, symmetry, swelling, skin color, deformity) → palpation (temperature, tenderness, consistency of the swelling, fluid — “ballottement” of the patella, crepitus) → determining the range of active and passive movements (with a goniometer). Joint pain may be **inflammatory** (morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes, lessening with movement — rheumatoid arthritis) or **mechanical** (worse on loading, relieved by rest, stiffness for less than 30 minutes — osteoarthritis).

blocks.title: Table 3.13. Characteristic joint changes in internal diseases
head: Disease
Nature of involvement
rows: Metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, symmetrical; “walrus flipper” (ulnar deviation) and “swan neck” deformities
Often an acute, extremely painful arthritis of the first joint of the big toe (at night), tophi
Knee and hip joints, distal (Heberden’s) and proximal (Bouchard’s) interphalangeal nodes
The spine and sacroiliac joints, the “beggar’s posture”

blocks.text: 12.1. Pathogenesis of fever

Exogenous pyrogens (bacterial endotoxin, viruses) and tissue breakdown products activate leukocytes and macrophages → **endogenous pyrogens** (interleukin-1, interleukin-6, tumor necrosis factor alpha) are released → **prostaglandin E~2~** is formed in the hypothalamus → the “set point” of the thermoregulatory center rises. Antipyretic drugs (paracetamol, NSAIDs) act precisely by blocking prostaglandin synthesis.

**The protective and harmful sides of fever:** fever enhances the immune response and slows the multiplication of many microbes; however, high fever increases oxygen consumption and places a burden on the heart (tachycardia), the nervous system (seizures in children) and metabolism.
12.2. Hypothermia and fever of unknown origin
**Hypothermia** — a core temperature below 35 °C: exposure to cold, hypothyroidism (myxedema coma), the severe stage of sepsis, alcohol intoxication, adrenal insufficiency.

**Fever of unknown origin** — a temperature above 38.3 °C lasting more than 3 weeks whose cause has not been found even after one week of investigation in hospital. The main groups of causes: **infections** (tuberculosis, infective endocarditis, occult abscesses), **tumors** (lymphomas, kidney cancer), **connective tissue diseases** (SLE, vasculitides, Still’s disease), **drug fever**.

parts.text: The three large groups of fever of unknown origin — **“INC”**: **I**nfection, **N**eoplasm (tumor), **C**onnective tissue (rheumatic) diseases.

head: Group

parts.text: If a lymph node is **larger than 2 cm**, **hard**, **fixed**, located **in the supraclavicular region**, or remains enlarged for **more than 4 weeks** and the patient is older than 40, there is a strong indication for biopsy. It is a mistake to keep observing such a node as “inflammation”.

sections.title: 14. General methods of palpation and palpation of the abdomen

blocks.label: Figure 3.16
blocks.caption: Superficial palpation of the abdomen (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 16)

blocks.text: Palpation is one of the oldest methods of propaedeutics, in which the physician’s hand serves as a “measuring instrument”. Different parts of the hand are sensitive to different sensations: **the fingertips** — small structures and consistency; **the base of the palm and the region of the metacarpophalangeal joints** — vibration (vocal fremitus, the “cat’s purr”); **the back of the hand** — temperature.

In the abdomen, **superficial orienting palpation** detects tension of the abdominal wall, tender areas, hernial openings and superficial masses, whereas **deep sliding methodical palpation** (Obraztsov–Strazhesko) makes it possible to examine the intestines, stomach, liver, spleen and kidneys in succession. This method is studied in detail in the next semester in the section on the digestive organs.

sections.title: 15. Clinical assessment of thyroid function

blocks.text: Along with palpation of the thyroid gland, its **function** must be assessed by clinical signs.

sections.title: 17. Additional methods of assessing body weight

blocks.text: **Broca index** — ideal weight = height (cm) − 100 (for people 155–165 cm tall); at 165–175 cm, − 105; above 175 cm, − 110. Exceeding the ideal weight by more than 10 % is overweight.

**Skinfold thickness** is measured with a special instrument (caliper) at several points (the back of the upper arm — triceps, below the shoulder blade, next to the umbilicus, over the iliac crest), and the proportion of fat in the body is calculated. Modern methods are **bioimpedance analysis** and **DEXA**.

parts.text: A BMI below 18.5 kg/m^2^ and marked weight loss over a short period are signs of **protein-energy malnutrition**. Malnutrition occurs in 20–40 percent of hospital patients, and it increases the risk of infectious complications, slow wound healing and death.

sections.title: 18. Additional features of conditions accompanied by fever

blocks.title: Table 3.18. Combinations of fever with other signs
head: Combination
Suspected condition
rows: Fever + chills + low back pain + dysuria
Fever + jaundice + pain in the right hypochondrium

blocks.text: **Pel–Ebstein fever** — periods of fever lasting several days alternate with fever-free periods — is characteristic of Hodgkin lymphoma (a variety of undulant fever).

sections.title: 19. Secondary elements of skin rashes

blocks.text: **Secondary elements** form as a result of changes in the primary elements (macule, papule, vesicle, pustule and others).

blocks.title: Table 3.19. Secondary skin elements
head: Element
Definition
rows: Shedding of the horny layer (psoriasis, ichthyosis)
Drying of the fluid of a vesicle or pustule
A superficial defect within the epidermis that heals without a scar
A defect reaching the dermis and deeper layers that heals with a scar (trophic ulcers — venous insufficiency, diabetes, arterial insufficiency)
Replacement by connective tissue (surgery, injury, tuberculous fistulas)
A change in color left at the site of an element

parts.text: The location of a trophic ulcer points to its cause: around the **medial malleolus**, with pigmentation and edema — **venous**; on the toes, the heel and pressure points, painful, with pale cold skin — **arterial**; under the heel and the metatarsophalangeal joints, painless, with impaired sensation — **neuropathic (diabetic)**.

sections.title: 20. Clinical part

blocks.text: Sample case history entry

**The skin** is pale yellowish, dry, with reduced turgor. Isolated “spider angiomas” on the chest and shoulders, erythema of the palms. No rashes or scars. The nails are unchanged. **The subcutaneous fat** is poorly developed; the skinfold next to the umbilicus is 0.8 cm thick. Soft edema of the lower legs. **Lymph nodes:** the peripheral groups are not palpable. **The thyroid gland** is not palpable (grade 0). **The muscles** are atrophied, with reduced tone. The joints are of normal shape, with a full range of movement. **Body temperature** 37.4 °C. Height 172 cm, weight 61 kg, BMI 20.6 kg/m^2^.
**Conclusion:** jaundice, “spider angiomas” and liver palms suggest a chronic liver disease (cirrhosis).

skills.title: Skill: measuring body temperature in the axilla

items: Wash your hands and explain the procedure to the patient.
Check the thermometer (shake the reading of a mercury thermometer down below 35 °C; switch on an electronic thermometer).
Wipe the axillary fossa with a dry napkin.
Place the tip of the thermometer in the center of the axillary fossa and press the patient’s arm against the chest.
Wait 10 minutes with a mercury thermometer, or until the signal sounds with an electronic thermometer.
Read the result, record it on the temperature chart (morning and evening) and draw the curve.
Disinfect the thermometer.

skills.title: Skill: calculating the body mass index

items: Measure height in the morning, without shoes, with the heels, buttocks and shoulder blades touching the wall.
Measure weight on an empty stomach, in light clothing.
Calculate according to the formula BMI = weight (kg) / height^2^ (m^2^). Example: 85 kg / (1.70 m)^2^ = 85 / 2.89 = 29.4 kg/m^2^ — overweight.
Measure the waist circumference and compare it with the criteria of abdominal obesity.

skills.title: Skill: palpation of the peripheral lymph nodes

items: Position the patient sitting, with the neck and shoulder girdle uncovered.
Palpate symmetrical areas at the same time with fingers 2–4 of both hands, using circular movements.
Order: occipital, postauricular, preauricular, submandibular, submental, anterior and posterior triangles of the neck, supraclavicular and infraclavicular.

When palpating the axillary nodes, the patient raises the arm slightly to the side; the physician inserts the fingers deep into the axillary fossa and, after the patient lowers the arm, slides them downward along the chest wall.
Palpate the cubital, inguinal and popliteal nodes.
Describe the nodes found according to the criteria (size, consistency, tenderness, mobility, matting, skin).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 28-year-old patient has had a body temperature of 36.8 °C in the morning rising to 40.1 °C in the evening for 7 days. When the temperature falls, he sweats profusely and changes his shirt several times. A tooth was extracted two weeks ago.
cases.ask: What is the type of fever? Which processes is such a fever characteristic of? What signs should be looked for on the skin and nails?
cases.answer: A daily fluctuation of more than 3 °C with profuse sweating is a hectic (exhausting) fever. It is characteristic of suppurative processes and sepsis. Its development after a tooth extraction raises suspicion of infective endocarditis, so one should look for petechiae, Osler’s nodes, Janeway lesions, clubbing and pallor of the skin (“café au lait” color) and examine the heart.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 55-year-old man complains that he has lost 9 kg in the last 3 months and has no appetite. On examination, a 2 cm hard, painless, fixed lymph node is palpated in the left supraclavicular fossa.
cases.ask: Describe the node found. What might it indicate? What investigations are needed?
cases.answer: A stony hard, painless enlarged node fixed to the surrounding tissues is Virchow’s node. Together with the weight loss and loss of appetite, it gives grounds to suspect metastasis of gastric (or other abdominal) cancer. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy, abdominal US/CT and biopsy of the node are needed.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 45-year-old woman is 160 cm tall, weighs 82 kg and has a waist circumference of 98 cm. Her blood pressure is 150/95 mm Hg.
cases.ask: Calculate and interpret the BMI. What type of obesity is this? What risk does this condition pose?
cases.answer: BMI = 82 / (1.60)^2^ = 82 / 2.56 = 32.0 kg/m^2^ — obesity class I. A waist circumference of 98 cm (more than 88 cm in women) indicates abdominal (visceral) obesity. Abdominal obesity together with arterial hypertension is a sign of the metabolic syndrome and increases the risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus, atherosclerosis and ischemic heart disease.

topics.title: Methods of examining patients with respiratory diseases. History taking. Inspection and palpation of the chest

goals.text: To teach the student to identify and analyze the main complaints in respiratory diseases, to perform static and dynamic inspection of the chest, and to assess tender areas, chest wall resistance and vocal fremitus by palpation.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the main complaints in respiratory diseases: cough, sputum, dyspnea, choking attacks, hemoptysis, chest pain;
the types of sputum and their diagnostic significance;
the types of dyspnea (inspiratory, expiratory, mixed);
the normal and pathological shapes of the chest;
the types, rate, depth and rhythm of breathing and the pathological types of breathing;
the causes of increased and decreased vocal fremitus.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: take the history of a patient with a respiratory disease according to a plan;
perform static and dynamic inspection of the chest;
count the respiratory rate without the patient noticing;
determine chest wall resistance and vocal fremitus and interpret the result.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: When purulent sputum is left to settle in a container, it separates into layers. According to the textbook, **two layers** (pus and serous fluid) are characteristic of lung abscess, and **three layers** (pus at the bottom, serous fluid in the middle, frothy mucus on top) of bronchiectasis and cavitary tuberculosis.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In Russian-language textbooks (Grebenev, Mukhin), three-layered sputum is given as a common sign of **lung abscess, lung gangrene and bronchiectasis**. Hence the number of layers does not strictly distinguish an abscess from bronchiectasis; the decisive investigation is radiography and CT.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: In a healthy adult at rest, the respiratory rate is **16–20** per minute (12–14 during sleep), and in a newborn 40–45. A respiratory rate of more than 20 per minute is **tachypnea**, less than 12 is **bradypnea**, and cessation of breathing is **apnea**. The ratio of the respiratory rate to the pulse rate is normally **1:4**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **“Kussmaul — Ketoacidosis”**: deep, noisy breathing in acidosis. **“Cheyne–Stokes — Crescendo-decrescendo wave + Cessation”**. **“Biot — Bursts of equal Breaths, Blank pauses”**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Vocal fremitus is **increased over solid tissue and dampened by fluid and air**: “Solid — Strong, Fluid and Air — Faint”.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: For vocal fremitus to be increased, bronchial patency must be preserved. If the bronchus of the consolidated area is blocked by a tumor or a foreign body (obstructive atelectasis), the fremitus is **decreased** even though the tissue is dense.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Loss of **more than 100–200 ml** of blood per day (500 ml in some sources), or bleeding accompanied by airway obstruction and hemodynamic instability, is **massive pulmonary hemorrhage**; it is life-threatening and requires urgent bronchoscopy and bronchial artery embolization. The patient is laid on the bleeding side (so that blood does not flow into the healthy lung).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Pulse oximetry** is the painless measurement of the oxygen saturation of arterial blood (SpO2) and the pulse with a sensor placed on a finger. Normal is **95–98 %**. An SpO2 below 90 % is hypoxemia (an indication for oxygen therapy). In patients with COPD, the target SpO2 is 88–92 %.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: What is examined by palpation — **“TREV”**: **T**enderness, **R**esistance, **E**xpansion (participation in breathing), **V**ocal fremitus.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Vocal fremitus is easy to examine in men with a low voice, whereas in women and children with a high-pitched voice it is felt only weakly. That is why **comparing the two sides** is important: it is not the absolute strength of the fremitus but its **asymmetry** that has diagnostic significance.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The production of a large amount of sputum at once (“a mouthful”) is a sign of the **rupture of a cavity in the lung into a bronchus** (abscess) or of **bronchiectasis**; an increase in sputum in the morning and its dependence on position are characteristic of bronchiectasis.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In an elderly patient, a respiratory rate of **more than 25** per minute is often the earliest and most sensitive sign of pneumonia. That is why the respiratory rate must be counted accurately in every elderly patient.

sections.title: 1. Brief anatomy and physiology of the respiratory organs

blocks.text: The respiratory system consists of the upper airways (nose, pharynx, larynx), the trachea, the bronchi and the lungs. At the level of the IV–V thoracic vertebrae, the trachea divides into the right and left main bronchi (the bifurcation). The right lung has three lobes and the left lung two; each lung is divided into 10 segments. The main structure of gas exchange is the **acinus** (respiratory bronchiole, alveolar ducts and alveoli).

The three stages of external respiration are **ventilation** (the movement of air into and out of the alveoli), **diffusion** (the exchange of O2 and CO2 across the alveolar-capillary membrane) and **perfusion** (blood flow in the pulmonary capillaries). Impairment of any of them leads to respiratory failure.

sections.title: 2. History taking: the main complaints

blocks.text: 2.1. Cough (tussis)

Cough is a protective reflex that clears the airways of sputum, foreign bodies and other irritants. Cough receptors are most numerous in the larynx, the tracheal bifurcation, the large bronchi and the pleura; there are no cough receptors in the alveoli.

blocks.title: Table 4.1. Characteristics of cough
head: Feature
Type
Diagnostic significance
rows: Onset of bronchitis, dry pleurisy, tracheitis, bronchial asthma, lung tumor, foreign body, taking ACE inhibitors
Chronic bronchitis, pneumonia, bronchiectasis, rupture of an abscess
Chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis (the sputum accumulated overnight is expelled)
Bronchial asthma, left ventricular failure (cardiac asthma), gastroesophageal reflux
Compression of a large bronchus by a tumor or enlarged lymph nodes
Chronic bronchitis, COPD, asthma, tuberculosis, lung cancer

blocks.text: 2.2. Sputum
When sputum is described, its **amount** (single and daily), **character**, **color**, **odor**, **consistency**, **separation into layers** and **admixtures** (blood) are determined.

blocks.title: Table 4.2. Types of sputum
head: Type
Appearance
Diseases
rows: Onset of acute bronchitis, bronchial asthma (with Curschmann spirals)
Bronchiectasis, rupture of a lung abscess
Streaks of blood or pure blood
Tuberculosis, lung cancer, bronchiectasis, pulmonary infarction, mitral stenosis

parts.text: When purulent sputum is left to settle in a container, it separates into layers. According to the textbook, **two layers** (pus and serous fluid) are characteristic of lung abscess, and **three layers** (pus at the bottom, serous fluid in the middle, frothy mucus on top) of bronchiectasis and cavitary tuberculosis.

In Russian-language textbooks (Grebenev, Mukhin), three-layered sputum is given as a common sign of **lung abscess, lung gangrene and bronchiectasis**. Hence the number of layers does not strictly distinguish an abscess from bronchiectasis; the decisive investigation is radiography and CT.

blocks.text: 2.3. Dyspnea

Dyspnea is a disturbance of the rate, depth and rhythm of breathing in which the patient feels short of air. It may be **subjective** (felt by the patient), **objective** (detected by the physician) or **mixed**.

blocks.title: Table 4.3. Types of dyspnea
head: Type
Content
Causes
rows: Narrowing of the upper airways (larynx, trachea): edema, foreign body, tumor, diphtheria
Obstruction of the small bronchi: bronchial asthma, COPD, pulmonary emphysema
Reduction of the respiratory surface: pneumonia, pleurisy, pneumothorax; heart failure

blocks.text: The dyspnea scale of the Medical Research Council (mMRC):

blocks.title: Table 4.4. The mMRC dyspnea scale
head: Grade
Definition
rows: Breathless when hurrying or walking up a slight hill
Walks slower than people of the same age because of breathlessness, or has to stop for breath when walking at own pace on level ground
Stops for breath after walking about 100 m or after a few minutes on level ground
Too breathless to leave the house, or breathless when dressing

blocks.text: 2.4. Choking attacks (asthma)
A **choking attack** is a suddenly developing attack of severe dyspnea. Two types are distinguished:

items: **An attack of bronchial asthma** — expiratory dyspnea, wheezes audible at a distance, expectoration of glassy viscous sputum at the end of the attack;

**Cardiac asthma** — the result of acute left ventricular failure, usually at night; inspiratory or mixed dyspnea, the orthopnea position, moist rales in the lower parts of the lungs, and in severe cases pink frothy sputum (pulmonary edema).

blocks.text: 2.5. Hemoptysis (haemoptysis)

Hemoptysis is the expectoration of blood with sputum on coughing. If more than 50 ml of blood is expectorated per day, it is called **pulmonary hemorrhage**. Causes: tuberculosis, lung cancer, bronchiectasis, lung abscess, pulmonary infarction, mitral stenosis, lobar pneumonia.

blocks.title: Table 4.5. Differences between pulmonary and gastric bleeding
head: Feature
Pulmonary bleeding
Gastric bleeding

blocks.text: 2.6. Chest pain
In respiratory diseases, pain arises mainly from irritation of the **parietal pleura** (the lung tissue has no pain receptors).

parts.text: **Pleuritic pain** is stabbing, increases with deep inspiration and coughing, and lessens when the patient lies on the affected side or presses the chest with the hand (dry pleurisy, lobar pneumonia, pulmonary infarction, pneumothorax). In **intercostal neuralgia**, the pain spreads along the intercostal space and increases when the trunk bends to the healthy side. **The pain of angina pectoris**, by contrast, does not depend on breathing and appears on physical exertion.

blocks.text: 2.7. Features of the history

In the history of present illness, the link of the disease with chilling or influenza and the periods of exacerbation and remission are established. In the life history, **smoking** (pack-years), **occupational hazards** (dust, silica, asbestos, chemicals), **allergic diseases** (pollinosis, eczema), past tuberculosis, contact with a tuberculosis patient and bronchial asthma in the family must always be asked about.

sections.title: 3. Inspection of the chest

blocks.text: The chest is inspected **statically** (shape, symmetry, supraclavicular and infraclavicular fossae, position of the shoulder blades, direction of the ribs, epigastric angle) and **dynamically** (type, rate, depth and rhythm of breathing, equal participation of both sides in breathing, use of the accessory muscles). The patient stands or sits, undressed to the waist.
3.1. Shape of the chest
The normal shapes correspond to the constitutional type: **normosthenic** (conical), **hypersthenic** (cylindrical, broad and short) and **asthenic** (long, narrow, flat).

blocks.text: 3.2. Asymmetry of the chest

items: **Enlargement (bulging) of one side** — accumulation of a large amount of fluid (exudative pleurisy, hydrothorax) or air (pneumothorax) in the pleural cavity. On this side the intercostal spaces are smoothed out or bulge, and the side lags behind in breathing.

**Reduction (retraction) of one side** — obstructive atelectasis, removal of a lung (pneumonectomy), pleural adhesions (schwartes), pneumosclerosis. The shoulder is lowered, the shoulder blade protrudes backward, and the intercostal spaces are narrowed.

blocks.text: 3.3. Type, rate, depth and rhythm of breathing

**Types of breathing:** the thoracic (costal) type — mainly in women; the abdominal (diaphragmatic) type — mainly in men; the mixed type — in the elderly. A change from the thoracic to the abdominal type is seen in pleurisy, rib fractures and intercostal neuralgia; a change from the abdominal to the thoracic type in diaphragmatic paralysis, peritonitis, ascites and meteorism.
**The respiratory rate** is counted for one minute without the patient noticing (for example, as if counting the pulse), with the hand placed on the chest or abdominal wall.

blocks.label: Figure 4.5
blocks.caption: Counting the respiratory rate (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 10)

parts.text: In a healthy adult at rest, the respiratory rate is **16–20** per minute (12–14 during sleep), and in a newborn 40–45. A respiratory rate of more than 20 per minute is **tachypnea**, less than 12 is **bradypnea**, and cessation of breathing is **apnea**. The ratio of the respiratory rate to the pulse rate is normally **1:4**.

sections.title: 4. Palpation of the chest

blocks.text: Palpation determines the following: tender areas, the resistance (elasticity) of the chest, the equal participation of both sides in the respiratory movements and **vocal fremitus** (fremitus vocalis).
4.1. Detecting tender areas

The chest is palpated with the palms of both hands over symmetrical areas from above downward. Localized tenderness is found in rib fractures (a “grating” on pressure — crepitus), intercostal neuralgia (Valleix points: next to the spine, on the axillary line, next to the sternum) and muscle inflammation.

blocks.label: Figure 4.10
blocks.caption: Palpation of the chest from the front (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 15)

blocks.text: 4.2. Determining the resistance (elasticity) of the chest

Standing beside the patient, the physician places one palm on the sternum and the other on the interscapular region and compresses the chest from front to back; then the two hands are placed on the sides and the chest is compressed from the sides. Normally the chest is elastic — it yields when compressed.

blocks.label: Figure 4.11
blocks.caption: Determining the elasticity of the chest in the anteroposterior direction (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 17)

blocks.label: Figure 4.12
blocks.caption: Assessing the participation of the chest in breathing from behind (same source, Fig. 18)

blocks.text: Causes of increased resistance (a “rigid” chest): pulmonary emphysema, a large amount of fluid in the pleural cavity, a pleural tumor, calcification of the costal cartilages in old age.
4.3. Determining vocal fremitus

**Vocal fremitus** is the transmission of the sound vibrations generated in the larynx during speech through the bronchi and lung tissue to the chest wall. The patient is asked to say, in a low (bass) voice, words containing the letter “r” (“thirty-three”, “ninety-nine”, “tractor”). The physician places the palms on symmetrical areas, compares the fremitus on the two sides, then swaps the hands and examines again.
**Areas examined:** in front — the supraclavicular and infraclavicular regions and the lateral surfaces of the chest; behind — the suprascapular, interscapular and infrascapular regions.

blocks.label: Figure 4.15
blocks.caption: In the infrascapular region (same source, Fig. 23)

blocks.label: Figure 4.13
blocks.caption: Determining vocal fremitus from the front (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 20)

blocks.label: Figure 4.14
blocks.caption: In the suprascapular region (same source, Fig. 21)

blocks.text: Normally vocal fremitus is equal on both sides; it is stronger in men with a low voice and in thin people and weaker in women, children and obese people. Over the right apex it is somewhat stronger than on the left (because the right main bronchus is short and wide).

blocks.title: Table 4.8. Changes in vocal fremitus
head: Change
Mechanism
Causes
rows: Consolidated lung tissue conducts sound well (bronchial patency preserved)
Lobar pneumonia, pulmonary infarction, compression atelectasis
A superficially located air-filled cavity communicating with a bronchus acts as a resonator
Fluid or air in the pleural cavity damps the vibrations
The bronchus is blocked, and sound does not pass into the lung
Increased air content of the lung tissue

parts.text: Vocal fremitus is **increased over solid tissue and dampened by fluid and air**: “Solid — Strong, Fluid and Air — Faint”.

For vocal fremitus to be increased, bronchial patency must be preserved. If the bronchus of the consolidated area is blocked by a tumor or a foreign body (obstructive atelectasis), the fremitus is **decreased** even though the tissue is dense.

sections.title: 5. Anatomical and physiological basis of the respiratory system

blocks.label: Figure 4.16
blocks.caption: General structure of the respiratory system (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 1)

blocks.label: Figure 4.17
blocks.caption: Gas exchange between the air in the alveoli and the red cells (same source, Fig. 2)

blocks.text: The airways are divided into the **conducting** part (from the nasal cavity to the terminal bronchioles — it does not take part in gas exchange; the “anatomical dead space”, about 150 ml) and the **respiratory** part (respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveoli). The two lungs contain about **300 million alveoli** with a total surface area of **70–100 m^2^**. The alveolar-capillary membrane is only **0.5 µm** thick, so gas diffusion is very rapid.

**The pleura** is a serous membrane consisting of two layers: the **visceral** layer (covers the lung and has no pain receptors) and the **parietal** layer (lines the inner surface of the chest wall, the diaphragm and the mediastinum and is rich in pain receptors). Between the layers there is 5–15 ml of fluid, and the pressure between them is negative — this keeps the lung in the expanded state.

blocks.title: Table 4.9. Lung volumes and capacities (in an average young man)
head: Parameter
Definition
Normal
rows: Air that can be additionally inhaled after a quiet inspiration
Air that can be additionally exhaled after a quiet expiration
Air remaining in the lungs after a maximal expiration
TV + the inspiratory and expiratory reserve volumes

blocks.text: **Regulation of breathing:** the respiratory center in the medulla oblongata responds to the levels of CO2 (central chemoreceptors) and O2 (peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid bodies) in the blood. A rise in blood CO2 (hypercapnia) is the strongest stimulus to breathing.

sections.title: 6. Pathogenesis of the main complaints

blocks.text: 6.1. Mechanisms of dyspnea
Dyspnea is a multifactorial sensation that arises through the following mechanisms:

items: **Impaired gas exchange** — hypoxemia and hypercapnia stimulate the chemoreceptors and excite the respiratory center.

**Impaired respiratory mechanics** — increased bronchial resistance (obstruction) or decreased lung compliance (fibrosis, congestion) requires greater work of the respiratory muscles; the “mismatch between the effort required and the result obtained” is felt as dyspnea.
**Stimulation of receptors in the lungs** — the interstitial J receptors (pulmonary edema, fibrosis) and stretch receptors.
**Metabolic acidosis** — Kussmaul breathing.
**Psychological factors** — anxiety, panic attacks (hyperventilation syndrome: “unable to take a full breath”, sighing).

blocks.title: Table 4.10. Causes of dyspnea by system
head: System
Causes
rows: COPD, bronchial asthma, pneumonia, pleurisy, pneumothorax, pulmonary fibrosis, lung cancer
Heart failure, valvular heart disease, arrhythmias, pericarditis, pulmonary embolism
Diaphragmatic paralysis, myasthenia gravis, Guillain–Barré syndrome

parts.text: Dyspnea of sudden onset — pneumothorax, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary edema, an asthma attack, aspiration of a foreign body; increasing over several days — pneumonia, pleurisy, decompensated heart failure; increasing gradually over months and years — COPD, pulmonary fibrosis, valvular heart disease, anemia.

blocks.text: 6.2. Causes and severity of hemoptysis

blocks.title: Table 4.11. Causes of hemoptysis
head: Group
Causes
rows: Tuberculosis (one of the most common causes), bronchiectasis, lung abscess, pneumonia (especially lobar and Klebsiella), aspergilloma
Mitral stenosis, left ventricular failure (pulmonary edema), pulmonary embolism and pulmonary infarction
Chest injury, foreign body, hemorrhagic diatheses, anticoagulants, Goodpasture’s syndrome, granulomatosis with polyangiitis

parts.text: Loss of **more than 100–200 ml** of blood per day (500 ml in some sources), or bleeding accompanied by airway obstruction and hemodynamic instability, is **massive pulmonary hemorrhage**; it is life-threatening and requires urgent bronchoscopy and bronchial artery embolization. The patient is laid on the bleeding side (so that blood does not flow into the healthy lung).

sections.title: 7. Additional aspects of the inspection of the chest

blocks.text: 7.1. Topographic lines of the chest

Conventional vertical lines are used to localize changes on the chest precisely: the **anterior midline**, the **sternal line**, the **parasternal line** (midway between the sternal and midclavicular lines), the **midclavicular line** (through the middle of the clavicle), the **anterior, middle and posterior axillary lines**, the **scapular line** (through the angle of the scapula), the **paravertebral line** and the **posterior midline**.

**Counting the ribs:** in front — the II rib joins the sternum at the level of the sternal angle (the angle of Louis, where the manubrium joins the body of the sternum), and counting proceeds downward from it; behind — with the arms lowered, the angles of the shoulder blades correspond to the VII rib; the spinous process of the VII cervical vertebra is the most prominent when the head is bent forward.
7.2. Additional examples of chest deformities

blocks.caption: Paralytic chest with cachexia (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 6)

blocks.label: Figure 4.19
blocks.caption: Kyphosis (same source, Fig. 8)

parts.text: In severe kyphoscoliosis the volume of the chest is sharply reduced and the respiratory muscles work under unfavorable conditions — **restrictive respiratory failure** and, later, **cor pulmonale** (the “kyphoscoliotic heart”) develop. In such patients it is also harder to determine the borders of the heart and lungs.

blocks.text: 7.3. Signs of respiratory failure detected on inspection

items: Tachypnea (more than 25–30 per minute), use of the accessory muscles (sternocleidomastoid, trapezius, abdominal muscles) during inspiration;
indrawing of the intercostal spaces during inspiration;
**paradoxical abdominal movement** — indrawing of the abdominal wall during inspiration (diaphragmatic fatigue, severe respiratory failure);
movement of the nasal alae with breathing;
diffuse (central) cyanosis, sweating, tachycardia;
in hypercapnia — warm and moist skin, headache, drowsiness, a “flapping” tremor of the hands, impaired consciousness (hypercapnic encephalopathy).

blocks.title: Table 4.13. Grades of respiratory failure (by blood gases and pulse oximetry)
head: Grade
PaO2, mm Hg
SpO2, %

blocks.text: Clinically, the textbook divides respiratory failure into three grades: **I** — dyspnea on heavy or moderate physical exertion; **II** — on slight exertion, with the compensatory mechanisms working even at rest; **III** — dyspnea and cyanosis at rest.

parts.text: **Pulse oximetry** is the painless measurement of the oxygen saturation of arterial blood (SpO2) and the pulse with a sensor placed on a finger. Normal is **95–98 %**. An SpO2 below 90 % is hypoxemia (an indication for oxygen therapy). In patients with COPD, the target SpO2 is 88–92 %.

sections.title: 8. Detailed description of the palpation technique

blocks.text: 8.1. Palpation of the back and lateral regions

blocks.label: Figure 4.22
blocks.caption: Determining the elasticity of the chest from the side (same source, Fig. 17)

blocks.label: Figure 4.21
blocks.caption: Palpation of the chest from behind (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 16)

blocks.text: To assess the equal participation (excursion) of both sides of the chest in breathing, the physician stands behind the patient and places the palms of both hands below the angles of the shoulder blades, with the thumbs close together beside the spine. When the patient takes a deep breath, the thumbs should move the same distance away from the spine; a lag of one side indicates pathology on that side (pleurisy, pneumonia, atelectasis, pneumothorax).

blocks.label: Figure 4.23
blocks.caption: Assessing chest excursion with the thumbs (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 18)

blocks.text: 8.2. Examining vocal fremitus from behind

blocks.label: Figure 4.24
blocks.caption: Determining vocal fremitus in the interscapular region (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 22)

parts.text: What is examined by palpation — **“TREV”**: **T**enderness, **R**esistance, **E**xpansion (participation in breathing), **V**ocal fremitus.

Vocal fremitus is easy to examine in men with a low voice, whereas in women and children with a high-pitched voice it is felt only weakly. That is why **comparing the two sides** is important: it is not the absolute strength of the fremitus but its **asymmetry** that has diagnostic significance.

sections.title: 9. Lung diseases related to occupational and environmental factors

blocks.text: In respiratory diseases, a careful occupational history is often the key to the diagnosis.

parts.text: When occupational asthma is suspected, the most important question is: **“Do the symptoms lessen at weekends and on holiday?”** Symptoms that get worse at work and lessen at home point to an occupational factor. The diagnosis is confirmed by serial PEF measurements at work and during time off.

sections.title: 10. Detailed analysis of cough and sputum

blocks.text: 10.1. Mechanism of the cough reflex

When the cough receptors are stimulated (mechanically, chemically, thermally, by inflammation), impulses travel along the vagus nerve to the cough center in the medulla oblongata. A cough consists of three phases: **a deep inspiration** → **closure of the glottis and contraction of the expiratory muscles** (the intrathoracic pressure rises to 100–300 mm Hg) → **sudden opening of the glottis** and expulsion of air at high speed (hundreds of km per hour) together with the secretions.

blocks.title: Table 4.15. Causes of chronic cough outside the respiratory system
head: Cause
Features
rows: At night, after meals, on lying down; with heartburn
A feeling of something running down the throat, frequent throat clearing; rhinitis, sinusitis
Dry, tickling; resolves 1–4 weeks after the drug is stopped
Worse on lying down, with dyspnea
Disappears during sleep, worse with excitement

blocks.text: 10.2. The amount of sputum and its significance

items: **A small amount** (a few spittings a day) — acute bronchitis, bronchial asthma, the onset of pneumonia;
**a moderate amount** (50–100 ml) — chronic bronchitis, pneumonia;
**a large amount** (more than 100–150 ml, sometimes up to 1 l) — lung abscess (after rupture), bronchiectasis, lung gangrene, pulmonary edema, cavitary tuberculosis.

parts.text: The production of a large amount of sputum at once (“a mouthful”) is a sign of the **rupture of a cavity in the lung into a bronchus** (abscess) or of **bronchiectasis**; an increase in sputum in the morning and its dependence on position are characteristic of bronchiectasis.

sections.title: 11. Measuring the dimensions of the chest

blocks.text: The chest circumference is measured with a centimeter tape: behind, the tape passes below the angles of the shoulder blades, and in front, at the level of the nipples in men and at the junction of the IV rib with the sternum in women. Normally the circumference equals half the height or is slightly greater. The **anteroposterior** and **transverse** diameters of the chest are determined with a special caliper (pelvimeter); normally the ratio of the anteroposterior to the transverse diameter (the chest index) is **0.65–0.75**; in emphysema it approaches 1.0.

sections.title: 13. Features of the respiratory system in the elderly

blocks.text: With age, the chest becomes rigid (the costal cartilages calcify), the strength of the respiratory muscles and the elasticity of the lungs decrease, mucociliary clearance weakens and the cough reflex diminishes. As a result:

items: chest excursion decreases and resistance increases;
the lower borders of the lungs descend slightly (“senile emphysema”), and vesicular breathing is diminished;
pneumonia often runs an **asymptomatic or atypical** course: without fever, with only weakness, confusion, loss of appetite, falls;
isolated crackles in the lower parts of the lungs that disappear after coughing may be normal (basal atelectasis).

parts.text: In an elderly patient, a respiratory rate of **more than 25** per minute is often the earliest and most sensitive sign of pneumonia. That is why the respiratory rate must be counted accurately in every elderly patient.

blocks.text: Sample case history entry

**The chest** is emphysematous in shape and symmetrical. The epigastric angle is obtuse, the ribs run horizontally, the intercostal spaces are widened, and the supraclavicular fossae bulge. Breathing is of the mixed type, respiratory rate 24 per minute, rhythmic, shallow. The accessory muscles take part in inspiration. Both sides take part equally in breathing. **On palpation** the chest is painless, with increased resistance. Vocal fremitus is symmetrically decreased on both sides.
**Conclusion:** signs characteristic of the syndrome of increased air content of the lung tissue (emphysema).

skills.title: Skill: counting the respiratory rate

items: Lay or seat the patient in a comfortable position.
Hold the patient’s hand as if counting the pulse (so that the patient does not consciously change his or her breathing).
Place your other hand on the lower part of the chest or on the abdominal wall.
Count the respiratory movements for one minute (one inspiration and one expiration — one movement).
At the same time, assess the type, depth and rhythm of breathing.
Record the result on the temperature chart.

skills.title: Skill: determining vocal fremitus

items: Undress the patient to the waist, standing or sitting.
Place the palms of both hands lightly on symmetrical areas of the chest, with the fingers directed along the ribs.
Ask the patient to say “thirty-three” or “ninety-nine” in a low voice.
Compare the fremitus on the two sides; then swap the hands and examine again.
Examine the areas in turn: supraclavicular, infraclavicular, lateral surfaces, suprascapular, interscapular, infrascapular.
Interpret the result: equal, increased or decreased (in which area).

skills.title: Skill: measuring chest excursion

items: Pass the centimeter tape behind below the angles of the shoulder blades, and in front at the level of the nipples in men and below the breasts in women.
Measure the chest circumference during quiet breathing, at maximal inspiration and at maximal expiration.
The difference between the circumferences at maximal inspiration and expiration is the excursion, normally 6–8 cm. It is reduced in emphysema, pleural adhesions and ankylosing spondylitis.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 60-year-old man has complained of a morning productive cough for 15 years and, in recent years, of dyspnea on climbing stairs. He has smoked a pack of cigarettes a day for 40 years. On inspection: the chest is barrel-shaped, the supraclavicular fossae bulge, the accessory muscles take part in inspiration, and he exhales through pursed lips. On palpation the chest is rigid, and vocal fremitus is decreased on both sides.
cases.ask: Calculate the smoking index. What type of dyspnea is it? Which syndrome are the inspection and palpation findings characteristic of?
cases.answer: Smoking index = 20 × 40 / 20 = 40 pack-years. The dyspnea is expiratory (bronchial obstruction). A barrel chest, increased resistance and symmetrically decreased vocal fremitus are characteristic of the syndrome of increased air content of the lung tissue (emphysema). The clinical picture suggests COPD (chronic obstructive bronchitis and emphysema).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 35-year-old patient developed sudden chills, a fever of 39.8 °C and stabbing pain on the right side that increased on deep inspiration 3 days ago. Today he began to expectorate viscous rust-colored sputum. Vocal fremitus is increased in the right infrascapular region.
cases.ask: Explain the character of the sputum and of the pain. Why is vocal fremitus increased?
cases.answer: The rust-colored sputum is due to the breakdown of red cells with the formation of hemosiderin and is characteristic of lobar pneumonia. Stabbing pain that increases on deep inspiration is pleuritic pain (inflammation of the parietal pleura). Increased vocal fremitus indicates consolidation of the lung tissue: the alveoli are filled with exudate, bronchial patency is preserved, and the dense tissue conducts sound well.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: On inspection of a 42-year-old woman, the left side of the chest is enlarged, the intercostal spaces are smoothed out, and the left side lags behind in breathing. On palpation, vocal fremitus is not detected in the lower part of the left side.
cases.ask: In which conditions is such a picture observed? What investigations are needed?
cases.answer: Enlargement of one side of the chest, its lagging behind in breathing and the absence of vocal fremitus are characteristic of the accumulation of fluid (exudative pleurisy, hydrothorax) or air (pneumothorax) in the pleural cavity. Changes in the lower parts suggest fluid rather than air. Percussion (a dull note and the Damoiseau line), auscultation, radiography, pleural US and pleural puncture are needed.

cards.back: Waxing and waning + apnea — heart failure, cerebral ischemia
Equal breaths + long pause — meningitis, brain injury

topics.title: Percussion as a method of objective examination. Comparative and topographic percussion of the lungs

goals.text: To teach the student the physical basis, methods and rules of percussion, the types of percussion notes, and how to perform comparative and topographic percussion of the lungs in a healthy person and in respiratory diseases and interpret the results.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the physical basis of percussion and the history of its discovery;
the methods of direct and indirect (finger-on-finger) percussion;
the general rules of performing percussion;
the features of the main percussion notes (resonant, dull, tympanic) and their intermediate types;
the points of comparative percussion and the causes of changes;
the normal values for the height of the lung apices, Krönig’s isthmus, the lower borders of the lungs and their mobility.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: perform finger-on-finger percussion with the correct technique;
perform comparative percussion of the lungs and assess the result;
perform topographic percussion of the lungs, mark the borders and compare them with the normal values.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Percussion sets the tissues into vibration to a **depth of 5–7 cm** and **2–4 cm to the side** of the point struck. That is why deep-seated foci or foci smaller than 2–3 cm in diameter are not detected by percussion.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Common mistakes: striking with movement at the elbow or shoulder joint (the blow becomes heavy and imprecise), keeping the plexor finger on the pleximeter (the sound is damped), other fingers touching the body under the pleximeter, and long nails (the nail of the plexor finger must be short).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The rule of topographic percussion: **“From resonant to dull, parallel, gently, the border on the resonant side”**.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Even in a healthy person, the note may differ slightly at symmetrical points: over the right apex the note is somewhat duller than on the left (the right apex lies lower, and the muscles of the right shoulder girdle are better developed); on the left in the II–III intercostal spaces it is somewhat duller because of the proximity of the heart; on the right in the lower parts it is dulled because of the proximity of the liver; on the left below it has a tympanic tinge because of Traube’s space (the fundus of the stomach).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The normal width of Krönig’s isthmus is **5–6 cm** (individual variation 3.5–8 cm). The textbook gives the normal value as **3–8 cm**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Remember the lower border of the right lung from front to back: **“5-6-7-8-9-10-11”** — the parasternal line in the V intercostal space, the midclavicular VI, the anterior axillary VII, the mid-axillary VIII, the posterior axillary IX, the scapular X, and the paravertebral line at the XI vertebra. On the left along the mid-axillary line, it is one rib lower — **IX**.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The total mobility of the lower edge of the lung: **4–6 cm along the midclavicular and scapular lines**, **6–8 cm along the mid-axillary line** (3–4 cm each on inspiration and on expiration).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Percussion is not performed over the scapula: the thick bone and muscles damp the sound, and the result is unreliable. In the interscapular region the pleximeter is placed **vertically**, and in the infrascapular regions it is again placed parallel to the ribs (horizontally).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Textbooks give different normal values for Krönig’s isthmus: Gadayev — **3–8 cm**, Grebenev and Mukhin — **5–6 cm** (individual variation 3.5–8 cm). In practice, **comparing the two sides** matters more than the absolute figure: unilateral narrowing (for example, 3 cm on the right and 6 cm on the left) raises suspicion of apical tuberculosis or pneumosclerosis.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The lower border: **“up — pushed from below, down — the lung is inflated”**: its rise is most often due to pressure from below (ascites, meteorism, an enlarged liver) or to shrinkage of the lung; its descent is a sign of increased lung volume (emphysema).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The absence of changes on percussion does not mean the absence of disease. If there is clinical suspicion, radiography, US or CT is performed. However, percussion and auscultation are the first step: they direct the investigation correctly and make it possible to follow the dynamics at the bedside.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The “triad” of physical signs: **Percussion — Fremitus — Breath sounds**. It is enough to remember each syndrome by these three parameters: consolidation — “Dull, Increased, Bronchial”; fluid — “Dull, Absent, Absent”; air — “Tympanic, Absent, Absent”; emphysema — “Hyperresonant, Decreased, Decreased”.

sections.title: 1. General information on percussion

blocks.text: **Percussion** (Latin percussio — tapping) is a method of determining the physical state, borders and size of the underlying organs by tapping the body surface and assessing the characteristics of the resulting sound.

The method was discovered in 1761 by the Austrian physician **Leopold Auenbrugger** (“Inventum novum”). He was inspired by his father, a wine producer, who determined the amount of wine in barrels by tapping them. In 1808 the French physician **J. Corvisart** introduced the method widely into practice. After percussion with a pleximeter (1828, P. Piorry) and a hammer, **finger-on-finger percussion** eventually prevailed; Russian clinicians (G. Sokolov, F. Yanovsky, V. Obraztsov) played a large role in its development.
1.1. Physical basis of percussion
When tapped, the body tissues vibrate and produce a sound. The character of the sound depends on the **density**, **air content** and **elasticity** of the tissue.

parts.text: Percussion sets the tissues into vibration to a **depth of 5–7 cm** and **2–4 cm to the side** of the point struck. That is why deep-seated foci or foci smaller than 2–3 cm in diameter are not detected by percussion.

blocks.label: Figure 5.1
blocks.caption: Technique of finger-on-finger percussion (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 17)

blocks.text: 2.1. Technique of finger-on-finger percussion

items: The **pleximeter finger** (the middle finger of the left hand) is applied closely to the body surface, but without excessive pressure; the other fingers are slightly separated and do not touch the body.
The **plexor finger** (the middle finger of the right hand) is bent and strikes the **middle phalanx** of the pleximeter perpendicularly, using movement at the **wrist joint** only.
The blow is short and sharp, and the finger is withdrawn at once after striking (it “bounces back”).
**Two** blows of equal strength are delivered at each point.
The strength of the blows is kept the same throughout the examination.

blocks.label: Figure 5.2
blocks.caption: Performing percussion (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 18)

parts.text: Common mistakes: striking with movement at the elbow or shoulder joint (the blow becomes heavy and imprecise), keeping the plexor finger on the pleximeter (the sound is damped), other fingers touching the body under the pleximeter, and long nails (the nail of the plexor finger must be short).

blocks.text: 2.2. Strength of percussion

items: **Loud (strong, deep) percussion** — for examining deep-seated organs (up to 7 cm); used in comparative percussion.
**Moderate percussion** — the strength most often used in comparative percussion.
**Quiet (weak) percussion** — for determining the borders of organs (topographic percussion).
**The quietest (threshold) percussion** — Goldscheider’s method; for determining the absolute cardiac dullness, with sound at the threshold of hearing.

sections.title: 3. General rules of performing percussion

items: The room should be warm and quiet.
The patient is in a comfortable position (standing, sitting or lying), with the muscles relaxed.
The physician’s hands are warm and the nails short.
In **comparative percussion**, symmetrical points are compared alternately.

In **topographic percussion**, percussion proceeds from the resonant note (clear lung note) toward the dull note; the pleximeter is placed **parallel** to the border being determined, and each step does not exceed **1–2 cm**.
The border is marked **on the side of the resonant note** (along the edge of the pleximeter facing the resonant side).

parts.text: The rule of topographic percussion: **“From resonant to dull, parallel, gently, the border on the resonant side”**.

parts.text: In lobar pneumonia the percussion note changes with the stage: **stage I** (congestion) — dull-tympanic; **stage II** (hepatization) — dull; **stage III** (resolution) — dull-tympanic again, and then it returns to the clear lung note. These changes are explained by the ratio of air to exudate in the alveoli.

sections.title: 5. Comparative percussion of the lungs

blocks.text: **Purpose** — to detect a pathological focus by comparing the percussion note at symmetrical points of the chest. Percussion is performed with moderate or loud strength.
5.1. Order of comparative percussion
**In front** (the patient stands or sits with the arms lowered):

items: The supraclavicular fossae (pleximeter parallel to the clavicle).
The clavicles themselves (direct percussion — the finger strikes the middle part of the clavicle).
The I and II intercostal spaces along the midclavicular line.
Because the heart lies lower down on the left, comparative percussion is performed symmetrically only down to the III intercostal space.

blocks.text: **From the side** (the patient places the hands on the head): starting from the axillary fossa, the IV and V intercostal spaces along the mid-axillary line.
**From behind** (the patient crosses the arms over the chest and bends the head slightly — the shoulder blades move apart):

items: The suprascapular regions (pleximeter parallel to the spine of the scapula).
The interscapular region — the pleximeter is placed **vertically** (parallel to the spine), at three points from above downward.
The infrascapular regions — in the VII, VIII and IX intercostal spaces below the angle of the scapula, with the pleximeter parallel to the ribs.

sections.title: 6. Topographic percussion of the lungs

blocks.text: **Purpose:** to determine the height and width of the lung apices (Krönig’s isthmus), the lower borders of the lungs and the respiratory mobility of their lower edges. Percussion is performed with **quiet** strength.
6.1. Determining the height of the lung apices

**In front:** the pleximeter is placed in the supraclavicular fossa parallel to the clavicle, and percussion proceeds from the middle of the clavicle upward and medially (toward the sternocleidomastoid muscle) until a dull note appears. Normally the apex is **3–4 cm** above the clavicle.

**Behind:** the pleximeter is moved horizontally from the middle of the spine of the scapula toward the spinous process of the VII cervical vertebra. Normally the apex is at the level of the **spinous process of the VII cervical vertebra**.

blocks.label: Figure 5.7
blocks.caption: Determining the height of the lung apex from behind (same source, Fig. 32)

blocks.label: Figure 5.6
blocks.caption: Determining the height of the lung apex from the front (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 31)

blocks.text: 6.2. Determining Krönig’s isthmus

**Krönig’s isthmus** is the width of the area of clear lung note over the lung apex along the anterior edge of the trapezius muscle. The pleximeter is placed perpendicular to the middle of the edge of the trapezius, and percussion proceeds first medially (toward the neck) and then laterally (toward the shoulder) until a dull note appears. The distance between the two points is measured.

blocks.label: Figure 5.8
blocks.caption: Determining Krönig’s isthmus (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 33)

parts.text: The normal width of Krönig’s isthmus is **5–6 cm** (individual variation 3.5–8 cm). The textbook gives the normal value as **3–8 cm**.

blocks.text: Changes:

items: Increased height of the apices and widening of Krönig’s isthmus — **pulmonary emphysema**.
Decreased height of the apices and narrowing of Krönig’s isthmus — **tuberculous infiltrate or pneumosclerosis** of the apex, shrinkage of the apex. A unilateral change is especially significant.

blocks.text: 6.3. Determining the lower borders of the lungs

Percussion proceeds along the topographic lines from above downward, starting from the II–III intercostal space (behind, from the angle of the scapula), until the clear lung note changes to a dull note (on the right, liver dullness) or, on the left, to a tympanic note (Traube’s space). The pleximeter is placed in the intercostal space, parallel to the ribs. The rib or intercostal space to which the border corresponds is counted.

blocks.label: Figure 5.9
blocks.caption: Topographic lines used to determine the lower borders of the lungs (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 36)

parts.text: Remember the lower border of the right lung from front to back: **“5-6-7-8-9-10-11”** — the parasternal line in the V intercostal space, the midclavicular VI, the anterior axillary VII, the mid-axillary VIII, the posterior axillary IX, the scapular X, and the paravertebral line at the XI vertebra. On the left along the mid-axillary line, it is one rib lower — **IX**.

blocks.text: In hypersthenic persons the border is one rib higher, and in asthenic persons one rib lower.

blocks.title: Table 5.7. Causes of displacement of the lower border of the lung
head: Displacement
Unilateral
Bilateral
rows: Vicarious (compensatory) emphysema — when the other lung has stopped functioning
Pulmonary emphysema, an attack of bronchial asthma, prolapse of the internal organs (splanchnoptosis)
Fluid or air in the pleural cavity, obstructive atelectasis, pneumosclerosis, diaphragmatic paralysis, marked enlargement of the liver or spleen

blocks.text: 6.4. Determining the mobility of the lower edge of the lung

Along the midclavicular (on the right only), mid-axillary and scapular lines, the lower border is first determined during quiet breathing. Then the patient takes a deep breath and holds it — the border is determined again and marked. Next the patient exhales maximally and holds the breath — the border is determined once more. The distance between the borders at maximal inspiration and expiration is measured.

blocks.label: Figure 5.10
blocks.caption: Assessing the mobility of the lower border of the lung (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 37)

parts.text: The total mobility of the lower edge of the lung: **4–6 cm along the midclavicular and scapular lines**, **6–8 cm along the mid-axillary line** (3–4 cm each on inspiration and on expiration).

blocks.text: **Causes of decreased mobility:** decreased elasticity of the lung tissue (emphysema), inflammatory infiltrate, pulmonary congestion, pneumosclerosis, pleural adhesions, diaphragmatic paralysis. **Absent mobility:** a large amount of fluid or air in the pleural cavity, complete fusion of the pleural layers (obliteration).

sections.title: 7. Physical basis of percussion: a deeper analysis

blocks.text: According to their acoustic properties, the body tissues fall into three groups:

items: **Airless and dense tissues** (muscles, liver, spleen, heart, fluid) — damp vibrations quickly and give a low-amplitude, short sound (dull, the thigh note).

**Air-containing tissue with elastic walls** (the lung) — the alveoli with their tense walls hold the air; the vibrations are irregular (of different frequencies), so the sound is loud and long but not tympanic (the clear lung note).
**Large air-filled cavities with smooth walls** (stomach, intestines, a large cavern, pneumothorax) — the vibrations are of a single frequency (harmonic), hence the tympanic note.

blocks.text: The character of the percussion note depends on the ratio of the amount of air to the tension and elasticity of the tissue. For example, **when the tension of the lung tissue decreases** (the onset of pulmonary edema, stage I of lobar pneumonia, compression atelectasis), the alveolar walls slacken even though air is preserved, and a **dull-tympanic** note appears. **When the tension increases** and the air increases (emphysema), a **hyperresonant (box-like)** note results.

parts.text: **Škoda’s tympany** is the dull-tympanic note heard in exudative pleurisy above the fluid level, over the compressed lung (in Garland’s triangle and above it). When the lung tissue is compressed, its tension decreases, while air is partly preserved in the alveoli.

blocks.text: 8.3. Typical mistakes in comparative percussion

items: Choosing symmetrical points incorrectly (one over a rib, the other over an intercostal space).
Percussing one side strongly and the other quietly.
Incorrect position of the patient: trunk turned, shoulders at different heights, muscles tense.
Pressing the pleximeter finger with varying pressure.
Examining only the anterior surface and missing the posterior and lateral regions — whereas pneumonia and pleurisy are most often located in the **lower posterior** regions.
