blocks.text: 9.3. Traube’s space

**Traube’s space** (the semilunar tympanic area) is the area of tympanic note on the left in the lower part of the chest produced by the gas bubble of the fundus of the stomach. Its borders: above — the lower edge of the left lung; on the right — the left lobe of the liver; on the left — the spleen; below — the costal arch.

blocks.title: Table 5.8. Changes in Traube’s space
head: Change
Causes
rows: Reduced or absent (dullness instead of tympany)
Left-sided exudative pleurisy (the most important cause), marked enlargement of the spleen, enlargement of the left lobe of the liver, a large amount of pericardial fluid, a full stomach
Distension of the stomach with gas, aerophagia

parts.text: Traube’s space helps to distinguish left-sided exudative pleurisy from **left lower lobe pneumonia**: when there is fluid in the pleura, the space is “filled” with a dull note, whereas in pneumonia it is usually preserved.

sections.title: 10. Changes in the lung borders under various conditions

blocks.title: Table 5.9. Lung borders in physiological states
head: Condition
Change
rows: The lower borders rise slightly (the abdominal organs push the diaphragm upward), especially on the dependent side
The lower border of the dependent lung rises by 2–3 cm, and the border of the upper lung descends
The lower borders descend by 2–4 cm
The lower borders descend slightly, and mobility decreases (senile emphysema)

blocks.text: Relation between the lung and liver borders
The lower border of the right lung along the midclavicular line is at the same time the **upper border of the relative liver dullness**. Therefore:

items: when the lung border **descends** (emphysema), the liver is also pushed downward and may be palpable below the costal arch — this is **false hepatomegaly**;
**disappearance** of liver dullness (tympany over the liver on percussion) is a sign of free air in the abdominal cavity (perforation of a gastric or intestinal ulcer), a surgical emergency.

parts.text: The lower border: **“up — pushed from below, down — the lung is inflated”**: its rise is most often due to pressure from below (ascites, meteorism, an enlarged liver) or to shrinkage of the lung; its descent is a sign of increased lung volume (emphysema).

sections.title: 11. Comparing percussion findings with modern methods

blocks.text: The accuracy of percussion is limited: it detects superficial (5–7 cm) changes larger than 2–3 cm. Fluid in the pleural cavity is usually detected by percussion when it exceeds **300–500 ml**; on the radiograph, blunting of the costophrenic sinus appears at 200–300 ml, whereas **on US even 50 ml** of fluid is visible.

blocks.title: Table 5.10. Sensitivity of the physical methods and modern investigations (approximate)
head: Condition
Physical examination
X-ray (radiography)
US / CT
rows: A lobe or a large segment

parts.text: The absence of changes on percussion does not mean the absence of disease. If there is clinical suspicion, radiography, US or CT is performed. However, percussion and auscultation are the first step: they direct the investigation correctly and make it possible to follow the dynamics at the bedside.

sections.title: 12. Features of percussion in children and the elderly

blocks.text: **In children**, because the chest wall is thin and elastic, percussion is performed **more quietly** (often directly or with a fingertip); a strong blow also sets neighboring areas into vibration and masks small foci. In children the lung borders are one rib higher than in adults, and the percussion note may have a slight tympanic tinge.

**In the elderly**, the chest is rigid and the air content of the lungs is increased (senile emphysema) — the note has a box-like tinge, the lower borders have descended, and mobility is decreased. A functional investigation is needed to distinguish these changes from pathological emphysema.

sections.title: 13. Additional methods of percussion

blocks.text: 13.1. Auscultatory percussion

The stethoscope is placed over the organ, and a sound is produced around it by light flicking (or by rubbing with a finger). The sound changes sharply on crossing the border of the organ. The method is used to determine the borders of the liver, stomach and heart, as well as in bedridden patients and in situations where percussion is difficult.
13.2. Additional methods of detecting pleural fluid

items: **Positional percussion:** free fluid (transudate) shifts when the patient’s position changes — dullness appears at the bottom when sitting and on the dependent side when lying on the side.
**Independence of the fluid border from breathing:** the fluid level does not change with breathing, whereas the lung border shifts.

sections.title: 14. Drawing a conclusion from percussion

blocks.text: Percussion findings are never assessed in isolation. For example, a dull note is found in three different conditions — consolidation of the lung, pleural fluid and atelectasis — and to distinguish them, **inspection** (size of the hemithorax), **palpation** (vocal fremitus), **auscultation** (type of breath sounds) and **the position of the mediastinum** are analyzed together.

blocks.title: Table 5.11. Combinations of the percussion note with other physical signs
head: Percussion note
Vocal fremitus
Respiration
Conclusion
rows: Absent, mediastinum shifted to the affected side
Stage I or III of lobar pneumonia

parts.text: The “triad” of physical signs: **Percussion — Fremitus — Breath sounds**. It is enough to remember each syndrome by these three parameters: consolidation — “Dull, Increased, Bronchial”; fluid — “Dull, Absent, Absent”; air — “Tympanic, Absent, Absent”; emphysema — “Hyperresonant, Decreased, Decreased”.

sections.title: 15. The influence of the diaphragm and abdominal organs on the lung borders

items: **Unilateral elevation of the diaphragm** — phrenic nerve paralysis (tumor, surgery), subphrenic abscess, marked enlargement of the liver or spleen, lobar atelectasis. On percussion the lower border of the lung is raised on the affected side, and mobility is absent or paradoxical (the diaphragm rises on inspiration).
**Subphrenic abscess** — the lower border of the right lung rises, and reactive pleural fluid sometimes appears; fever, pain in the right hypochondrium, pain radiating to the shoulder.
**Meteorism and ascites** — bilateral elevation, shallow breathing.

parts.text: After abdominal operations, patients do not breathe deeply because of pain; diaphragmatic movement is restricted, and **atelectasis** and **hypostatic pneumonia** develop in the lower parts. Percussion reveals dulling and decreased mobility in the lower posterior regions. Prevention — early mobilization, breathing exercises, adequate pain relief.

blocks.text: Sample case history entry

**On comparative percussion** a hyperresonant (box-like) note is found over all symmetrical areas of the lungs. **On topographic percussion**: the lung apices are 5 cm above the clavicle in front and 1 cm above the VII cervical vertebra behind. Krönig’s isthmus is 9 cm on both sides. The lower borders of the lungs are lowered by one rib (on the right, the VII rib along the midclavicular line and the XI rib along the scapular line). The mobility of the lower edge of the lung along the mid-axillary line is 2 cm.
**Conclusion:** the syndrome of increased air content of the lung tissue (emphysema).

skills.title: Skill: comparative percussion of the lungs

items: Undress the patient to the waist, standing or sitting; stand in front of the patient.
Begin in front: supraclavicular fossae → clavicles (directly) → I and II intercostal spaces along the midclavicular line.
At each level, percuss first the right and then the left side (or vice versa) with the same strength and compare the notes.
Move to the lateral regions: the patient places the hands on the head; the IV–V intercostal spaces, starting from the axilla.

Move to the back: the patient crosses the arms in front of the chest. The suprascapular regions, the interscapular region (pleximeter vertical, three points), the infrascapular regions (VII–IX intercostal spaces).
Record the result: what note over which area, symmetrical or asymmetrical.

skills.title: Skill: determining the lower borders of the lungs and their mobility

items: On the right, percuss quietly downward along the parasternal line from the II intercostal space, and mark the place where the resonant note changes to a dull note along the upper edge of the pleximeter.
In the same way, determine the border along the midclavicular line, the anterior, mid- and posterior axillary lines (with the patient’s hands on the head), and the scapular and paravertebral lines.
On the left, do the same, starting from the anterior axillary line.

Compare the borders found with the normal values by counting the ribs and intercostal spaces (start counting the ribs in front from the II rib — next to the sternal angle, and behind from the angle of the scapula — the VII rib).

To determine mobility, find the border during quiet breathing along the mid-axillary line, then have the patient hold the breath at deep inspiration and at full expiration and determine the border again.
Measure the distance between the points of maximal inspiration and expiration with a centimeter tape and compare it with the normal value.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: In a 65-year-old patient, comparative percussion revealed a hyperresonant (box-like) note over all areas. On topographic percussion, Krönig’s isthmus was 10 cm, the lower border of the right lung along the midclavicular line was at the VII rib, and the mobility along the mid-axillary line was 2 cm.
cases.ask: Interpret the percussion findings. Which syndrome is involved?
cases.answer: A hyperresonant note, widening of Krönig’s isthmus (normal 5–6 cm), descent of the lower border by one rib (normal VI rib) and a sharp decrease in mobility (normal 6–8 cm) are characteristic of the syndrome of increased air content of the lung tissue, that is, pulmonary emphysema.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: In a 40-year-old patient, a dull note is found on the right below the infrascapular region. The upper border of the dullness runs along an oblique line: it rises upward and laterally from the spine, reaches its highest point at the posterior axillary line and then descends forward. In this area the mobility of the lower edge of the lung cannot be determined.
cases.ask: What do these findings indicate? What is the oblique line of the border called?
cases.answer: Accumulation of fluid in the pleural cavity (exudative pleurisy or hydrothorax). The oblique line of the upper border of the fluid is the Damoiseau line (Ellis–Damoiseau–Sokolov line); it is characteristic of an exudate. The absent mobility shows that the edge of the lung is compressed by the fluid. The diagnosis is confirmed by radiography, US and pleural puncture.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: In a tall, thin 25-year-old man, severe pain on the left side and dyspnea appeared suddenly after lifting a heavy load. On percussion there is a tympanic note on the left, and the lower border of the left lung cannot be determined.
cases.ask: Which condition can be considered? Interpret the percussion findings.
cases.answer: Spontaneous pneumothorax. As a result of air entering the pleural cavity, the lung collapses and a layer of air forms under the chest wall — that is why a tympanic note is heard and the lung border and its mobility cannot be determined. Urgent radiography is performed for confirmation.

topics.title: Auscultation as a method of objective examination. Auscultation of the lungs: the main and added breath sounds

goals.text: To teach the student the history, technique and rules of auscultation, the main breath sounds heard on auscultation of the lungs (vesicular, bronchial) and their changes, the added breath sounds (dry and moist rales, crepitation, pleural friction rub), and how to examine and interpret bronchophony.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: direct and indirect auscultation and the structure of the stethoscope and phonendoscope;
the rules of auscultation and the points of auscultation of the lungs;
the mechanism of production, features and sites of audibility of vesicular and bronchial breathing;
the physiological and pathological changes of vesicular breathing;
the types of pathological bronchial breathing and their causes;
the mechanism of production and distinguishing features of rales, crepitation and pleural friction rub;
bronchophony and its diagnostic significance.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: perform auscultation of the lungs in accordance with the rules;
identify and assess the main breath sound;
detect added sounds and apply the methods of distinguishing them from one another;
examine bronchophony.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: In vesicular breathing the ratio of the inspiratory to the expiratory phase is **3:1** (inspiration long and loud, expiration short and soft). It is best heard over the anterior lower parts of the chest, the axillary regions and the infrascapular regions (where the layer of lung tissue is thickest).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: In a healthy person, bronchial breathing is heard only **over the larynx and trachea and in the region of the manubrium**, and behind in the interscapular region at the level of the **VII cervical to the III–IV thoracic vertebrae**. If bronchial breathing is heard over other parts of the chest, it is considered **pathological**.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In obstructive atelectasis (a bronchus blocked by a tumor), bronchial breathing is **not heard** even though the lung tissue is dense, because there is no airflow — breath sounds are markedly diminished or absent. In compression atelectasis (when fluid compresses the lung), bronchial patency is preserved, so soft bronchial breathing is heard over the upper border of the fluid.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Three tests distinguish the three sounds: **“Cough — Pressure — Sham breathing”**. If the sound changes after coughing, it is **rales**; if it increases when pressing with the stethoscope and is heard even during sham breathing, it is a **pleural friction rub**; if it occurs only at the end of inspiration and does not change after coughing, it is **crepitation**.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In modern English-language textbooks (ATS/ERS nomenclature, Bates, Macleod) the terms are different: **crackles** are divided into fine and coarse types and cover moist rales and crepitation together; **wheezes** are high-pitched dry rales; **rhonchi** are low-pitched dry rales; **stridor** is a loud inspiratory sound in narrowing of the upper airways. The “crepitation” of the Russian and Uzbek school roughly corresponds to the English fine end-inspiratory crackles. Keep this difference in mind when reading the literature.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: “Artifact” sounds on auscultation: rubbing of the stethoscope head against clothing or hair (resembles crepitation), muscle tremor (in a cold room, with fear — a low rumble), the patient swallowing, the tubes touching each other, intestinal peristalsis (in the left lower region). If a doubtful sound is detected, press the stethoscope more firmly, ask the patient not to move and listen again.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The easiest way to distinguish bronchial from vesicular breathing is **the pause between the phases of respiration**: in bronchial breathing there is a short silence between inspiration and expiration, whereas in vesicular breathing there is no pause (inspiration passes without a break into expiration).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Vocal fremitus, bronchophony and egophony obey the same rule: **they are increased in consolidation and decreased in fluid, air, obstruction and emphysema**. All three confirm one another.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: On auscultation, always keep to the order **“Type — Intensity — Phases — Added sounds — Bronchophony”**: first the type of breathing, then its intensity, the ratio of the respiratory phases, the added sounds and, last of all, bronchophony.

sections.title: 1. General information on auscultation

blocks.text: **Auscultation** (Latin auscultatio — listening) is a method of assessing the state of organs by listening to the sounds produced during their activity.

**Direct auscultation** (with the ear placed directly on the body) has been known since the time of Hippocrates. **Indirect auscultation** was discovered in 1816 by the French physician **René Laennec**: while examining a young woman, he rolled a sheet of paper into a tube, placed it on her chest and found that the heart sounds were clearly audible. He then made a wooden stethoscope and in 1819 published the book “On Mediate Auscultation”, in which many terms still in use today (rales, bronchial breathing, egophony) were described.

sections.title: 2. General rules of auscultation

items: The room should be warm and quiet.
The patient stands or sits, undressed to the waist; severely ill patients are examined lying down, being turned onto each side in turn.
The stethoscope head is applied to the skin closely but without excessive pressure; it must not be placed over clothing (friction sounds are produced).
The stethoscope head should be warm (a cold head causes muscle tremor).
Thick chest hair produces a crackling that resembles added sounds; it can be moistened or greased.
The patient breathes through the mouth, somewhat deeply and evenly.
At least 2–3 respiratory cycles are listened to at each point.
Symmetrical points are compared, and the examination follows the points of comparative percussion.
The main breath sound is assessed first, and then the added sounds.

blocks.text: Points of auscultation of the lungs

Auscultation is performed at the points where comparative percussion was carried out: **in front** — the supraclavicular fossae and the I–II (on the right, down to the III–IV) intercostal spaces along the midclavicular line; **from the side** — the axillary fossae and the IV–VI intercostal spaces along the mid-axillary line; **behind** — the suprascapular, interscapular (three points) and infrascapular regions.

sections.title: 3. The main breath sounds

blocks.text: 3.1. Vesicular (alveolar) breathing

**Mechanism of production:** during inspiration, air enters the alveoli and rapidly tenses their walls — the vibrations of the walls of millions of alveoli add up to produce vesicular breathing. At the beginning of expiration it continues briefly owing to the relaxation of the alveolar walls.

**Features:** a soft, blowing sound, resembling the sound produced when saying the letter “f” or drawing air inward. It is heard **throughout** inspiration and only during the **first third** of expiration.

parts.text: In vesicular breathing the ratio of the inspiratory to the expiratory phase is **3:1** (inspiration long and loud, expiration short and soft). It is best heard over the anterior lower parts of the chest, the axillary regions and the infrascapular regions (where the layer of lung tissue is thickest).

blocks.title: Table 6.2. Changes of vesicular breathing

Type
Causes
rows: In children (“puerile” breathing), in thin people, during physical exertion
In the unaffected lung when the other lung does not take part in breathing (pleurisy, pneumothorax)
Inflammation and unevenness of the bronchial mucosa (bronchitis, focal pneumonia): expiration is also loud and prolonged, and the sound is coarse
Obesity, strong development of the chest wall muscles

Pathological — decreased entry of air into the alveoli
The onset and resolution stage of lobar pneumonia (swollen alveolar walls), bronchial obstruction, the onset of atelectasis
Fluid or air in the pleural cavity, pleural thickening
Rib fracture, dry pleurisy (pain), diaphragmatic paralysis, weakness

Uneven narrowing of the small bronchi, uneven contraction of the respiratory muscles (chilling, nervousness)

blocks.text: 3.2. Bronchial (laryngotracheal) breathing

**Mechanism of production:** when air passes through the narrow glottis in the larynx, the airflow becomes turbulent and a sound is produced. Because the glottis is narrower during expiration, the expiratory phase of bronchial breathing is louder, harsher and longer.
**Features:** harsh and loud, resembling the sound made when saying the letter “h”; it is heard **throughout** inspiration and expiration, and the expiratory phase is stronger and longer.

parts.text: In a healthy person, bronchial breathing is heard only **over the larynx and trachea and in the region of the manubrium**, and behind in the interscapular region at the level of the **VII cervical to the III–IV thoracic vertebrae**. If bronchial breathing is heard over other parts of the chest, it is considered **pathological**.

blocks.text: **Pathological bronchial breathing** is heard when the lung tissue has come to conduct sound well.

blocks.title: Table 6.3. Types of pathological bronchial breathing
head: Type
Mechanism
Diseases
rows: The alveoli are airless, and the consolidated tissue conducts the laryngotracheal sound in the bronchi well to the chest wall
The hepatization stage of lobar pneumonia, pulmonary infarction, compression atelectasis
Resonance in a smooth-walled cavity more than 5–6 cm in diameter communicating with a bronchus; resembles the sound of blowing across the mouth of an empty bottle
A large cavern, an emptied abscess
Very loud, with a metallic ring
Narrowing of the trachea or a large bronchus, a loud sound

parts.text: In obstructive atelectasis (a bronchus blocked by a tumor), bronchial breathing is **not heard** even though the lung tissue is dense, because there is no airflow — breath sounds are markedly diminished or absent. In compression atelectasis (when fluid compresses the lung), bronchial patency is preserved, so soft bronchial breathing is heard over the upper border of the fluid.

blocks.text: 3.3. Mixed (bronchovesicular) breathing

It combines the features of vesicular and bronchial breathing: the inspiratory phase resembles vesicular and the expiratory phase bronchial breathing. It is heard when the lung tissue is consolidated in small foci, deep down or unevenly (focal pneumonia, tuberculous infiltrate, pneumosclerosis). In a healthy person it may also be heard over the right apex.

sections.title: 4. Added (adventitious) breath sounds

blocks.text: The added breath sounds include **rales** (dry and moist), **crepitation** and the **pleural friction rub**. They are heard against the background of the main breath sound and are always considered pathological.

blocks.label: Figure 6.5
blocks.caption: Classification of rales (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 41)

blocks.text: 4.1. Dry rales (rhonchi sicci)

**Mechanism:** narrowing of the bronchial lumen (mucosal edema, bronchospasm, viscous sputum) leads to acceleration and turbulence of the airflow; viscous sputum stretched like threads across the bronchial lumen vibrates in the airflow like a “string”.

blocks.title: Table 6.4. Types of dry rales
head: Type
Where they arise
Character
Diseases
rows: High, thin, like a whistle; most often during expiration

blocks.text: Characteristic features of dry rales: they are changeable — after coughing they may increase, decrease or change location; they are heard in both phases of respiration. In an attack of bronchial asthma, whistling rales are sometimes heard even at a distance (“distant wheezes”).
4.2. Moist rales (rhonchi humidi)
**Mechanism:** liquid secretions (sputum, blood, transudate) accumulate in the bronchial lumen; as air passes through them, bubbles form and burst — a sound “like blowing into water through a straw”.

blocks.title: Table 6.5. Types of moist rales
head: Classification
Type
Content
rows: By the caliber of the bronchus where they arise
In the small bronchi and bronchioles; short, numerous
In the large bronchi, the trachea and cavities (cavern, abscess); longer, low-pitched
The surrounding lung tissue is consolidated or there is cavity resonance — the sound is conducted well and heard “right under the ear”: pneumonia, cavern, abscess
The lung tissue is air-filled and the sound is damped, heard “from afar”: bronchitis, pulmonary congestion (heart failure), pulmonary edema

parts.text: **Consonating fine-bubbling moist rales** over a limited area are an important sign of focal pneumonia. Bilateral, symmetrical **nonconsonating fine-bubbling** rales in the lower parts of the lungs indicate congestion in the pulmonary circulation (left ventricular failure). In pulmonary edema, coarse-bubbling rales are heard at a distance, like a “boiling samovar”.

blocks.text: 4.3. Crepitation (crepitatio)

**Mechanism:** when there is a sticky secretion (exudate) on the inner surface of the alveoli, the alveolar walls stick together during expiration; at the **very end** of a deep inspiration, air enters and separates them simultaneously — a faint “crackling” is heard. This sound is likened to rubbing a lock of hair between the fingers next to the ear or to throwing salt onto a fire.
**Causes:** stages I (crepitatio indux) and III (crepitatio redux) of lobar pneumonia, pulmonary infarction, pulmonary congestion and the onset of pulmonary edema, fibrosing alveolitis.
4.4. Pleural friction rub (frictio pleurae)

**Mechanism:** normally the smooth, moist layers of the pleura slide silently during breathing. In inflammation of the pleura (fibrin deposits), its drying (dehydration, uremia), tumors and tuberculous tubercles, the surfaces of the layers become rough — and a sound is produced when they rub together. This sound resembles the crunching of snow underfoot or the creaking of new leather.

**Causes:** dry (fibrinous) pleurisy, lobar pneumonia (the pleura is also involved), pulmonary infarction, pleural tumors and tuberculosis, uremia, severe dehydration. In exudative pleurisy, it reappears during the period of fluid resorption.

The pleural friction rub is most often heard **in the lower part of the axillary region** (where the lung moves most during breathing). When the pleura next to the heart is inflamed, a **pleuropericardial rub** related to both the heartbeat and breathing is heard.

parts.text: Three tests distinguish the three sounds: **“Cough — Pressure — Sham breathing”**. If the sound changes after coughing, it is **rales**; if it increases when pressing with the stethoscope and is heard even during sham breathing, it is a **pleural friction rub**; if it occurs only at the end of inspiration and does not change after coughing, it is **crepitation**.

In modern English-language textbooks (ATS/ERS nomenclature, Bates, Macleod) the terms are different: **crackles** are divided into fine and coarse types and cover moist rales and crepitation together; **wheezes** are high-pitched dry rales; **rhonchi** are low-pitched dry rales; **stridor** is a loud inspiratory sound in narrowing of the upper airways. The “crepitation” of the Russian and Uzbek school roughly corresponds to the English fine end-inspiratory crackles. Keep this difference in mind when reading the literature.

sections.title: 6. Bronchophony

blocks.text: **Bronchophony** is the audibility with a stethoscope, over the chest wall, of words whispered by the patient. It has the same mechanism as vocal fremitus but is more sensitive in detecting smaller foci.

**Method:** the stethoscope is placed on symmetrical points, and the patient is asked to whisper words containing hissing sounds (“cup of tea”, “sixty-six”, “hush”). Normally the words are not heard clearly; only an indistinct murmur is perceived.

**Increased bronchophony** (the words are heard clearly) — in consolidation of the lung tissue and in a cavity communicating with a bronchus (the same conditions as increased vocal fremitus). **Decreased** — fluid or air in the pleural cavity, obstructive atelectasis, emphysema.

parts.text: English-language textbooks distinguish two types of bronchophony: **whispered pectoriloquy** — clear audibility of whispered words, and **egophony** — the sound “ee” heard like “ay”, resembling the bleating of a goat; egophony is observed at the upper border of fluid (over the compressed lung) and in consolidation.

sections.title: 7. Structure and correct use of the phonendoscope

blocks.text: A modern stethophonendoscope consists of the following parts: **earpieces** (soft; they must fit snugly into the ear canal), **ear tubes** (they should be angled forward, toward the nose, because the external ear canal is directed forward), **flexible tubing** (50–70 cm long; long tubing attenuates the sound) and the **chest piece** (diaphragm and bell).

Diaphragm

parts.text: “Artifact” sounds on auscultation: rubbing of the stethoscope head against clothing or hair (resembles crepitation), muscle tremor (in a cold room, with fear — a low rumble), the patient swallowing, the tubes touching each other, intestinal peristalsis (in the left lower region). If a doubtful sound is detected, press the stethoscope more firmly, ask the patient not to move and listen again.

parts.text: The easiest way to distinguish bronchial from vesicular breathing is **the pause between the phases of respiration**: in bronchial breathing there is a short silence between inspiration and expiration, whereas in vesicular breathing there is no pause (inspiration passes without a break into expiration).

blocks.text: 8.1. Conditions for the occurrence of pathological bronchial breathing
For bronchial breathing to be heard over the chest wall, three conditions must be met:

items: the lung tissue must be **consolidated** (airless);
the consolidated area must be connected with a **patent bronchus**;
the area of consolidation must be **close** to the chest wall and sufficiently **large**.

blocks.text: That is why bronchial breathing is rarely heard in focal pneumonia (small, deep foci), whereas in lobar pneumonia it is always heard.

sections.title: 9. Modern classification and mechanisms of the added sounds

blocks.text: 9.1. Timing of crackles

blocks.title: Table 6.9. Crackles and their timing
head: Type
Phase of respiration
Mechanism

parts.text: The **late inspiratory fine crackles** heard over the basal areas in pulmonary fibrosis resemble the “Velcro” sound (the sound of a strip of Velcro being pulled apart). They do not change after coughing and often occur together with **clubbing**. In Russian-language textbooks this sound is described as “crepitation” or “consonating fine-bubbling rales”.

blocks.text: 9.2. Wheezes and stridor

items: **Polyphonic** wheezes (of different pitches at the same time) — diffuse narrowing of many bronchi (bronchial asthma, COPD).
**Monophonic** (a single pitch, always in the same place) — local narrowing of a single bronchus (tumor, foreign body). If such a wheeze does not change after coughing, bronchoscopy is needed.

**Stridor** is a loud, harsh sound heard at a distance, mainly **during inspiration**, in narrowing of the upper airways (larynx, trachea). It is a life-threatening sign: angioedema, foreign body, laryngeal tumor, epiglottitis, false croup.

blocks.text: 9.3. Other added sounds

items: **Pleuropericardial rub** — a sound related to the heartbeat and to breathing when the pleura next to the heart is inflamed; it diminishes when the breath is held.
**“Falling drop” sound** — a resonant dripping sound heard when the patient changes position in a large cavity containing air and fluid (hydropneumothorax, a large cavern).
**Hippocratic succussion splash** — heard in hydropneumothorax when the patient is shaken by the shoulders.
**“Mediastinal crunch”** (Hamman’s sign) — a crunching sound heard in time with the heartbeat in mediastinal emphysema.

parts.text: Vocal fremitus, bronchophony and egophony obey the same rule: **they are increased in consolidation and decreased in fluid, air, obstruction and emphysema**. All three confirm one another.

sections.title: 11. Points of auscultation on the anterior surface and special methods

blocks.label: Figure 6.8
blocks.caption: Points of auscultation of the lungs from the front (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 38)

blocks.text: Special methods:

items: **Listening after a forced cough** — to detect changes in rales (bronchial secretions) and to “awaken” latent crepitation.
**Deep breathing and forced expiration** — to detect latent bronchial obstruction (wheezes).
**Listening with the patient turned onto the side** — to examine the lower posterior regions in bedridden patients (hypostatic pneumonia, congestion).

parts.text: In modern practice, **lung ultrasound** is becoming widespread as a rapid bedside method: B-lines indicate pulmonary edema and the interstitial syndrome, the absence of the “lung sliding” sign indicates pneumothorax, and consolidation indicates pneumonia. However, it does not replace auscultation but complements it.

sections.title: 12. Standard form for recording auscultatory findings

blocks.text: The result of auscultation is recorded in the following order:

items: The type and intensity of the main breath sound (vesicular, diminished, increased, harsh, bronchial, mixed, amphoric).
The ratio of the respiratory phases (whether expiration is prolonged or not).

Added sounds: type (dry — whistling or humming; moist — fine-, medium- or coarse-bubbling, consonating or nonconsonating; crepitation; pleural friction rub), amount (isolated, numerous), location, phase of respiration, change after coughing.

Bronchophony. **Example:** “Vesicular breathing over the upper parts of the lungs. On the right in the infrascapular region, below the VII rib, breath sounds are diminished; in this area numerous consonating fine-bubbling moist rales are heard at the end of inspiration, unchanged after coughing. Bronchophony is increased in the right infrascapular region.”

sections.title: 13. Dynamics of the auscultatory picture in various diseases

blocks.text: Auscultatory signs change during the course of a disease; observing them daily helps to assess the effectiveness of treatment.

blocks.title: Table 6.11. Auscultation in the dynamics of diseases
head: Disease
Onset
Height of the disease
Recovery period
rows: Diminished vesicular breathing, crepitation (indux), pleural friction rub
Crepitation (redux), consonating moist rales, vesicular breathing returns
After rupture, amphoric breathing and coarse-bubbling rales
The rales decrease and breath sounds are restored
Crepitation and fine rales in the lower parts

The rales decrease from below upward

parts.text: In pulmonary edema, **how high** the rales extend indicates the severity of the edema: only in the lower parts — initial; up to the angle of the scapula — moderate; over the whole lung — severe (alveolar edema). This is a very convenient indicator for following the effect of treatment.

sections.title: 14. Changes in breath sounds related to complications

items: **When pleurisy complicates pneumonia** — a pleural friction rub appears; later, if fluid accumulates, breath sounds disappear over this area.
**Transformation of pneumonia into an abscess** — amphoric breathing in place of bronchial breathing, numerous coarse-bubbling rales; the sputum increases.
**Development of pneumothorax** (for example, in a patient with COPD) — breath sounds suddenly disappear on one side.
**Atelectasis** (blockage by sputum) — breath sounds suddenly disappear; they may return after coughing and expectoration.

sections.title: 15. Typical errors in describing the results of auscultation in the case history

items: Writing “breathing vesicular, no rales” without listening to the lower posterior regions.
Not distinguishing crepitation from moist rales (not examining after coughing).
Not describing the rales: type, caliber, resonance, amount, location.
Confusing a pleural friction rub with a pericardial rub — not examining with the breath held.
Confusing bronchial breathing with “harsh breathing” (in bronchial breathing the expiratory phase is long and loud, and there is a pause).

parts.text: On auscultation, always keep to the order **“Type — Intensity — Phases — Added sounds — Bronchophony”**: first the type of breathing, then its intensity, the ratio of the respiratory phases, the added sounds and, last of all, bronchophony.

blocks.text: Sample case history entry

**On auscultation**, bronchial breathing is heard over the right infrascapular region of the lung, and in this area crepitation at the end of inspiration and a pleural friction rub are detected. Bronchophony is increased in the right infrascapular region. Over the other areas, vesicular breathing without added sounds.

**Conclusion:** the syndrome of consolidation of the lung tissue in the lower lobe of the right lung with inflammatory involvement of the pleura — characteristic of right-sided lower lobe lobar pneumonia.

skills.title: Skill: auscultation of the lungs

items: Check the stethophonendoscope, warm the chest piece and put on the earpieces facing forward (matching the ear canals).
Undress the patient to the waist, standing or sitting; ask him or her to breathe evenly and somewhat deeply through the mouth.
Begin in front: the supraclavicular fossae, the I–II intercostal spaces; listen to 2–3 respiratory cycles at each point and compare with the symmetrical point.
Listen over the lateral regions: the patient places the hands on the head; from the axillary fossae downward.
Listen over the posterior regions: the patient crosses the arms in front of the chest; the suprascapular, interscapular and infrascapular regions.
At each point, assess first the main breath sound (type, intensity, ratio of the phases) and then the added sounds.
If an added sound is detected, perform the distinguishing tests: have the patient cough, press with the stethoscope, perform the sham-breathing test.
Record the result in the case history.

skills.title: Skill: examining bronchophony

items: Place the stethoscope on symmetrical points in turn.
Ask the patient to whisper “cup of tea” or “sixty-six”.
Compare the clarity of the words on the two sides.
Interpret the result: normal, increased or decreased.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 30-year-old patient suddenly developed a choking attack. He is sitting leaning forward with his hands propped on the edge of a table. On auscultation, harsh breathing is heard over the whole lung with markedly prolonged expiration and numerous whistling dry rales in both phases; they are also heard at a distance.
cases.ask: Interpret the auscultatory findings. Where and by what mechanism are the rales produced?
cases.answer: Prolonged expiration and whistling (high-pitched) dry rales are characteristic of obstruction of the small bronchi (bronchospasm, mucosal edema, viscous sputum). The airflow through the narrowed bronchi accelerates and becomes turbulent, producing a high-frequency sound. The clinical picture corresponds to an attack of bronchial asthma.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: On auscultation of a 70-year-old patient, a moist sound was heard over the right infrascapular region. The sound did not change after the patient coughed; it is heard only at the end of a deep inspiration as a uniform fine crackling and does not increase on pressing with the stethoscope.
cases.ask: Which added sound is this? How is it produced, and in which conditions is it heard?
cases.answer: Crepitation. It is produced by the simultaneous separation, at the end of inspiration, of alveoli that stuck together during expiration because of exudate adhering to the alveolar walls. Its not changing after coughing distinguishes it from moist rales, and its not increasing under pressure of the stethoscope and its being heard only at the end of inspiration distinguish it from the pleural friction rub. The onset or resolution stage of lobar pneumonia, pulmonary congestion and alveolitis should be considered.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 45-year-old patient has stabbing pain on the left that increases on deep inspiration. In the lower part of the left axillary region, a sound resembling the crunching of snow underfoot is heard in both phases of respiration; it increases on pressing with the stethoscope and does not change after coughing.
cases.ask: Which sound has been detected? What is its cause, and what is the confirmatory test?
cases.answer: A pleural friction rub — characteristic of dry (fibrinous) pleurisy. To confirm it, the “sham breathing” test is performed: the patient closes the mouth and nose and makes breathing movements with the abdominal wall — even without airflow, the pleural layers move and the rub is heard (whereas rales are not). The pain also confirms pleural involvement.

topics.title: The syndrome of impaired bronchial patency. Acute and chronic bronchitis. The syndrome of increased air content of the lung tissue. Bronchial asthma. Pulmonary emphysema

goals.text: To teach the student the pathogenesis and clinical signs of the syndromes of bronchial obstruction and increased air content of the lung tissue, the symptomatology of acute and chronic bronchitis, bronchial asthma and pulmonary emphysema, as well as how to examine patients with obstructive diseases and interpret the results of spirometry and peak flowmetry.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the main mechanisms of bronchial obstruction (reversible and irreversible components);
the physical signs of the syndromes of bronchial obstruction and emphysema;
the definition, causes and clinical signs of acute and chronic bronchitis;
the definition, the periods of an attack, and the physical and laboratory signs of bronchial asthma, and status asthmaticus;
the main signs of COPD and pulmonary emphysema;
the main parameters and normal values of spirometry and peak flowmetry (GINA 2025, GOLD 2026).

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: take the history of and physically examine a patient with an obstructive disease;
identify the syndromes of bronchial obstruction and emphysema on the basis of physical signs;
perform peak flowmetry and interpret the result;
interpret the conclusion of a spirogram.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The small bronchi **less than 2 mm** in diameter, which have no cartilaginous skeleton, are held open by the elastic recoil of the lung tissue. When elasticity is lost in emphysema, they collapse and close during expiration (**expiratory collapse**) — air is “trapped” in the alveoli.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In acute bronchitis the auscultatory findings are diffuse and symmetrical. If **consonating** fine-bubbling moist rales or crepitation appear over a limited area, this is a sign not of bronchitis but of pneumonia — radiography is mandatory.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: By the WHO criterion, chronic bronchitis is a productive cough **for at least 3 months a year in at least 2 consecutive years**, with other causes of cough (tuberculosis, bronchiectasis, tumor and others) excluded.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: According to GOLD 2026, spirometry is mandatory for the diagnosis of COPD: the **post-bronchodilator FEV~1~/FVC ratio must be less than 0.70**. The severity of obstruction is assessed by FEV1 as a percentage of the predicted value.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Older textbooks (including the textbook used here) grouped chronic bronchitis, bronchial asthma, bronchiectasis and emphysema together as “chronic obstructive lung diseases”. In modern classifications, **bronchial asthma and bronchiectasis are separate diseases**, and COPD is only a condition with persistent (not fully reversible) airflow limitation.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: For asthmatic sputum, **“E + C + C”**: **E**osinophils, **C**urschmann spirals, **C**harcot–Leyden crystals — “Eosinophil, Curschmann, Charcot”.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: GINA 2025 uses the concepts of a **severe and a life-threatening exacerbation** instead of the term “status asthmaticus”. Signs of a threat to life: impaired consciousness (drowsiness), a **“silent chest”**, cyanosis, bradycardia or hypotension, SpO2 below 90 %, PEF less than 25–50 % of the predicted value. Such a patient is transferred urgently to the intensive care unit.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The **“traffic light” system** of asthma control by PEF: **green zone** — PEF more than 80 % of the personal best (controlled); **yellow zone** — 50–80 % (caution, treatment needs to be stepped up); **red zone** — less than 50 % (a dangerous condition, urgent help).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Number of “yes” answers: **0 — well controlled**, **1–2 — partly controlled**, **3–4 — uncontrolled asthma**. Together with control, future risk factors (exacerbations, low FEV1, smoking, eosinophilia) are also assessed.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The **diurnal variability** of PEF = (highest PEF during the day − lowest PEF) / their mean × 100 %. If it averages **more than 10 %** over two weeks (13 % in children), it confirms the diagnosis of bronchial asthma.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The main principle of GINA 2025: in adults and adolescents, treating asthma **with short-acting beta~2~-agonists alone is not recommended**; every patient receives ICS-containing treatment (the preferred track is low-dose budesonide-formoterol “as needed” and as maintenance treatment). Treatment with salbutamol alone increases the risk of severe exacerbations and death.

sections.title: 1. The syndrome of impaired bronchial patency (bronchial obstruction)

blocks.text: **Bronchial obstruction** is an increase in resistance to airflow and impaired ventilation of the lungs as a result of narrowing of the bronchial lumen. Clinically it is manifested mainly by expiratory dyspnea and dry rales.

blocks.title: Table 7.1. Mechanisms of bronchial obstruction
head: Component
Mechanism
Example
rows: Spasm of the bronchial smooth muscle
Inflammatory edema and infiltration of the mucosa
Fibrosis and deformity of the bronchial wall
Expiratory collapse of the small bronchi (when lung elasticity is lost)
Blockage of the bronchial lumen by a tumor or foreign body (local obstruction)

parts.text: The small bronchi **less than 2 mm** in diameter, which have no cartilaginous skeleton, are held open by the elastic recoil of the lung tissue. When elasticity is lost in emphysema, they collapse and close during expiration (**expiratory collapse**) — air is “trapped” in the alveoli.

blocks.text: Signs of the syndrome of bronchial obstruction

blocks.title: Table 7.2. Signs of the syndrome of bronchial obstruction (bronchospasm)
head: Method of examination
Signs
rows: Expiratory dyspnea or choking attacks, cough with viscous, hard-to-expectorate sputum, a feeling of “tightness” in the chest

Forced position (sitting propped on the hands), use of the accessory muscles, prolonged expiration, exhalation through pursed lips, diffuse cyanosis, the neck veins distend during expiration; the chest is “in the position of inspiration”
Vocal fremitus symmetrically decreased, resistance increased
Hyperresonant (box-like) note, lower borders lowered, mobility decreased
Harsh or diminished vesicular breathing, prolonged expiration, numerous dry whistling rales (especially during expiration)
FEV1, the Tiffeneau index (FEV1/FVC) and PEF decreased

parts.text: **The forced expiratory time test** is a simple bedside test: the patient takes a deep breath and breathes out as fast and as completely as possible with the mouth open, while the physician places the stethoscope over the trachea and measures the time. Normally expiration takes **less than 4 seconds**; more than 6 seconds indicates bronchial obstruction.

sections.title: 2. Acute bronchitis

blocks.text: **Acute bronchitis** is an acute diffuse inflammation of the bronchial mucosa. It most often develops as a manifestation of acute respiratory viral infections and accounts for 20–25 percent of acute nonspecific respiratory diseases.

**Causes:** viruses (respiratory syncytial virus, rhinoviruses, adenoviruses, influenza), bacteria (pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae), physical and chemical factors (cold air, dust, acid and alkali vapors). Predisposing factors: chilling, smoking, alcohol, foci of infection in the nasopharynx.

**Clinical picture:** the disease often begins with a runny nose, low-grade fever and weakness. A scratchy feeling behind the sternum and a dry or scantily productive cough appear; after 2–3 days the cough loosens and mucoid or mucopurulent sputum is produced. In the uncomplicated course there is no dyspnea; its appearance indicates involvement of the small bronchi and bronchioles (bronchiolitis).
**Physical signs:** a clear lung note on percussion; on auscultation, harsh breathing, dry (humming and whistling) rales and, when the sputum increases, nonconsonating moist rales.
**Laboratory and X-ray:** no changes in the blood, or mild leukocytosis and a raised ESR (15–20 mm/h); no changes on X-ray, or an accentuated lung pattern.

**Course:** usually 10–14 days, ending in complete recovery. The most common complication is focal pneumonia. Fever lasting more than 3–4 days and a sharp rise in leukocytosis indicate that pneumonia has developed.

parts.text: In acute bronchitis the auscultatory findings are diffuse and symmetrical. If **consonating** fine-bubbling moist rales or crepitation appear over a limited area, this is a sign not of bronchitis but of pneumonia — radiography is mandatory.

sections.title: 3. Chronic bronchitis

blocks.text: **Chronic bronchitis** is a diffuse, long-standing inflammation of the bronchi accompanied by hypersecretion of mucus and impaired drainage function.

parts.text: By the WHO criterion, chronic bronchitis is a productive cough **for at least 3 months a year in at least 2 consecutive years**, with other causes of cough (tuberculosis, bronchiectasis, tumor and others) excluded.

blocks.text: **Causes:** tobacco smoking (the main cause in about 80 percent of patients), occupational factors (cotton, coal and cement dust, chemical vapors), air pollution, recurrent respiratory infections, difficulty breathing through the nose.
**Classification:** by the nature of the exudate — catarrhal and purulent; by external respiratory function — obstructive and nonobstructive; by the course — phases of exacerbation and remission.

**Clinical picture:** the main sign is **cough**. At first it occurs in the morning after waking, with a small amount of sputum (the “smoker’s cough”); it gets worse in the cold, damp season. Later the sputum becomes mucopurulent and purulent. When obstruction and emphysema develop, **exertional dyspnea** appears and gradually increases.

**Physical signs:** in the uncomplicated course there are no changes on percussion; on auscultation, harsh breathing, dry rales and nonconsonating moist rales. In the obstructive form, prolonged expiration and wheezes; when emphysema develops, its signs appear.
**Complications:** pulmonary emphysema, respiratory failure, pulmonary hypertension and chronic cor pulmonale, pneumonia, bronchiectasis.

sections.title: 4. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)

blocks.text: In current international practice, chronic obstructive bronchitis and emphysema are considered within a single disease — **COPD**.

parts.text: According to GOLD 2026, spirometry is mandatory for the diagnosis of COPD: the **post-bronchodilator FEV~1~/FVC ratio must be less than 0.70**. The severity of obstruction is assessed by FEV1 as a percentage of the predicted value.

blocks.title: Table 7.3. Severity of airflow limitation in COPD (GOLD, when FEV1/FVC is less than 0.70)
head: Grade
Definition
FEV1, % of predicted

blocks.text: Patients are divided into groups **A, B and E** according to their symptoms (mMRC, CAT questionnaire) and the risk of exacerbations. In GOLD 2026, even a single moderate or severe exacerbation is assessed as a factor increasing the risk of further exacerbations.

parts.text: Older textbooks (including the textbook used here) grouped chronic bronchitis, bronchial asthma, bronchiectasis and emphysema together as “chronic obstructive lung diseases”. In modern classifications, **bronchial asthma and bronchiectasis are separate diseases**, and COPD is only a condition with persistent (not fully reversible) airflow limitation.

sections.title: 5. Bronchial asthma

blocks.text: **Bronchial asthma** is a heterogeneous disease with chronic inflammation of the airways. It is characterized by respiratory symptoms that vary over time and in intensity (wheezing, dyspnea, chest tightness, cough) and by **variable expiratory airflow** (GINA 2025).

**Etiology:** exogenous allergens (plant pollen, house dust and mites, particles from pets’ fur, molds, foods), infections, drugs (aspirin and other NSAIDs, beta-blockers), occupational factors, physical exertion, cold air, psychological factors, hereditary predisposition.

**Pathogenesis:** it is based on sensitization of the organism and an IgE-dependent immediate (type I) allergic reaction. When the allergen binds to IgE fixed on the mast cells of the bronchial mucosa, histamine, leukotrienes and other mediators are released, causing **bronchospasm, mucosal edema and hypersecretion**. Eosinophilic inflammation and bronchial hyperreactivity form the basis of the disease.

blocks.title: Table 7.4. Clinical forms (phenotypes) of bronchial asthma
head: Shape
Features
rows: Begins in childhood, a history of allergic diseases (eczema, rhinitis), eosinophilia in the blood and sputum, raised IgE
In adults, after infections, without an allergic history
The “aspirin triad”: choking attacks + aspirin intolerance + polyposis of the nose and paranasal sinuses
Attacks appear with physical exertion (running), especially in cold air
In adults, more often in women

blocks.text: Periods of an attack of bronchial asthma

items: **Prodromal period** — sneezing, watery nasal discharge, dry cough, a feeling of chest tightness.

**Period of the height of the attack** — choking: inspiration is short, expiration is long and difficult, wheezes are audible at a distance. The patient is in a forced position — sitting leaning forward with the hands propped on a table or the knees; the accessory muscles take part; the face is slightly puffy, there is cyanosis, and the neck veins are distended. The chest seems fixed in the position of maximal inspiration. On percussion, a hyperresonant (box-like) note, lowered lower borders and markedly decreased mobility; on auscultation, diminished vesicular breathing with prolonged expiration and numerous dry whistling rales. The absolute cardiac dullness is reduced; tachycardia.
**Period of resolution** — viscous, glassy sputum is expectorated, and the choking gradually passes.

blocks.text: Laboratory signs

**Eosinophilia** in the blood; in the sputum, **eosinophils**, **Curschmann spirals** (casts of the mucus of the small bronchi) and **Charcot–Leyden crystals** (crystals formed from the breakdown of eosinophils).

blocks.label: Figure 7.1
blocks.caption: Sputum microscopy: a — Curschmann spiral, Charcot–Leyden crystals and other elements (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 59)

parts.text: For asthmatic sputum, **“E + C + C”**: **E**osinophils, **C**urschmann spirals, **C**harcot–Leyden crystals — “Eosinophil, Curschmann, Charcot”.

blocks.text: Status asthmaticus and severe exacerbation

The textbook divides status asthmaticus (prolonged severe choking that does not respond to the usual bronchodilators) into three stages: **I** — relative compensation (resistance to bronchodilators, hypocapnia); **II** — decompensation, the **“silent chest”**: the bronchi are plugged with viscous mucus, the previously heard rales disappear, hypoxemia and hypercapnia; **III** — hypercapnic coma.

parts.text: GINA 2025 uses the concepts of a **severe and a life-threatening exacerbation** instead of the term “status asthmaticus”. Signs of a threat to life: impaired consciousness (drowsiness), a **“silent chest”**, cyanosis, bradycardia or hypotension, SpO2 below 90 %, PEF less than 25–50 % of the predicted value. Such a patient is transferred urgently to the intensive care unit.

blocks.text: Functional criteria in the diagnosis of bronchial asthma (GINA 2025)

blocks.title: Table 7.5. Tests confirming variable expiratory airflow
head: Test
Criterion in adults
rows: An increase in FEV1 of more than 12 % and more than 200 ml from baseline
Diurnal variability of PEF (2 weeks, twice a day)
An increase in FEV1 of more than 12 % and 200 ml
A fall in FEV1 of more than 10 % and 200 ml
A fall in FEV1 of 20 % (at a low dose)

sections.title: 6. The syndrome of increased air content of the lung tissue. Pulmonary emphysema

blocks.text: **Pulmonary emphysema** is a permanent enlargement of the air spaces distal to the terminal bronchioles with destruction of the alveolar walls. As a result, the lung tissue loses its elasticity, its air content increases and the gas-exchange surface decreases.
Causes and types:

items: **Primary (diffuse, panacinar)** — congenital alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency; in young people, in the lower parts of the lungs.
**Secondary (centriacinar)** — chronic obstructive bronchitis, long-standing bronchial asthma, smoking; more often in the upper lobes.
**Vicarious (compensatory)** — in the remaining part of the lung when part of it has been removed or is not functioning.
**Senile emphysema** — age-related decrease in elasticity.
**Bullous emphysema** — large air-filled blebs (bullae); if they rupture, pneumothorax.

blocks.title: Table 7.6. Signs of the syndrome of increased air content of the lung tissue (emphysema)
head: Method of examination
Signs
rows: Gradually increasing expiratory dyspnea (first on exertion, then at rest)

Barrel chest, bulging supraclavicular fossae, horizontal ribs, obtuse epigastric angle, decreased respiratory excursion of the chest, use of the accessory muscles; exhalation through pursed lips (the “puffer”); cyanosis; clubbing may be present
Increased resistance of the chest, vocal fremitus equally decreased on both sides

Hyperresonant (box-like) note; increased height of the apices, widened Krönig’s isthmus, lowered lower borders, markedly decreased mobility of the lower edge; the absolute cardiac dullness reduced or undetectable, the liver dullness shifted downward

Vesicular breathing equally diminished on both sides; when combined with obstructive bronchitis — prolonged expiration, dry rales; muffled heart sounds, accentuation of the II sound over the pulmonary artery
Increased transparency of the lung fields, a low, flattened, poorly mobile diaphragm, horizontal ribs, a “hanging” (drop-shaped) heart, widened retrosternal space
FEV1 and FEV1/FVC decreased; total lung capacity and residual volume increased

parts.text: Two classic phenotypes of patients with COPD are distinguished: the **“pink puffer”** (emphysematous type) — thin, very breathless, exhales through pursed lips, little cyanosis; the **“blue bloater”** (bronchitic type) — heavier, coughs a lot and produces sputum, with diffuse cyanosis and early right ventricular failure (edema). This division is conventional; most patients have mixed features.

sections.title: 7. Examination of external respiratory function: spirometry and peak flowmetry

blocks.text: **Peak flowmetry** is the measurement of the peak expiratory flow (PEF) with a special device (peak flow meter). Performed by the patient at home twice a day, it makes it possible to monitor the course of asthma and detect an exacerbation early.

sections.title: 8. Pathogenesis of bronchial asthma: a deeper analysis

blocks.text: Bronchial asthma is based on **chronic inflammation**, which persists even in the periods without symptoms. That is why the mainstay of treatment is not bronchodilators but **anti-inflammatory** agents (inhaled glucocorticosteroids).

blocks.title: Table 7.9. The main participants in inflammation in asthma
head: Cell or substance
Role
rows: Activated via IgE, they release histamine, leukotrienes and prostaglandin D2 — immediate bronchospasm
Major basic protein and cytotoxic proteins — damage to the epithelium; eosinophilia in the blood and sputum
IL-4 (IgE synthesis), IL-5 (eosinophils), IL-13 (mucus hypersecretion, hyperreactivity)
Powerful bronchoconstrictors (1000 times stronger than histamine), mucus secretion and edema

blocks.text: **Airway remodeling** — irreversible changes in the bronchial wall in long-untreated asthma: thickening of the basement membrane, smooth muscle hypertrophy, hyperplasia of the mucous glands, subepithelial fibrosis. As a result, the obstruction becomes partly irreversible.

**Early and late asthmatic reactions:** 10–20 minutes after exposure to the allergen comes the **early reaction** (bronchospasm lasting 1–2 hours), and after 4–8 hours the **late reaction** (eosinophilic inflammation, long-lasting, increasing hyperreactivity).

sections.title: 9. COPD: clinical forms, exacerbation and complications

blocks.text: **An exacerbation of COPD** is a worsening of dyspnea and/or cough with increased sputum within 14 days; its causes are most often viral and bacterial infections and air pollution. The **Anthonisen criteria** of exacerbation: increased dyspnea, increased sputum volume and purulent sputum; if all three signs are present, an antibiotic is indicated.
Complications of COPD:

items: **Chronic respiratory failure** — hypoxemia, secondary erythrocytosis;

**Pulmonary hypertension and chronic cor pulmonale** — alveolar hypoxia causes spasm of the pulmonary arterioles (the Euler–Liljestrand reflex); the right ventricle hypertrophies, and failure develops later;
spontaneous pneumothorax (rupture of bullae), pneumonias, an increased risk of lung cancer.

The right ventricle dilated and hypertrophied, the pulmonary artery pressure raised

sections.title: 10. Pathogenesis of pulmonary emphysema

blocks.text: The main theory of the development of emphysema is **an imbalance between proteases and antiproteases**. Under the influence of smoking and other irritants, neutrophils and macrophages accumulate in the lung and release **elastase** and other proteases, which destroy the elastic fibers in the alveolar walls. Normally this process is stopped by **alpha~1~-antitrypsin**. In its congenital deficiency or in smoking (the smoke inactivates the antiproteases), the alveolar walls are destroyed, and the alveoli merge into large air spaces.

As a result: the elastic recoil of the lung decreases → the small bronchi collapse during expiration (**expiratory collapse**, “air trapping”) → the residual volume and total lung capacity increase (**hyperinflation**) → the diaphragm flattens and works inefficiently → dyspnea increases; the gas-exchange surface and the capillaries decrease → diffusion is impaired.

parts.text: **Pursed-lip breathing** (“puffing”) is a useful technique that emphysema patients discover themselves: the resistance created at the mouth raises the pressure in the airways and prevents early collapse of the small bronchi. This technique is also taught in breathing exercises.

sections.title: 11. Instrumental methods of examining the respiratory organs

blocks.text: 11.1. Radiological examination

blocks.label: Figure 7.4
blocks.caption: Normal radiograph of the lungs (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 46)

blocks.label: Figure 7.5
blocks.caption: Pathological changes on a lung radiograph (same source, Fig. 46)

blocks.text: Chest radiography is performed in two views (frontal and lateral). The following are assessed: the transparency of the lung fields, the lung pattern, the hila, the position and sharpness of the outline of the diaphragm, the costophrenic sinuses, the mediastinum and the cardiac shadow. Common syndromes: **opacity** (pneumonia, atelectasis, fluid, tumor), **lucency** (cavity, pneumothorax, emphysema, bulla), **accentuation of the lung pattern** (bronchitis, congestion, interstitial diseases), **widening of the hila** (lymphadenopathy, pulmonary hypertension).

**Computed tomography (CT)** shows the lung tissue, bronchi and mediastinum layer by layer with high resolution; it is the main method for detecting bronchiectasis, interstitial diseases, small tumors and pulmonary embolism (CT angiography).
11.2. Bronchoscopy

blocks.label: Figure 7.7
blocks.caption: Diagram of bronchoscopy (same source, Fig. 50)

blocks.label: Figure 7.6
blocks.caption: Fiberoptic bronchoscope (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 49)

blocks.text: **Bronchoscopy** is the inspection of the trachea and bronchi with a flexible fiberoptic bronchoscope. Diagnostic purposes: detecting tumors and taking biopsies, finding the source of bleeding, detecting a foreign body, obtaining bronchoalveolar lavage. Therapeutic purposes: removing a foreign body and viscous sputum, sanitation of the bronchi (bronchiectasis, abscess), stopping bleeding.
11.3. Spirometry and peak flowmetry: practical aspects

blocks.label: Figure 7.9
blocks.caption: Computerized spirometer (same source, Fig. 52)

blocks.label: Figure 7.8
blocks.caption: Spirograph (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 51)

blocks.text: **Rules for performing spirometry:** short-acting bronchodilators are withheld for 4–6 hours and long-acting ones for 12–24 hours before the test; no smoking for 1 hour beforehand; the patient sits, with a nose clip; after a maximal deep inspiration, he or she breathes out through the mouthpiece as forcefully as possible for at least 6 seconds; at least 3 satisfactory attempts are made. **Bronchodilator test:** the test is repeated 15–20 minutes after inhalation of salbutamol 400 µg.

blocks.label: Figure 7.10
blocks.caption: Peak flow meter scale (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 55)

blocks.label: Figure 7.11
blocks.caption: Predicted values of PEF by age, sex and height (same source)

parts.text: The **diurnal variability** of PEF = (highest PEF during the day − lowest PEF) / their mean × 100 %. If it averages **more than 10 %** over two weeks (13 % in children), it confirms the diagnosis of bronchial asthma.

blocks.text: 11.4. Blood gases and other investigations

**Arterial blood gases:** PaO2 (normal 80–100 mm Hg), PaCO2 (35–45), pH (7.35–7.45). In hypoxemic (type I) respiratory failure, PaO2 is decreased and PaCO2 normal or low; in hypercapnic (type II) respiratory failure, PaCO2 is above 45 (severe COPD, a severe asthma attack, respiratory muscle fatigue).

**Allergological investigations:** skin tests (prick test), total and specific IgE in the blood, the blood eosinophil count; **FeNO** — fractional exhaled nitric oxide (an indicator of eosinophilic inflammation).

sections.title: 12. Principles of treating bronchial asthma and COPD (in brief)

blocks.text: Knowing the principles of treatment consolidates the student’s understanding of the pathogenesis of the disease.

parts.text: The main principle of GINA 2025: in adults and adolescents, treating asthma **with short-acting beta~2~-agonists alone is not recommended**; every patient receives ICS-containing treatment (the preferred track is low-dose budesonide-formoterol “as needed” and as maintenance treatment). Treatment with salbutamol alone increases the risk of severe exacerbations and death.

blocks.text: 12.1. Inhaler technique

The most common cause of treatment failure is **incorrect use** of the inhaler. For a metered-dose aerosol inhaler: shake → breathe out fully → close the lips around the mouthpiece → press the canister at the same time as starting a slow deep inspiration → hold the breath for 10 seconds → rinse the mouth after ICS (to prevent candidiasis). A **spacer** is recommended for children and the elderly.

sections.title: 13. Differential diagnosis of wheezing

blocks.text: “Not all wheezing is asthma” — this clinical rule is important.

sections.title: 14. When bronchiectasis, bronchial asthma and COPD coexist

blocks.text: In practice, diseases often coexist:

items: **Asthma–COPD overlap** — in an asthma patient who smokes, or in a COPD patient showing eosinophilia and high reversibility; according to the GINA and GOLD recommendations, such patients must be given ICS.
**COPD and bronchiectasis** — detected on CT; runs a course with frequent bacterial exacerbations and much purulent sputum.
**COPD and heart failure** — both cause dyspnea; echocardiography, NT-proBNP and spirometry are used together for the diagnosis.

sections.title: 15. Complications of pulmonary emphysema and bullae

blocks.text: **Bullae** are thin-walled air spaces more than 1 cm in diameter. Large bullae (more than a third of the lung field) compress the healthy tissue (the “vanishing lung” syndrome). Complications: **spontaneous pneumothorax** (rupture of a bulla — sudden severe dyspnea in a COPD patient) and infection. On physical examination, a tympanic note and markedly diminished breath sounds over a large bulla resemble pneumothorax; they are distinguished by CT.

blocks.text: Sample case history entry

The patient is in a forced position — sitting with the hands propped on the edge of the bed. Respiratory rate 26 per minute, expiration markedly prolonged, wheezes heard at a distance, the accessory muscles take part in breathing, diffuse cyanosis. The chest is emphysematous. Vocal fremitus is symmetrically decreased. On percussion, a hyperresonant (box-like) note; the lower borders of the lungs are lowered by one rib, mobility 2 cm. On auscultation, diminished vesicular breathing with prolonged expiration and numerous dry whistling rales over the whole lung. PEF 180 l/min (40 % of the predicted value).
**Conclusion:** the syndromes of bronchial obstruction and increased air content of the lung tissue — characteristic of a severe attack of bronchial asthma.

skills.title: Skill: performing peak flowmetry

items: Set the pointer of the peak flow meter to the beginning of the scale.
The patient stands or sits upright and holds the peak flow meter horizontally, with the fingers not touching the scale.
The patient takes a deep breath and closes the lips tightly around the mouthpiece.
He or she breathes out (blows) as hard and as fast as possible.
Record the result and return the pointer to the beginning.
Repeat the test 3 times and record the highest reading.
Compare the result with the predicted or personal best value and determine the zone.

skills.title: Skill: identifying the syndrome of bronchial obstruction by physical examination

items: Establish the complaints: type of dyspnea (expiratory), attacks, character of the sputum.
Inspect: position, respiratory rate and ratio of the respiratory phases, accessory muscles, cyanosis, shape of the chest.
Palpation: resistance and vocal fremitus.
Percussion: comparative (hyperresonant note) and topographic (borders, mobility).
Auscultation: prolonged expiration, dry rales.
Determine the forced expiratory time.
Draw a syndromic conclusion and plan spirometry and peak flowmetry.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 22-year-old female student complains of choking attacks at night in spring, when the apple trees are in blossom. She has had eczema since childhood, and her mother has pollinosis. During an attack the patient sits with her hands propped on the table, expiration is prolonged, and wheezes are heard at a distance. At the end of the attack a small amount of glassy, viscous sputum was expectorated. Blood eosinophils 12 %.
cases.ask: Which disease and which form of it can be considered? What is expected to be found in the sputum? Which functional test confirms the diagnosis?
cases.answer: Allergic (atopic) bronchial asthma — the seasonality, the atopic history (eczema, pollinosis in the family), the attacks of expiratory choking and the eosinophilia are characteristic of it. Eosinophils, Curschmann spirals and Charcot–Leyden crystals are expected in the sputum. The diagnosis is confirmed on spirometry by the bronchodilator test (an increase in FEV1 of more than 12 % and 200 ml) or by a diurnal variability of PEF of more than 10 %.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 64-year-old man has smoked a pack of cigarettes a day for 45 years. For 20 years he has been bothered by a morning productive cough and, over the last 5 years, by increasing dyspnea. On spirometry, the post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC is 0.58 and FEV1 is 42 % of the predicted value.
cases.ask: Calculate the smoking index. What is the diagnosis? Assess the degree of obstruction according to GOLD. What signs are expected on physical examination?
cases.answer: Smoking index 20 × 45 / 20 = 45 pack-years. FEV1/FVC less than 0.70 — the diagnosis of COPD is confirmed; FEV1 42 % — GOLD 3 (severe obstruction). On physical examination: an emphysematous chest, symmetrically decreased vocal fremitus, a hyperresonant (box-like) note, lowered lower borders and decreased mobility, diminished vesicular breathing with prolonged expiration, dry rales.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 35-year-old woman with bronchial asthma complains of choking that has lasted for 18 hours; salbutamol inhalations are not helping. The patient is drowsy, cannot speak, and has diffuse cyanosis. On auscultation, breath sounds are markedly diminished, and the previously heard rales are almost inaudible. SpO2 84 %.
cases.ask: Assess the condition. Is the disappearance of the rales a good or a bad sign?
cases.answer: This is a life-threatening severe asthma exacerbation (stage II of status asthmaticus in the old terminology). The disappearance of the rales — the “silent chest” — is not an improvement but a very dangerous sign showing that the bronchi are completely plugged with viscous mucus and ventilation has fallen sharply. Together with the drowsiness, cyanosis and an SpO2 below 90 %, it means the patient must be transferred immediately to the intensive care unit.
