topics.title: The syndrome of consolidation of the lung tissue. Lobar and focal pneumonia. The syndromes of fluid and air accumulation in the pleural cavity. Hydrothorax. Pneumothorax. Dry and exudative pleurisy

goals.text: To teach the student the pathogenesis and physical signs of the syndromes of consolidation of the lung tissue and of fluid and air accumulation in the pleural cavity, the symptomatology of lobar and focal pneumonia, dry and exudative pleurisy, hydrothorax and pneumothorax, and how to examine and interpret pleural fluid.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the causes and physical signs of the syndrome of consolidation of the lung tissue;
the stages of lobar pneumonia and the physical signs at each stage;
the differences between lobar and focal pneumonia, the CURB-65 score;
the syndrome of fluid accumulation in the pleural cavity, the Damoiseau line, and Garland’s and Rauchfuss–Grocco triangles;
the differences between a transudate and an exudate (Rivalta test, Light’s criteria);
the clinical signs of dry and exudative pleurisy;
the types of pneumothorax and the syndrome of air accumulation in the pleural cavity.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: identify and distinguish the syndromes of consolidation and of fluid and air accumulation by physical examination;
interpret the analysis of pleural fluid;
explain the steps of pleural puncture (demonstrate them on a manikin).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: If the bronchus of the consolidated area is blocked by a tumor or a foreign body (**obstructive atelectasis**), then even though the percussion note is dull, vocal fremitus, bronchophony and breath sounds are **decreased or absent**, bronchial breathing is not heard, and the mediastinum shifts to the affected side. It is very important to distinguish this condition from pneumonia (especially in elderly smokers — lung cancer).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The stages of lobar pneumonia: **“Crepitation — Bronchial — Crepitation”** (indux — hepatization — redux), and on percussion **“Dull-tympanic — Dull — Dull-tympanic”**.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: By CURB-65, **0–1 point** — outpatient treatment is possible; **2 points** — hospital admission is recommended; **3–5 points** — severe pneumonia, intensive care is likely. Where urea cannot be measured, the **CRB-65** variant is used.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In a **transudate** (hydrothorax), the fluid moves freely and its upper border is usually **horizontal**; the border also shifts when the patient changes position. In an **exudate**, because of adhesion of the pleural layers and fibrin, the border is **oblique** (the Damoiseau line) and depends little on position. This difference is relative; they are distinguished precisely by pleural puncture and fluid analysis.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Light’s criteria** (1972): the fluid is an **exudate** if **at least one** of the following is present: 1) the ratio of pleural fluid protein to serum protein is **more than 0.5**; 2) the ratio of fluid LDH to serum LDH is **more than 0.6**; 3) the fluid LDH is **more than 2/3** of the upper limit of normal for serum LDH.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The dynamics of pleurisy: **“The pain goes — the dyspnea comes”** — when dry pleurisy turns into exudative pleurisy, the fluid separates the pleural layers and the pain lessens, but the lung is compressed and the dyspnea increases.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Usually **no more than 1–1.5 liters** of fluid are removed in a single procedure: rapid removal of a large amount of fluid may lead to an abrupt mediastinal shift, collapse and “re-expansion” pulmonary edema. The fluid obtained is sent for physicochemical, cytological and bacteriological examination.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The term “atypical” does not mean a mild or unusual course of pneumonia but refers to the intracellular pathogens **insensitive to the usual antibiotics (beta-lactams)** (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila, Legionella). Macrolides or respiratory fluoroquinolones are used for them.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The rule of mediastinal shift: **“Volume added — it moves away, volume lost — it is pulled toward”**. Fluid, air or a large tumor in the pleura (volume added) — the mediastinum shifts to the **healthy** side; obstructive and contraction atelectasis, pneumonectomy (volume lost) — to the **affected** side.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The most common cause of a transudate is **heart failure** (often bilateral or right-sided), and of an exudate, **pneumonia, tumor and tuberculosis**. A unilateral, large, rapidly reaccumulating hemorrhagic exudate raises suspicion of a **tumor** first of all.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Signs of tension pneumothorax: severe dyspnea and cyanosis, tachycardia, **hypotension**, distended neck veins, deviation of the trachea to the **healthy** side, a tympanic note and absent breath sounds on the affected side. This condition requires urgent **needle decompression** without waiting for an X-ray (the II intercostal space in the midclavicular line or the IV–V space in the anterior axillary line).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: If there are clinical signs but no infiltrate is found on X-ray (the initial stage, dehydration, neutropenia, a very small focus), pneumonia is considered “probable”, and the X-ray is repeated after 24–48 hours or CT is performed. Conversely, an infiltrate on X-ray is not always pneumonia: it must be distinguished from pulmonary infarction, tumor, tuberculosis and eosinophilic infiltrate.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The **“4C”** order of pleural fluid analysis: **C**olor (appearance), **C**hemistry (Rivalta test and protein — transudate or exudate), **C**ells (neutrophils, lymphocytes, eosinophils, atypical cells), **C**ulture (microbiology: bacteria, tuberculosis).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The key to distinguishing the three syndromes is **vocal fremitus**: it is **increased in consolidation and decreased in fluid and air**. Fluid and air, in turn, are distinguished by **percussion**: fluid — dull, air — tympanic.

sections.title: 1. The syndrome of consolidation of the lung tissue

blocks.text: **Consolidation of the lung tissue** is the loss of air from the lung as a result of the filling of the alveoli with exudate (inflammation), transudate, blood, tumor or connective tissue, or their collapse.
**Causes:** pneumonia (lobar — by lobe, focal — small foci), pulmonary infarction, tuberculous infiltrate, lung tumor, compression atelectasis, pneumosclerosis, pulmonary edema.

It is very important to distinguish this condition from pneumonia (especially in elderly smokers — lung cancer).

sections.title: 2. Pneumonias: general information

blocks.text: **Pneumonia** is an acute infectious (mainly bacterial) inflammation of the respiratory parts of the lung, accompanied by exudation into the alveoli and confirmed radiologically.

blocks.text: Classic propaedeutics textbooks distinguish, on morphological and clinical grounds, **lobar** and **focal (bronchopneumonia)** pneumonia.

sections.title: 3. Lobar pneumonia

blocks.text: **Lobar pneumonia (pleuropneumonia)** is an acute inflammation involving one or several lobes (segments) of the lung and accompanied by inflammation of the pleura. Its causative agent is most often **pneumococcus** (Streptococcus pneumoniae). Fibrinous exudate enters the alveoli.
3.1. Pathological stages and physical signs

blocks.title: Table 8.3. Physical signs in the stages of lobar pneumonia

Morphology

II. Red and gray hepatization, 3–7 days

parts.text: The stages of lobar pneumonia: **“Crepitation — Bronchial — Crepitation”** (indux — hepatization — redux), and on percussion **“Dull-tympanic — Dull — Dull-tympanic”**.

blocks.text: 3.2. Clinical picture

items: **Sudden onset**: severe chills (shivering), the body temperature rises to 39–40 °C within a few hours.

**Stabbing pain** on the affected side, worse on deep inspiration and coughing (inflammation of the parietal pleura). In lower lobe pneumonia the pain may radiate to the abdomen and resemble an “acute abdomen”.
**Cough**: dry at first, with viscous **“rusty”** sputum from the 2nd–3rd day.
**Dyspnea**, tachycardia, sometimes severe intoxication and delirium.

blocks.text: **On inspection**: a febrile face, flushing of the cheek on the affected side, **herpes** eruptions on the lips and nasal alae, movement of the nasal alae with breathing, cyanosis; the affected side lags behind in breathing.

**The fever** is of the continuous type (febris continua); untreated, it lasts 7–10 days and falls by **crisis** (within a few hours) or **lysis**. During a crisis there is a risk of collapse. In the present era of antibiotics, the fever usually falls by lysis within 2–3 days.

**Laboratory and instrumental signs:** neutrophilic leukocytosis in the blood (15–30·10^9^/l), a shift of the differential to the left, toxic granulation of the neutrophils, a raised ESR, raised C-reactive protein and procalcitonin; pneumococci, fibrin and red cells in the sputum; a homogeneous opacity of a lobe or segment on X-ray; febrile proteinuria in the urine.
**Complications:** exudative pleurisy (parapneumonic), lung abscess, infectious-toxic shock, acute respiratory failure, myocarditis, meningitis, pericarditis.

sections.title: 4. Focal pneumonia (bronchopneumonia)

blocks.text: In focal pneumonia the inflammation begins in a bronchus and involves one or several lobules or segments; the pleura is rarely involved; the exudate is serous or mucopurulent.

rows: Respiratory rate 30 per minute or more
Systolic BP below 90 or diastolic BP 60 mm Hg or below

parts.text: By CURB-65, **0–1 point** — outpatient treatment is possible; **2 points** — hospital admission is recommended; **3–5 points** — severe pneumonia, intensive care is likely. Where urea cannot be measured, the **CRB-65** variant is used.

sections.title: 5. The syndrome of fluid accumulation in the pleural cavity

blocks.text: The accumulation of fluid in the pleural cavity may be **noninflammatory** (transudate — hydrothorax) or **inflammatory** (exudate — exudative pleurisy); blood (hemothorax), lymph (chylothorax) and pus (empyema, pyothorax) may also accumulate.

blocks.title: Table 8.6. Signs of the syndrome of fluid accumulation in the pleural cavity
head: Method of examination
Signs
rows: Dyspnea, a feeling of heaviness in the chest; with an exudate — fever and, at the onset, stabbing pain (the pain lessens once fluid has accumulated)
Forced position — lying on the affected side; the affected side is enlarged, the intercostal spaces are smoothed out or bulge, and it lags behind in breathing
Vocal fremitus markedly decreased or absent over the fluid; resistance increased
A dull (thigh) note over the fluid; an oblique upper border — the Damoiseau line; no mobility of the lower edge
Breath sounds markedly diminished or absent over the fluid; soft bronchial breathing at the upper border (compressed lung); no bronchophony
With a large amount of fluid (more than 1.5–2 l) it shifts to the healthy side
A homogeneous opacity in the lower part with an oblique upper border; the costophrenic sinus is filled

blocks.label: Figure 8.2
blocks.caption: Fluid accumulation in the pleural cavity: a homogeneous opacity on the left (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 62)

blocks.text: 5.1. Percussion borders of an exudate

blocks.label: Figure 8.3
blocks.caption: Percussion and auscultation in left-sided exudative pleurisy: 1 — exudate; 2 — the Ellis–Damoiseau–Sokolov line; 3 — Garland’s triangle; 4 — the Grocco–Rauchfuss triangle (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 64)

items: **The Ellis–Damoiseau–Sokolov line** is the oblique upper border of an exudate: it starts at the spine, rises upward and laterally, reaches its highest point at the posterior axillary line and then descends forward. This shape arises because the fluid compresses the lung obliquely.

**Garland’s triangle** is the area on the affected side between the Damoiseau line, the spine and a straight line dropped from the highest point of the line to the spine. Because the compressed lung lies here, percussion reveals a **dull-tympanic** note and auscultation **soft bronchial breathing**.

**The Grocco–Rauchfuss triangle** is a triangle of dullness on the **healthy** side, next to the spine. It is formed by the shift of the mediastinal organs to the healthy side; vocal fremitus is decreased here.

parts.text: In a **transudate** (hydrothorax), the fluid moves freely and its upper border is usually **horizontal**; the border also shifts when the patient changes position. In an **exudate**, because of adhesion of the pleural layers and fibrin, the border is **oblique** (the Damoiseau line) and depends little on position. This difference is relative; they are distinguished precisely by pleural puncture and fluid analysis.

blocks.text: 5.2. Distinguishing a transudate from an exudate

blocks.title: Table 8.7. Differences between a transudate and an exudate
head: Parameter
Transudate
Exudate
rows: Increased hydrostatic pressure or decreased oncotic pressure
Inflammation or tumor of the pleura, increased capillary permeability
Heart failure, liver cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminemia
Pneumonia, tuberculosis, tumor, pulmonary infarction, SLE, rheumatoid arthritis
Turbid, serous, serofibrinous, purulent or hemorrhagic
Less than 2/3 of the upper limit of serum LDH

parts.text: **Light’s criteria** (1972): the fluid is an **exudate** if **at least one** of the following is present: 1) the ratio of pleural fluid protein to serum protein is **more than 0.5**; 2) the ratio of fluid LDH to serum LDH is **more than 0.6**; 3) the fluid LDH is **more than 2/3** of the upper limit of normal for serum LDH.

**Rivalta test**: a few drops of acetic acid are added to 100 ml of distilled water in a cylinder, and then one drop of pleural fluid is let fall into it. In an exudate, the drop sinks forming a white cloud like “cigarette smoke” (positive); in a transudate, it dissolves without a trace (negative). The test is based on the presence of seromucoid proteins.

sections.title: 6. Pleurisy

blocks.text: **Pleurisy** is inflammation of the pleural layers. **Dry (fibrinous)** and **exudative (effusive)** pleurisy are distinguished. It is most often not an independent disease but a complication or manifestation of other diseases (pneumonia, tuberculosis, tumor, rheumatism, SLE, pulmonary infarction, uremia).
6.1. Dry (fibrinous) pleurisy

**Complaints:** **stabbing pain** on the affected side of the chest, worse on deep inspiration, coughing, sneezing and bending to the healthy side; dry cough, low-grade fever. The pain of diaphragmatic pleurisy may radiate to the abdomen and shoulder.
**Inspection:** the patient lies on the affected side or presses the chest with the hand (to restrict movement); the affected side lags behind in breathing; breathing is shallow and rapid.
**Palpation:** a tender area; sometimes the pleural friction is felt with the hand.
**Percussion:** the note is unchanged or slightly impaired; on the affected side the mobility of the lower edge is decreased (because of pain).
**Auscultation: the pleural friction rub** is the main sign; breath sounds are diminished.
6.2. Exudative pleurisy

It often begins as dry pleurisy: as fluid begins to accumulate, the pain lessens and the **dyspnea** increases. Fever, weakness, sweating. The physical signs correspond to the syndrome of fluid accumulation in the pleural cavity (see section 5). During the resorption of the fluid, the pleural friction rub reappears.

parts.text: The dynamics of pleurisy: **“The pain goes — the dyspnea comes”** — when dry pleurisy turns into exudative pleurisy, the fluid separates the pleural layers and the pain lessens, but the lung is compressed and the dyspnea increases.

sections.title: 7. The syndrome of air accumulation in the pleural cavity. Pneumothorax

blocks.text: **Pneumothorax** is the entry of air into the pleural cavity with collapse of the lung.

blocks.title: Table 8.8. Types of pneumothorax
head: Classification
Type
Content
rows: In a healthy person, most often in tall, thin young men, from rupture of subpleural bullae
Against the background of lung diseases: COPD, emphysema, tuberculosis, abscess, bronchial asthma
Chest injury, puncture, central venous catheterization
By communication with the external environment
The opening through which air entered has closed; the amount of air does not change
The pleural cavity communicates permanently with the external environment or a bronchus
Air enters on inspiration but does not leave on expiration — the pressure rises and the mediastinum shifts; life-threatening

blocks.title: Table 8.9. Signs of the syndrome of air accumulation in the pleural cavity
head: Method of examination
Signs
rows: Sudden severe stabbing pain, severe dyspnea, dry cough
The affected side is enlarged, does not take part in breathing, the intercostal spaces are smoothed out; in tension — cyanosis, distended neck veins, hypotension
Vocal fremitus markedly decreased or absent
Tympanic note; the lower border of the lung and its mobility cannot be determined; the mediastinum and heart are shifted to the healthy side
Breath sounds markedly diminished or absent; in open pneumothorax, amphoric or metallic breathing
A lucent area without lung markings; the collapsed lung compressed toward the hilum

blocks.label: Figure 8.4
blocks.caption: Air accumulation in the pleural cavity: the border of the collapsed lung is shown by an arrow (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 63)

parts.text: **Hydropneumothorax** is the presence of both air and fluid in the pleural cavity. On percussion there is a tympanic note above and a dull note below; the border between them is **horizontal** and shifts when the patient changes position. When the patient is shaken (the Hippocratic test), a “succussion splash” (succussio Hippocratis) is heard.

sections.title: 8. Pleural puncture

blocks.text: **Indications:** diagnostic (to determine the nature of the fluid) and therapeutic (to remove fluid or air, to administer drugs).

**Site:** in the area where dullness on percussion is most pronounced, usually **in the VII–VIII intercostal space along the scapular or posterior axillary line**. The needle is inserted along the **upper edge** of the rib, because the intercostal vessels and nerves run along the lower edge of the rib. In pneumothorax, the puncture is performed in the II intercostal space along the midclavicular line.

blocks.label: Figure 8.5
blocks.caption: Technique of pleural puncture: the needle is inserted along the upper edge of the rib (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 58)

parts.text: Usually **no more than 1–1.5 liters** of fluid are removed in a single procedure: rapid removal of a large amount of fluid may lead to an abrupt mediastinal shift, collapse and “re-expansion” pulmonary edema. The fluid obtained is sent for physicochemical, cytological and bacteriological examination.

sections.title: 9. Pathogenesis and morphology of pneumonia

blocks.text: Normally the lower airways are almost sterile: they are protected by **mucociliary clearance** (ciliated epithelium and mucus), the **cough reflex**, alveolar macrophages, secretory IgA and surfactant. Pneumonia develops as a result of the route of entry of the microorganism and the weakening of the defense mechanisms.

blocks.title: Table 8.10. Routes by which microorganisms enter the lung
head: Route
Content
Examples
rows: Aspiration of oropharyngeal contents during sleep — the most common route
Aspiration of a large amount of gastric or oral contents
Alcoholism, stroke, epilepsy, anesthesia — anaerobes, aspiration pneumonia and abscess
Through the blood from a distant focus
Staphylococcus (infective endocarditis, injection drug use, sepsis) — multiple foci

blocks.title: Table 8.11. Factors predisposing to pneumonia
head: Group
Factors
rows: Old age (over 65), smoking, alcoholism, chilling, stress, malnutrition
COPD, bronchiectasis, heart failure, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney and liver diseases, tumors, HIV
Impaired consciousness, impaired swallowing, stroke, epilepsy, nasogastric tube
Mechanical ventilation (ventilator-associated pneumonia), immunosuppressive therapy, glucocorticoids, prolonged bed rest (hypostatic pneumonia)

blocks.text: 9.1. “Atypical” pneumonias

blocks.title: Table 8.12. Features of pneumonias caused by particular pathogens
head: Pathogen
Clinical features
rows: Classic lobar pneumonia: sudden onset, chills, pleuritic pain, rusty sputum, a lobar shadow
In young people and in groups (students, soldiers), gradual onset, prolonged dry cough, pharyngitis, few physical signs (“the X-ray is worse than the clinical picture”), myalgia
Air conditioners and water systems, severe course, high fever and relative bradycardia, diarrhea, impaired consciousness, hyponatremia
In alcoholism and diabetes mellitus, bloody viscous sputum like “red currant jelly”, in the upper lobes, rapid destruction (abscess)
After influenza, severe course, multiple cavities (bullae), pyopneumothorax
Bilateral interstitial changes (“ground glass”), hypoxemia, bacterial infection is often superimposed

parts.text: The term “atypical” does not mean a mild or unusual course of pneumonia but refers to the intracellular pathogens **insensitive to the usual antibiotics (beta-lactams)** (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila, Legionella). Macrolides or respiratory fluoroquinolones are used for them.

blocks.text: 9.2. Complications of pneumonia

blocks.title: Table 8.13. Pulmonary and extrapulmonary complications of pneumonia
head: Pulmonary complications
Extrapulmonary complications
rows: Parapneumonic exudative pleurisy and pleural empyema
Myocarditis, pericarditis, arrhythmias, decompensation of heart failure

parts.text: If the fever does not fall by the 3rd–5th day of treatment or rises again, the following must be excluded: **an antibiotic-resistant pathogen**, **a complication** (empyema, abscess), **a wrong diagnosis** (tuberculosis, lung cancer, pulmonary infarction, vasculitis) or **drug fever**.

sections.title: 10. Types of atelectasis

blocks.text: **Atelectasis** is the loss of air and collapse of lung tissue (a segment, a lobe or the whole lung).

blocks.title: Table 8.14. Types of atelectasis and their physical signs
head: Type
Mechanism
Causes
Physical signs
rows: The bronchial lumen is blocked, and the air distal to it is absorbed
Tumor, foreign body, viscous sputum (after surgery)
The affected side is smaller and lags behind in breathing; dull note; fremitus, breath sounds and bronchophony decreased or absent; the mediastinum shifts to the affected side
The lung is compressed from outside
A large amount of fluid or air in the pleura, a large tumor
Dull-tympanic note over the compressed area, soft bronchial breathing (the bronchus is patent)
The lung shrinks as a result of fibrosis
Retracted chest, impaired note, mediastinum shifted to the affected side
Diaphragmatic movement is restricted, and the lower parts collapse
After surgery, abdominal pain, prolonged bed rest
Often few physical signs; linear shadows on X-ray

parts.text: The rule of mediastinal shift: **“Volume added — it moves away, volume lost — it is pulled toward”**. Fluid, air or a large tumor in the pleura (volume added) — the mediastinum shifts to the **healthy** side; obstructive and contraction atelectasis, pneumonectomy (volume lost) — to the **affected** side.

sections.title: 11. Extended interpretation of pleural fluid analysis

blocks.title: Table 8.15. Additional parameters in pleural fluid analysis
head: Parameter
Interpretation
rows: Clear, pale yellow — transudate; turbid — exudate; purulent — empyema; hemorrhagic — tumor, pulmonary infarction, injury, tuberculosis; milky — chylothorax (triglycerides more than 1.24 mmol/l)
Below 7.2 — complicated parapneumonic pleurisy or empyema (an indication for drainage), as well as tumor, tuberculosis, rheumatoid pleurisy
Below 3.3 mmol/l — empyema, rheumatoid pleurisy, tuberculosis, tumor

Neutrophils predominate — an acute bacterial process (parapneumonic), pulmonary infarction; lymphocytes more than 50 % — tuberculosis, tumor, lymphoma, heart failure; eosinophils more than 10 % — air or blood in the pleural space, parasitic disease, drug effect
Above 40 U/l — strong suspicion of tuberculous pleurisy
Gram stain, culture, PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis

blocks.title: Table 8.16. The main causes of exudative pleurisy
head: Cause
Features
rows: With or after pneumonia, neutrophilic; the complicated type and empyema require drainage
More common in young people, low-grade fever, lymphocytic exudate, high ADA, mycobacteria rarely found
In the elderly, often hemorrhagic, reaccumulates rapidly; lung and breast cancer, lymphomas
Often small in amount, sometimes hemorrhagic
Acute pancreatitis (on the left, high amylase), subhepatic abscess

parts.text: The most common cause of a transudate is **heart failure** (often bilateral or right-sided), and of an exudate, **pneumonia, tumor and tuberculosis**. A unilateral, large, rapidly reaccumulating hemorrhagic exudate raises suspicion of a **tumor** first of all.

sections.title: 12. Pathophysiology of pneumothorax and danger signs

blocks.text: Normally the pressure in the pleural cavity is below atmospheric (negative) and keeps the lung expanded. When air enters, the pressure equalizes and the lung collapses owing to its elastic recoil. In **valvular (tension) pneumothorax**, air enters with each inspiration but does not leave: the intrapleural pressure becomes positive, the mediastinum shifts to the healthy side, the venae cavae kink and the venous return to the heart decreases → **obstructive shock**.

parts.text: Signs of tension pneumothorax: severe dyspnea and cyanosis, tachycardia, **hypotension**, distended neck veins, deviation of the trachea to the **healthy** side, a tympanic note and absent breath sounds on the affected side. This condition requires urgent **needle decompression** without waiting for an X-ray (the II intercostal space in the midclavicular line or the IV–V space in the anterior axillary line).

blocks.title: Table 8.17. Clinical comparison of the types of pneumothorax
head: Feature
Closed
Open
Valvular
rows: Markedly shifted to the healthy side

Lobar pneumonia

sections.title: 14. Criteria for the diagnosis of pneumonia

blocks.text: The diagnosis of pneumonia is based on a combination of **clinical and radiological** data.

blocks.title: Table 8.19. Diagnosis of community-acquired pneumonia
head: Group of criteria
Signs
rows: Fever of acute onset (above 38 °C); cough (productive); pleuritic chest pain; dyspnea
Signs of local consolidation: dull note, bronchial breathing, increased bronchophony and vocal fremitus, local consonating fine-bubbling rales or crepitation
Leukocytosis (more than 10·10^9^/l) and/or band neutrophils more than 10 %; CRP raised
A newly appeared focal or infiltrative change in the lung

parts.text: If there are clinical signs but no infiltrate is found on X-ray (the initial stage, dehydration, neutropenia, a very small focus), pneumonia is considered “probable”, and the X-ray is repeated after 24–48 hours or CT is performed. Conversely, an infiltrate on X-ray is not always pneumonia: it must be distinguished from pulmonary infarction, tumor, tuberculosis and eosinophilic infiltrate.

blocks.text: 14.1. Radiological types of pneumonia

blocks.title: Table 8.20. Radiological appearances of pneumonia
head: Type
Appearance
Pathogens
rows: Homogeneous opacity of a whole lobe, an “air bronchogram”

blocks.text: **The “air bronchogram”** is the visualization of air-containing bronchi as lucent bands against the background of consolidated lung tissue; it shows that the consolidation is in the alveoli (pneumonia); this sign is absent when there is fluid in the pleura.

sections.title: 15. Pleural empyema

blocks.text: **Pleural empyema** (pyothorax) is the accumulation of pus in the pleural cavity. It most often develops after pneumonia, rupture of a lung abscess into the pleura, chest injury and operations. Signs: hectic fever, chills, profuse sweating, intoxication, pain and heaviness in the chest, signs of pleural fluid; sometimes swelling and redness of the chest wall. In the aspirate — thick pus, pH below 7.0, markedly low glucose, bacteria on culture. **Treatment:** drainage of the pleural cavity and antibiotics; if delayed, the pleura thickens and the lung becomes “encased in armor”.

sections.title: 16. Pulmonary embolism and pulmonary infarction

blocks.text: In the differential diagnosis of conditions with consolidation and pleuritic pain, **pulmonary embolism** (PE) must always be remembered.

**Risk factors:** prolonged bed rest, operations (especially orthopedic), leg injuries, tumors, pregnancy and the postpartum period, hormonal contraceptives, previous venous thrombosis, obesity, long flights.

blocks.title: Table 8.21. Signs of pulmonary embolism
head: Group
Signs
rows: Sudden dyspnea (the most common), chest pain (pleuritic or retrosternal), cough, hemoptysis, syncope
Tachypnea, tachycardia, cyanosis, distended neck veins, hypotension (massive PE); accentuation of the II sound over the pulmonary artery; signs of deep vein thrombosis in the leg
Pleuritic pain, hemoptysis, pleural friction rub, signs of limited consolidation, a small amount of hemorrhagic exudate
Raised D-dimer, right ventricular strain on the ECG (the SIQIIITIII pattern), right ventricular dilation on echocardiography; CT angiography is the confirmatory method

parts.text: In a patient who develops sudden dyspnea and tachycardia on the 5th–7th day after surgery, PE should be considered first of all, even if there are few physical changes in the lungs. In this situation the “mismatch between the physical signs and the degree of dyspnea” is an important diagnostic sign.

sections.title: 17. Hydrothorax and other noninflammatory fluids

blocks.title: Table 8.22. Types of noninflammatory pleural fluid
head: Type
Cause
Features
rows: Heart failure, liver cirrhosis (often on the right), nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminemia, peritoneal dialysis
Bilateral or on the right, clear, low protein
Injury, rupture of an aortic aneurysm, anticoagulants, tumor
Hematocrit more than 50 % of the blood hematocrit
Injury to the thoracic duct (trauma, surgery, lymphoma)

parts.text: The **“4C”** order of pleural fluid analysis: **C**olor (appearance), **C**hemistry (Rivalta test and protein — transudate or exudate), **C**ells (neutrophils, lymphocytes, eosinophils, atypical cells), **C**ulture (microbiology: bacteria, tuberculosis).

sections.title: 18. Clinical part

blocks.text: Distinguishing the three main syndromes

blocks.title: Table 8.23. Differences between the syndromes of consolidation and of fluid and air accumulation
head: Feature
Consolidation of the lung tissue
Fluid in the pleural cavity
Air in the pleural cavity

parts.text: The key to distinguishing the three syndromes is **vocal fremitus**: it is **increased in consolidation and decreased in fluid and air**. Fluid and air, in turn, are distinguished by **percussion**: fluid — dull, air — tympanic.

blocks.text: Sample case history entry

The right side of the chest is larger than the left and lags behind in breathing; the intercostal spaces in the lower part are smoothed out. On the right below the VI rib, vocal fremitus is not detected. On percussion there is a dull note over this area with an oblique upper border rising to the V rib along the posterior axillary line (the Damoiseau line); the mobility of the lower edge of the right lung cannot be determined. On the left beside the spine, there is a triangle of dullness (Grocco–Rauchfuss). On auscultation, no breath sounds are heard on the right below the VI rib, and there is soft bronchial breathing at the upper border of the dullness.
**Conclusion:** the syndrome of fluid accumulation in the right pleural cavity — exudative pleurisy (or hydrothorax); pleural puncture and fluid analysis are needed.

skills.title: Skill: distinguishing the syndromes of consolidation, fluid and air on physical examination

items: Inspect: the symmetry of the chest, the size of the affected side and its participation in breathing.
Compare vocal fremitus on the two sides: increased — consolidation; decreased — fluid, air or obstruction.
Perform comparative percussion: a dull (consolidation or fluid) or tympanic (air) note.
If dullness is found, determine the shape of its upper border (oblique — the Damoiseau line) and look for Garland’s and the Grocco–Rauchfuss triangles.
Auscultate: bronchial breathing (consolidation) or diminished/absent breath sounds (fluid, air).
Examine bronchophony.
Assess mediastinal shift by determining the position of the apex beat and the trachea.
Draw a syndromic conclusion and plan radiography, US and, if necessary, pleural puncture.

skills.title: Skill: the steps of pleural puncture (on a manikin)

items: Establish the indication, obtain the patient’s consent and mark the puncture site with X-ray or US.
Seat the patient leaning slightly forward with the arms resting on a pillow on a table.
Clean your hands and put on sterile gloves; treat the puncture area widely with an antiseptic and drape it with a sterile sheet.
Local anesthesia: inject novocaine (procaine) or lidocaine solution layer by layer.
Insert the needle perpendicularly along the upper edge of the rib; after the sensation of “entering a space”, pull back the syringe to check for fluid.
Withdraw the fluid slowly (no more than 1–1.5 l at a time) and prevent air entry (a clamp on the rubber tube or a three-way tap).
Remove the needle and apply a sterile dressing to the puncture site.
Record the amount and appearance of the fluid and send samples to the laboratory; observe the patient’s condition and perform a control radiograph.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: After chilling, a 38-year-old man fell ill suddenly with severe chills, a fever of 40 °C and pain on the right that increased on inspiration. On the third day he began to expectorate rust-colored sputum. On inspection: the right cheek is flushed, there is herpes on the lips. In the right infrascapular region vocal fremitus is increased, the percussion note is dull, and there is bronchial breathing and increased bronchophony. Blood leukocytes 22·10^9^/l, band neutrophils 15 %, ESR 48 mm/h. Age 38, consciousness clear, respiratory rate 24, BP 120/80, urea 5 mmol/l.
cases.ask: What are the syndrome and the diagnosis? At which stage is the disease? Assess it by CURB-65.
cases.answer: The syndrome of consolidation of the lung tissue — right-sided lower lobe lobar pneumonia, hepatization (II) stage (dull note, bronchial breathing, increased vocal fremitus and bronchophony). Neutrophilic leukocytosis and a shift of the differential to the left confirm bacterial inflammation. CURB-65 = 0 points (clear consciousness, normal urea, respiratory rate below 30, normal BP, age below 65). However, given the high fever and extensive involvement, X-ray confirmation and the start of treatment are needed.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: 2 weeks ago, a 50-year-old patient had pain on the left that increased with breathing; then the pain lessened and the dyspnea increased. On the left below the VII rib, vocal fremitus and breath sounds are not detected, and on percussion there is a dull note with an oblique border. Pleural puncture yielded 1000 ml of turbid yellowish fluid: specific gravity 1024, protein 42 g/l, Rivalta test positive, fluid/serum protein 0.68, many lymphocytes.
cases.ask: Is the fluid a transudate or an exudate? Explain the clinical dynamics. Which cause should be considered?
cases.answer: An exudate (specific gravity above 1015, protein above 30 g/l, positive Rivalta test, protein ratio above 0.5 — Light’s criterion). The replacement of pain by dyspnea shows that dry pleurisy has turned into exudative pleurisy: the fluid separates the pleural layers and lessens the pain but compresses the lung and causes dyspnea. A lymphocytic exudate raises suspicion of a tuberculous or tumor etiology — the fluid should be examined for mycobacteria and atypical cells.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 72-year-old patient has chronic heart failure: leg edema, an enlarged liver. There is dullness in the lower parts on both sides with an almost horizontal upper border. Puncture yielded a clear, pale yellow fluid: specific gravity 1010, protein 18 g/l, Rivalta test negative.
cases.ask: What is the type of fluid, and what is this condition called? By what mechanism did it develop?
cases.answer: A transudate; the condition is bilateral hydrothorax. In heart failure it develops as a result of a rise in venous (hydrostatic) pressure, with fluid leaving into the pleural cavity without inflammation. A transudate is most often bilateral or larger on the right, with a horizontal border that shifts with position.

topics.title: The syndrome of cavity formation in the lung. Lung abscess. Bronchiectasis. Patient curation. Writing case history 1

goals.text: To teach the student the causes and physical signs of the syndrome of cavity formation in the lung and the symptomatology of lung abscess and bronchiectasis; to develop the skills of independent curation of a patient with a respiratory disease and of writing the educational case history (case history 1).
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the causes of cavity formation in the lung and the conditions for detecting a cavity by physical methods;
the physical signs of the cavity syndrome;
the stages of lung abscess and the clinical signs at each stage;
the causes and the clinical and physical signs of bronchiectasis;
the signs distinguishing lung abscess from bronchiectasis;
the structure of the educational case history and the requirements for writing each section.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: take a full history from the patient and perform an objective examination;
combine the signs found into syndromes and justify the syndromic diagnosis;
interpret a sputum analysis and the conclusion of a radiograph;

sections.title: 1. The syndrome of cavity formation in the lung

blocks.text: **A cavity in the lung** is an air-filled space formed as a result of destruction of the lung tissue and most often communicating with a bronchus.
**Causes:** lung abscess (purulent destruction), tuberculous cavity, cavitating lung cancer, lung gangrene, a suppurating cyst, large bronchiectases, bullae.

parts.text: A cavity is detected by physical methods only under the following conditions:

items: it is **more than 4–5 cm** in diameter;
it lies **close to the chest wall (superficially)**;
it **communicates with a bronchus** and is filled with air (the pus has drained);
the lung tissue around it is consolidated (inflammatory infiltrate).

parts.text: A small, deep-seated or pus-filled cavity gives the picture of consolidation or no change at all on physical examination.

blocks.title: Table 9.1. Signs of the syndrome of cavity formation in the lung
head: Method of examination
Signs
rows: Cough with a large amount (especially in the morning, “a mouthful”) of purulent, often foul-smelling sputum; the sputum separates into layers; hemoptysis; fever, sweating
The affected side lags behind in breathing; in a long course, clubbing and watch-glass nails
Vocal fremitus increased over the cavity
Tympanic note; over a large smooth-walled cavity — metallic; when communicating with a bronchus through a narrow opening — the “cracked-pot” sound
Bronchial or amphoric breathing, coarse-bubbling consonating moist rales; bronchophony increased
A rounded lucent area (cavity) with a horizontal fluid level, with infiltration around it

blocks.label: Figure 9.1
blocks.caption: Cavity formation in the lung: a cavity with a fluid level in the right lung (arrow) (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 61)

parts.text: **Wintrich’s sign** — the pitch of the percussion note rises when the patient opens the mouth and falls when it is closed (showing that the cavity communicates with the outside air through a bronchus). **Gerhardt’s sign** — a change in the pitch of the tympanic note when the patient changes position (with the shifting of the fluid level in the cavity).

sections.title: 2. Lung abscess

blocks.text: **A lung abscess** is a nonspecific purulent-necrotic destruction of the lung tissue with the formation of one or more cavities bounded by granulation tissue (a capsule). It occurs most often in men aged 30–50.

**Causes and predisposing factors:** aspiration (alcohol intoxication, epilepsy, anesthesia, impaired swallowing, dental caries and periodontal disease), pneumonia (Staphylococcus, Klebsiella), bronchial obstruction (tumor, foreign body), septic embolism, diabetes mellitus, reduced immunity. Pathogens: anaerobes, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
The two periods of the course of an abscess

blocks.title: Table 9.2. Periods of lung abscess
head: Feature
Period I — formation of the abscess (before rupture)
Period II — after rupture of the abscess into a bronchus
rows: Suddenly, “a mouthful” — a large amount (200–1000 ml a day) of purulent, foul-smelling sputum
Improves rapidly once the pus has drained
Tympanic (if the cavity has emptied and is superficial and large)
Diminished or bronchial breathing, moist rales
Amphoric breathing, coarse-bubbling consonating moist rales
A cavity with a horizontal fluid level

blocks.text: **Laboratory signs:** marked neutrophilic leukocytosis in the blood (up to 20–30·10^9^/l), a shift of the differential to the left, a raised ESR; in the sputum, many leukocytes, **elastic fibers** (a sign of destruction of the lung tissue), hematoidin and cholesterol crystals and fatty acid crystals. When left to settle, the sputum **separates into layers**.

parts.text: The improvement of the condition and the fall in temperature after an abscess has ruptured into a bronchus may be deceptive. If the cavity drains poorly (a narrow or oblique draining bronchus), the fever and intoxication increase again. An abscess that has not healed in 2–3 months becomes a **chronic abscess**.

blocks.text: **Complications:** pyopneumothorax and pleural empyema, pulmonary hemorrhage, sepsis, brain abscess, amyloidosis, transition to a chronic abscess.

sections.title: 3. Bronchiectasis

blocks.text: **Bronchiectasis** is an irreversible dilation (bronchiectases) and deformity of the bronchi in which a chronic suppurative process takes place. The disease most often forms in childhood and adolescence (5–25 years) and is more common in males.

blocks.label: Figure 9.2
blocks.caption: Diagram of bronchiectases: a healthy lung (left) and bronchiectasis (right) (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 65)

blocks.text: **Causes:** severe pneumonias, measles and pertussis in childhood; congenital factors (developmental defects of the bronchial wall, cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia — Kartagener’s syndrome); bronchial obstruction (foreign body, tumor); immunodeficiency.
**Forms of bronchiectasis:** cylindrical, saccular, fusiform, mixed. **The lower lobes of the lungs** and the lingular segments of the left lung are most often affected (their drainage is poorer).
Clinical picture:

items: **Cough with a large amount of purulent sputum**, especially in the morning (“a mouthful”) and in the drainage position (lying on the healthy side with the head lower); the daily amount is 50–500 ml or more; when left to settle, the sputum separates into three layers and is often foul-smelling.
**Hemoptysis** (often recurrent), sometimes pulmonary hemorrhage.
Fever, weakness and sweating during exacerbations; exacerbations of the disease in spring and autumn are characteristic.
In a long course — dyspnea, weight loss, **clubbing** and watch-glass nails, cyanosis.

blocks.text: **Physical signs:** few changes during remission. During an exacerbation, over the affected area (most often the lower parts) percussion reveals an impaired note (surrounding pneumosclerosis and infiltration), and auscultation reveals harsh breathing and **medium- and coarse-bubbling moist rales**, which decrease or disappear after coughing and expectoration. When pneumosclerosis and emphysema develop, their signs appear.

**Diagnosis:** the “gold standard” is **high-resolution computed tomography** (a bronchial diameter larger than that of the adjacent artery, absence of tapering of the bronchus toward the periphery); bronchography was used previously. Bronchoscopy is used to find the source of pus and for sanitation.
**Complications:** pulmonary hemorrhage, respiratory failure, chronic cor pulmonale, amyloidosis (kidneys — nephrotic syndrome), lung abscess, brain abscess.

parts.text: The main signs of bronchiectasis — **“Pus, Blood, Clubs”**: a large amount of purulent sputum (in the morning), hemoptysis, clubbing.

sections.title: 4. Patient curation and writing case history 1

blocks.text: **Curation** is the student’s independent examination and observation of a patient and keeping of the case history under the supervision of the teacher. Case history 1 is written on a patient with a respiratory disease.
4.1. Stages of curation

items: A patient is assigned by the teacher; the student gets acquainted with the patient and obtains consent.
History taking (complaints, anamnesis morbi, anamnesis vitae) — according to the plan of topic 1.
General inspection and objective examination by systems (status praesens), with the main attention on the respiratory organs (status localis).
Combining the signs found into syndromes.
Formulating and justifying the syndromic and primary diagnosis.
Drawing up a plan of investigation and interpreting the available test results.
Keeping progress notes (the daily dynamics of the patient’s condition).
Discharge summary (epicrisis) and recommendations.
Submitting the case history to the teacher and defending it.

blocks.text: 4.2. Justifying the syndromic diagnosis

The syndromic diagnosis is written on the basis of the signs found in the following order: “On the basis of the patient’s complaints of ..., the history data ..., the signs found on inspection ..., on palpation ..., on percussion ... and on auscultation ..., the following syndromes can be identified: ...”

blocks.title: Table 9.4. The main syndromes in respiratory diseases
head: Syndrome
Main signs
Example diseases
rows: Increased fremitus, dull note, bronchial breathing
Increased air content of the lungs
Barrel chest, hyperresonant note, diminished breath sounds
No fremitus, dull note, no breath sounds
No fremitus, tympanic note, no breath sounds
Increased fremitus, tympanic note, amphoric breathing, coarse-bubbling rales
Signs of right ventricular failure, accentuation of the II sound over the pulmonary artery

parts.text: Typical errors in the case history: listing complaints without analysis; breaking the chronology of the history; writing a general “normal” in the objective examination (in fact, each parameter is written with an exact figure: respiratory rate, pulse, BP, borders); not justifying the syndromic diagnosis with signs; “copying” the diagnosis from the medical record before talking to the patient.

blocks.text: 4.3. Sample status localis of the respiratory system

**Respiratory system.** Breathing through the nose is free. The voice is unchanged. The chest is normosthenic in shape and asymmetrical: the left side lags behind in breathing. Breathing is of the mixed type, rhythmic, respiratory rate 24 per minute. The accessory muscles do not take part in inspiration.
Palpation: the chest is painless and elastic. Vocal fremitus is increased in the left infrascapular region.
Comparative percussion: a dull note in the left infrascapular region below the VII rib; a clear lung note over the other areas.

Topographic percussion: the lung apices are 3.5 cm above the clavicle in front and at the level of the VII cervical vertebra behind. Krönig’s isthmus is 5 cm on both sides. The lower borders of the lungs are normal (given in a table). The mobility of the lower edge of the lung along the mid-axillary line is 7 cm on the right and 3 cm on the left.

Auscultation: in the left infrascapular region, bronchial breathing, crepitation at the end of inspiration and consonating fine-bubbling moist rales; bronchophony increased. Vesicular breathing over the other areas.

**Syndromic conclusion:** the syndromes of inflammation and of consolidation of the lung tissue in the lower lobe of the left lung. **Primary diagnosis:** community-acquired left-sided lower lobe pneumonia.

Lung abscess

parts.text: In a smoker over 40, any cavity in the lung, especially one with a thick, irregular wall, is considered a **cavitating lung cancer** until proven otherwise: bronchoscopy and biopsy are performed. “Treating an abscess” with antibiotics may lead to a loss of time.

blocks.text: 5.1. Lung gangrene

**Lung gangrene** is a poorly demarcated, rapidly spreading putrefactive necrosis of the lung tissue. It differs from an abscess in that the patient’s condition is very severe (sepsis, shock), the sputum is very abundant (up to 1 liter a day), **very foul-smelling** (noticed even by those nearby), brownish-gray and multilayered; there is unbounded destruction in the lung with multiple cavities. Mortality is high, and surgical treatment is often needed.

sections.title: 6. Pathogenesis and diagnosis of bronchiectasis

blocks.text: Bronchiectases develop according to a **“vicious circle”** (P. Cole’s hypothesis): impaired mucociliary clearance → accumulation of mucus → bacterial colonization → chronic neutrophilic inflammation → neutrophil elastase and other enzymes destroy the elastic and muscle fibers of the bronchial wall → the bronchus dilates and becomes deformed → clearance is further impaired.

blocks.title: Table 9.6. Forms and causes of bronchiectases
head: Classification
Types
rows: Cylindrical (uniformly dilated), varicose (irregular, beaded), saccular (cystic — the most severe)

Congenital (developmental defect of the bronchial wall, cystic fibrosis, Kartagener’s syndrome) and acquired (childhood infections, obstruction, immunodeficiency, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis)

parts.text: **Kartagener’s syndrome** is the triad of **bronchiectasis + chronic sinusitis + reversed position of the internal organs** (situs inversus — the heart on the right). It is based on immobility of the ciliated epithelium (primary ciliary dyskinesia); infertility is also observed in men. If the heart sounds of a patient are heard on the right, this syndrome should be remembered.

blocks.label: Figure 9.3
blocks.caption: Bronchography: the normal structure of the bronchi (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 48)

blocks.label: Figure 9.4
blocks.caption: Bronchography: dilated bronchi (same source, Fig. 48)

blocks.text: Formerly, **bronchography** (radiography after a contrast agent has been introduced into the bronchi) was used to confirm bronchiectasis; it has now been replaced by **high-resolution CT**. CT signs: an internal bronchial diameter larger than the diameter of the adjacent artery (the “signet ring” sign), absence of tapering of the bronchus toward the periphery, visibility of bronchi within 1 cm of the pleura.

blocks.label: Figure 9.5
blocks.caption: Atypical (tumor) cells in the sputum (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 59, n)

sections.title: 7. Writing the main sections of the case history: a detailed sample

blocks.text: 7.1. Status praesens — general inspection
The status praesens (present status) is written systematically, with each parameter stated precisely:

items: **General condition** (satisfactory, moderately severe, severe), **consciousness** (clear, GCS score), **position** (active, passive, forced — which), **body build** (constitutional type, epigastric angle), **height, weight, BMI**, **body temperature**.
**Skin:** color, moisture, turgor, rashes, scars, vascular changes; **visible mucous membranes**; **hair and nails**.
**Subcutaneous fat:** development, skinfold thickness, edema (location, character).
**Lymph nodes:** by groups (size, consistency, tenderness, mobility).
**Muscles:** development, tone, strength, tenderness.
**Bones:** deformity, pain.
**Joints:** shape, range of movement, pain.
**Thyroid gland.**

blocks.text: 7.2. The respiratory system — in detail

items: **Inspection:** breathing through the nose, the voice; the shape and symmetry of the chest; the type, rate, depth and rhythm of breathing; use of the accessory muscles; participation of both sides in breathing.
**Palpation:** tender areas, resistance, vocal fremitus.
**Comparative percussion:** the character of the note by areas.
**Topographic percussion:** height of the apices (in front and behind), Krönig’s isthmus, the lower borders (table), the mobility of the lower edge (along three lines).
**Auscultation:** the main breath sound, added sounds, bronchophony.

blocks.title: Table 9.7. Form for recording the results of topographic percussion
head: Topographic line
Right lung
Left lung

blocks.text: 7.3. The other systems (in brief)

The cardiovascular system (inspection, apex beat, borders, heart sounds, murmurs, pulse, BP), the digestive system (tongue, inspection of the abdomen, superficial and deep palpation, the liver by Kurlov, the spleen), the urinary system (lumbar region, Pasternatsky’s sign, urination), the nervous system (reflexes, sleep, mental state).
7.4. Identifying the syndromes and justifying the primary diagnosis

The justification formula: **“On the basis of the complaints (...) + the history (...) + the objective findings (...), the following syndromes are identified: 1) ...; 2) ...; 3) .... The combination of these syndromes and the acute onset (or course) of the disease is characteristic of ... disease. Primary diagnosis: ...”**
7.5. Sample progress note

**Progress note (date, time):** The patient’s condition is moderately severe, with positive dynamics. Complaints: the cough has decreased, the sputum is mucopurulent, up to 20 ml a day, and dyspnea occurs only on climbing stairs. Body temperature 36.9 °C in the morning and 37.3 °C in the evening. Objectively: the skin is pink and moist. Respiratory rate 20 per minute. In the right infrascapular region the impaired percussion note persists; on auscultation breath sounds are diminished and crepitation (crepitatio redux) is heard. Heart sounds are clear and rhythmic, pulse 84/min, BP 120/80 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft and painless. Bowel movements and urination are normal. Treatment is continued.
7.6. Structure of the discharge summary

Briefly, the discharge summary gives: the patient’s full name and age, the date and reason for admission, the main complaints, the main objective and laboratory-instrumental findings that confirmed the diagnosis, the clinical diagnosis, the treatment given, the result of treatment and the patient’s condition at discharge, capacity for work, and further recommendations (regimen, diet, medicines, follow-up).

parts.text: It is convenient to write progress notes and conclusions according to the **SOAP** system of the English-language literature: **S**ubjective — the patient’s complaints; **O**bjective — objective findings; **A**ssessment — assessment (dynamics, diagnosis); **P**lan — plan (investigations and treatment).

sections.title: 8. Sputum examination: extended information

blocks.text: **Rules for collecting sputum:** in the morning, before eating, after rinsing the mouth with boiled water, by coughing deeply, into a sterile container (it must be sputum, not saliva). For bacteriological examination it is taken before antibiotics are started; for Mycobacterium tuberculosis it is collected on 3 consecutive days.

blocks.title: Table 9.8. Types of sputum examination
head: Examination
Content
rows: Amount, color, odor, consistency, separation into layers, admixtures (blood, Dittrich plugs, Curschmann spirals)
Leukocytes, red cells, epithelium, elastic fibers, Curschmann spirals, Charcot–Leyden crystals, cholesterol crystals
Gram stain (bacteria), Ziehl–Neelsen stain (Mycobacterium tuberculosis), Romanowsky stain (eosinophils), cytology (atypical cells)
PCR (Mycobacterium tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance — GeneXpert, viruses)

sections.title: 9. Postural drainage

blocks.text: **Postural drainage** is placing the patient in a special position so that sputum drains out of the affected bronchi. It is used in bronchiectasis, lung abscess and chronic purulent bronchitis. The procedure is performed 2–3 times a day for 15–30 minutes, before meals or 2 hours after them; it is more effective combined with vibratory massage (percussion) of the chest.

blocks.title: Table 9.9. Drainage positions according to the affected lobe
head: Affected area
Drainage position
rows: The apical segments of the upper lobes
Sitting, leaning slightly backward or forward
The anterior segments of the upper lobe
On the left side, turned slightly onto the back, with the foot of the bed raised by 15–20 cm
On the right side, turned slightly onto the back, with the foot of the bed raised
The basal segments of the lower lobes
Lying on the healthy side or on the abdomen, with the foot of the bed raised by 30–40 cm (“head down”)

parts.text: Postural drainage is **contraindicated** in pulmonary hemorrhage, severe heart failure, high arterial hypertension, acute cerebrovascular events and in the elderly in a severe condition.

sections.title: 10. Principles of treating lung abscess and bronchiectasis

items: **Lung abscess:** prolonged (4–6 weeks or more) antibiotic therapy (drugs active against anaerobes); postural drainage; bronchoscopic sanitation; if ineffective — percutaneous drainage or surgery (removal of a lobe of the lung).

**Bronchiectasis:** ensuring airway clearance (physiotherapy, drainage, mucolytics), antibiotics during exacerbations, long-term macrolides for frequent exacerbations; surgery for localized bronchiectasis; vaccination (influenza, pneumococcus).

sections.title: 11. Lung cancer: an important cause of the cavity and consolidation syndromes

blocks.text: Lung cancer is one of the most important diseases in modern pulmonology, and it may present as various syndromes (consolidation, atelectasis, pleural fluid, cavity).

blocks.title: Table 9.10. Clinical manifestations of lung cancer
head: Group
Signs
rows: Prolonged cough, a change in the character of the cough (in a smoker), hemoptysis (“raspberry jelly”), recurrent pneumonias in the same place, a monophonic wheeze, obstructive atelectasis
Chest pain (pleura, ribs), hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal nerve), superior vena cava syndrome, diaphragmatic paralysis, hemorrhagic pleural fluid, difficulty swallowing
Severe pain in the shoulder and arm, atrophy of the arm muscles, Horner’s triad
Brain (headache, seizures), bones (pain), liver, adrenal glands
Clubbing and hypertrophic osteoarthropathy, hypercalcemia, Cushing’s syndrome, hyponatremia, myasthenic syndrome, thrombophlebitis
Weight loss, weakness, loss of appetite, anemia, low-grade fever

parts.text: The most important risk factor for lung cancer is **smoking** (80–90 % of cases). In a smoker over 40 with a prolonged (more than 3 weeks) cough, hemoptysis or pneumonia recurring in the same place, chest CT and bronchoscopy are mandatory.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 42-year-old man abuses alcohol. 2 weeks ago he fell asleep in the street while drunk. Afterward, a hectic fever, chills, profuse sweating and pain on the right appeared. Today, after a bout of severe coughing, he expectorated “a mouthful” — 400 ml of purulent, foul-smelling sputum, and his temperature fell to 37.2 °C. In the right infrascapular region vocal fremitus is increased, there is a tympanic note on percussion, and amphoric breathing and coarse-bubbling moist rales are heard.
cases.ask: What are the syndrome and the diagnosis? In which period is the disease? What is found in the sputum? What is expected on X-ray?
cases.answer: The syndromes of cavity formation in the lung and of inflammation — an abscess of the right lung, period II (after rupture into a bronchus). Aspiration (intoxication) is the predisposing factor. When left to settle, the sputum separates into layers, and microscopy reveals elastic fibers and many leukocytes. A cavity with a horizontal fluid level is expected on X-ray.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 28-year-old woman has complained since childhood of producing a large amount (up to 200 ml a day) of purulent sputum in the morning and of occasional hemoptysis. At the age of 5 she had severe measles and pneumonia. The sputum increases when she lies on her right side. There is clubbing of the fingers. Over the lower part of the left lung there are medium- and coarse-bubbling moist rales, which decrease after coughing.
cases.ask: Which disease can be considered? Explain the dependence of the sputum on position. Which investigation confirms the diagnosis?
cases.answer: Bronchiectasis (measles and pneumonia in childhood, abundant purulent sputum in the morning, hemoptysis, clubbing, moist rales over the lower lobe). Pus from the bronchiectases in the left lower lobe drains out through the draining bronchi when she lies on her right side (the healthy side) — that is why the sputum increases. The diagnosis is confirmed by high-resolution CT.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A student wrote the objective examination in the case history as follows: “Lungs normal on percussion and auscultation. Diagnosis: pneumonia.” The patient has fever and cough, and when the teacher examined him, consonating fine-bubbling moist rales were found in the right infrascapular region.
cases.ask: What errors did the student make? What should the correct entry be?
cases.answer: 1) the results of the objective examination were written as a general “normal” — precise data must be written for each method (comparative and topographic percussion, the main and added breath sounds, the areas); 2) the pathological signs (consonating moist rales) were not detected — the examination was not performed completely; 3) the diagnosis was not based on syndromes and contradicts the objective data. The correct entry: describe the changes in the right infrascapular region precisely, identify the syndromes of inflammation and focal consolidation, and then justify the primary diagnosis.

topics.title: Methods of examining patients with cardiovascular diseases. History taking, inspection. Inspection of the heart region and peripheral vessels. Palpation of the heart region

goals.text: To teach the student to identify and analyze the main complaints in cardiovascular diseases, the signs characteristic of heart disease on general inspection, the inspection of the heart region and peripheral vessels, and the detection by palpation of the apex beat, the cardiac impulse and the “cat’s purr” (thrill).
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the projection of the heart and great vessels onto the chest and the main phases of the cardiac cycle;
the main complaints in cardiovascular diseases (pain, dyspnea, choking attacks, palpitations, edema) and their analysis;
the differences between chest pain in angina pectoris, myocardial infarction, pericarditis and other causes;
the NYHA functional classes of chronic heart failure;
the signs detected on inspection: forced position, cyanosis, edema, neck veins, pulsations;
the normal features of the apex beat and its changes;
the types of “cat’s purr” (thrill) and their diagnostic significance.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: take the history of a patient with a cardiovascular disease according to a plan;
inspect the heart region and the peripheral vessels;
palpate the apex beat and assess its location, area, height, force and resistance;
detect the cardiac impulse, epigastric pulsation and chest thrills.

sections.title: 1. Brief anatomy and physiology of the heart

blocks.text: The heart is a four-chambered muscular organ located in the anterior inferior part of the mediastinum, two-thirds of it to the left of the midline. The base of the heart faces upward, to the right and backward, and the apex downward, to the left and forward. The anterior surface of the chest is touched mainly by the **right ventricle**; the left ventricle forms the left contour only as a narrow strip.

blocks.label: Figure 10.1
blocks.caption: General structure of the heart and the direction of blood flow (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 2)

blocks.title: Table 10.1. The heart valves
head: Valve
Location
Function
rows: Between the left atrium and the left ventricle
Prevents the return of blood to the left atrium during systole
Between the right atrium and the right ventricle
Prevents the return of blood to the right atrium during systole
Between the left ventricle and the aorta
Prevents the return of blood to the left ventricle during diastole
Between the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery
Prevents the return of blood to the right ventricle during diastole

blocks.text: **The cardiac cycle** consists of systole and diastole. Ventricular systole: the periods of isovolumetric contraction (all valves closed) and ejection; diastole: the periods of isovolumetric relaxation, rapid and slow filling, and atrial systole. At a heart rate of 72 per minute, one cycle lasts about 0.8 seconds (systole 0.3, diastole 0.5 seconds).

parts.text: The atrioventricular (mitral and tricuspid) valves close **at the beginning of systole** (the I sound), and the semilunar (aortic and pulmonary) valves close **at the beginning of diastole** (the II sound). This rule is the key to understanding heart sounds and murmurs.

sections.title: 2. History taking: the main complaints

blocks.text: 2.1. Pain in the heart region and in the chest
Pain is the most important sign of heart disease. It is analyzed in detail according to a plan: site, character, radiation, circumstances of onset, duration, what relieves it, associated symptoms.

blocks.title: Table 10.2. Differences in chest pain of various causes
head: Feature
Angina pectoris
Myocardial infarction
Pericarditis
Aortic dissection
Cardialgia (functional)
rows: In the region of the cardiac apex, at a small point
Very severe, squeezing, “like a dagger stab”
Left arm, left shoulder blade, neck, lower jaw
Along the back, lower back, abdomen
Worse with breathing, coughing and lying down; lessens when leaning forward
Sudden, against a background of arterial hypertension
Cold sweat, fear, dyspnea, arrhythmia, hypotension
Asymmetry of the pulses in the limbs

parts.text: The three features of anginal pain — **“Squeezes, on Exertion, eased by Nitro”**. If all three are present, it is typical angina; if two, atypical; if one or none, cardialgia (non-anginal pain).

blocks.text: 2.2. Dyspnea and choking attacks (cardiac asthma)

In heart diseases, dyspnea most often develops as a result of **left ventricular failure** and congestion in the pulmonary circulation. It appears first on physical exertion, then on little exertion and at rest; it worsens on lying down and lessens on sitting up (**orthopnea**). A sudden choking attack at night is **cardiac asthma** (paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea); in severe cases, **pulmonary edema** with pink frothy sputum develops.

blocks.title: Table 10.3. Functional classes of chronic heart failure (NYHA)
head: Class
Definition
rows: No limitation of physical activity: ordinary exertion does not cause dyspnea, weakness or palpitations
Slight limitation of physical activity: no symptoms at rest; dyspnea and weakness on ordinary exertion
Marked limitation of physical activity: no symptoms at rest; symptoms appear on less than ordinary exertion
No physical activity can be carried out without symptoms; symptoms are present even at rest

blocks.text: 2.3. Palpitations and skipped beats

**Palpitations** are the sensation of the heartbeat. They are observed in tachycardia, extrasystole, atrial fibrillation, fever, anemia, thyrotoxicosis and neuroses. **Skipped beats** (the feeling that “the heart has stopped”) occur in extrasystole and AV blocks. Attacks of palpitations that begin and end suddenly are characteristic of paroxysmal tachycardia.
2.4. Edema

Cardiac edema is a sign of **right ventricular failure** (congestion in the systemic circulation): it first appears in the evening on the feet and ankles and lessens by the morning, then becomes permanent and spreads upward (thighs, lower back, abdominal wall); fluid accumulates in the body cavities (ascites, hydrothorax) — **anasarca**. In bedridden patients it is seen over the sacrum and lower back.

blocks.label: Figure 10.2
blocks.caption: Leg edema (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 10)

blocks.label: Figure 10.3
blocks.caption: Anasarca (same source, Fig. 11)

blocks.text: 2.5. Other complaints

items: **Heaviness and pain in the right hypochondrium** — liver enlargement and stretching of its capsule (right ventricular failure).
**Cough** (dry, often on lying down) and **hemoptysis** — congestion in the pulmonary circulation (mitral stenosis).
**Headache, dizziness, tinnitus, “floaters” before the eyes** — arterial hypertension; **syncope** — aortic stenosis, severe bradyarrhythmias (Morgagni–Adams–Stokes attack).
**Leg pain on walking, limping** (“intermittent claudication”) — atherosclerosis of the leg arteries.
**Weakness, easy fatigability, fever** — rheumatism, infective endocarditis, myocarditis.

blocks.text: 2.6. Features of the history

In the history of present illness, the following are established: when the pain began, how it has changed (increasing frequency of angina attacks — unstable angina), hospital admissions, ECG and echocardiography results, the medicines being taken. In the life history: **tonsillitis and joint pain in childhood** (rheumatism), risk factors — smoking, arterial hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, obesity, physical inactivity, psychological stress; **heredity** — premature ischemic heart disease in close relatives (men under 55, women under 65), sudden death.

sections.title: 4. Inspection of the heart region and the peripheral vessels

blocks.text: 4.1. Inspection of the heart region
The patient is inspected lying down or standing, with the light falling from the side. The following are assessed:

items: **The cardiac hump** (gibbus cardiacus) — a bulging of the chest over the heart region; it develops as a result of cardiac enlargement from childhood (congenital and early acquired defects), while the chest is not yet ossified.
**The apex beat** — normally visible in more than half of healthy people, on the left in the V intercostal space.
**The cardiac impulse** — a diffuse pulsation at the left sternal border in the III–IV intercostal spaces and below the xiphoid process — right ventricular hypertrophy and dilation.
**A negative (retracting) apex beat** — indrawing of the area of the apex beat during systole — **adhesive pericarditis** (the heart is adherent to the pericardium and the chest wall).

**Pulsations in the region of the base of the heart:** in the II intercostal space to the right of the sternum — dilation or aneurysm of the aorta, aortic regurgitation; in the II intercostal space on the left — dilation of the pulmonary artery (pulmonary hypertension, mitral stenosis); behind the manubrium (in the jugular notch) — dilation of the aortic arch.
**Epigastric pulsation** — see section 6.

blocks.text: 4.2. Inspection of the peripheral vessels
Arteries:

items: **The “carotid dance”** — strong pulsation of the carotid arteries; **de Musset’s sign** — nodding of the head in time with the pulse; **Quincke’s capillary pulse** — rhythmic alternation of redness and pallor under the nail; **pulsation of the pupils** (Landolfi’s sign). These are characteristic of **aortic regurgitation**.
Tortuous, thickened temporal arteries — atherosclerosis, giant cell arteritis.

blocks.text: Veins:

items: **Distension of the neck veins** — right ventricular failure, exudative and constrictive pericarditis, tricuspid valve defects, compression of the superior vena cava.

**Pulsation of the neck veins:** normally a visible negative venous pulse (corresponding to atrial systole); a **positive venous pulse** (the vein fills at the same time as ventricular systole) — **tricuspid regurgitation**.
**Kussmaul’s sign** — increased distension of the neck veins on inspiration (normally it decreases) — constrictive pericarditis, severe right ventricular failure.
**Hepatojugular reflux** — increased distension of the neck veins on pressing the right hypochondrium for 10–15 seconds — right ventricular failure.
Varicose veins of the legs; an infiltrate along a vessel with redness and pain — thrombophlebitis.

parts.text: When pulsation is seen in the neck, arterial and venous pulsation must be distinguished. **Venous pulsation** is soft, undulating, biphasic and visible but not palpable; it disappears when the vein is pressed above the clavicle and changes with the patient’s position and breathing. **Arterial pulsation** is abrupt, monophasic, easily palpable and does not disappear with pressure.

sections.title: 5. Palpation of the heart region

blocks.text: Palpation detects the apex beat, the cardiac impulse, chest thrills (the “cat’s purr”), other pulsations and the pericardial friction rub.
5.1. The apex beat
**The apex beat** is the striking of the apex of the left ventricle against the chest wall during systole (the contracting heart makes a rotary movement, and its apex rises forward).

**Method of palpation:** the patient lies on the back (with the head slightly raised) or stands. The physician places the palm of the right hand between the III and VI ribs, with the base of the palm toward the sternum and the fingers toward the axilla (orienting palpation). Once the impulse has been located, its exact site and features are assessed with the fingertips (2–3 fingers, bent). In women, the breast is moved upward and to the right.

blocks.label: Figure 10.4
blocks.caption: Orienting location of the apex beat with the palm (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 13)

blocks.label: Figure 10.5
blocks.caption: Precise assessment with the fingertips (same source, Fig. 14)

blocks.title: Table 10.5. Features of the apex beat
head: Property
Normal
Changes and causes
rows: On the left in the V intercostal space, 1–1.5 cm medial to the left midclavicular line

To the left — left ventricular dilation (mitral regurgitation, aortic valve defects, hypertension); to the left and downward (to the VI–VII space) — aortic regurgitation; with marked enlargement of the right ventricle — to the left (the left ventricle is pushed aside); fluid or air — to the healthy side; atelectasis, pleural adhesions — to the affected side; with a high diaphragm (ascites, pregnancy, obesity) — upward and to the left; with a low diaphragm (emphysema, asthenic build) — downward and medially
Broad (more than 2 cm, diffuse) — left ventricular dilation; limited — emphysema, obesity, pleural fluid
High — strong physical exertion, thyrotoxicosis, fever, left ventricular dilation; low — obesity, emphysema, pericardial fluid
Increased — left ventricular hypertrophy; decreased — myocardial damage, pericarditis
Resistant (“dome-shaped”, heaving) — concentric left ventricular hypertrophy (aortic stenosis, arterial hypertension)

parts.text: Displacement of the apex beat to the left and its widening are signs of **left ventricular dilation**, and its being resistant is a sign of **hypertrophy**. In aortic regurgitation the left ventricle is both dilated and hypertrophied — the impulse is **displaced to the left and downward, broad, high, forceful and resistant** (“dome-shaped”).
The 5 features of the apex beat — **“Location–Area–Height–Force–Resistance”**: “**L**azy **A**nts **H**ate **F**ast **R**unning”.

blocks.text: 5.2. The cardiac impulse

**The cardiac impulse** is a diffuse pulsation felt with the palm at the left sternal border in the III–IV intercostal spaces and in the epigastric region in hypertrophy and dilation of the right ventricle. It is not detected in a healthy person (except in children and thin people). It is observed in mitral stenosis, pulmonary hypertension, chronic cor pulmonale and congenital defects.

blocks.label: Figure 10.6
blocks.caption: Detecting the cardiac impulse (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 15)

blocks.text: 5.3. Chest thrill (the “cat’s purr”)

**The “cat’s purr”** (frémissement cataire) is a low-frequency vibration felt over the chest wall as a result of turbulence of the blood flow passing through a narrow opening; it resembles the purring of a stroked cat. It is detected by placing the palm over the points of cardiac auscultation.

blocks.label: Figure 10.7
blocks.caption: Detecting a chest thrill (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 17)

blocks.title: Table 10.6. Types of the “cat’s purr”
head: Site
Phase
Disease
rows: In the II intercostal space to the right of the sternum (over the aorta), radiating to the neck vessels
In the II intercostal space to the left of the sternum
At the left sternal border in the III–IV spaces
In the II space to the left of the sternum

parts.text: The “cat’s purr” is always a sign of an **organic** defect (it does not occur with functional murmurs). To determine which phase of the cardiac cycle it corresponds to, the pulse in the carotid artery is palpated at the same time: a thrill coinciding with the pulse is systolic, and one coinciding with the pause after the pulse is diastolic.

sections.title: 6. Other pulsations in and around the heart region

blocks.text: **Epigastric pulsation** is pulsation below the xiphoid process. It arises from three causes:

blocks.title: Table 10.7. Differentiation of epigastric pulsation
head: Cause
Method of determination
rows: When a finger is inserted under the xiphoid process directed upward (toward the heart), the pulsation strikes the fingertip and increases on inspiration
Pulsation of the abdominal aorta (in thin people, aneurysm)
The pulsation strikes the palmar surface of the finger (from above downward) and decreases on inspiration
When the liver is held with both hands, the whole liver expands and contracts (true pulsation — tricuspid regurgitation) or only moves forward (transmitted pulsation)

blocks.text: **The pericardial friction rub** is sometimes detected on palpation at the left sternal border as a rough vibration felt by the hand (dry pericarditis).

sections.title: 7. A detailed analysis of the circulations and the cardiac cycle

blocks.label: Figure 10.8
blocks.caption: General diagram of the cardiovascular system (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 1)

blocks.label: Figure 10.9
blocks.caption: The systemic and pulmonary circulations (same source, Fig. 3)

blocks.text: **The systemic circulation** begins from the left ventricle with the aorta, delivers arterial blood to all the organs and ends via the venae cavae in the right atrium. **The pulmonary circulation** begins from the right ventricle with the pulmonary artery; in the pulmonary capillaries the blood is saturated with oxygen and drains through the four pulmonary veins into the left atrium. The pulmonary circulation is a low-pressure system: the systolic pressure in the pulmonary artery is normally **15–30 mm Hg** (100–140 in the aorta).

blocks.label: Figure 10.10
blocks.caption: Ventricular diastole (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 5)

blocks.label: Figure 10.11

Systole — the interval between the I and II sounds (systolic murmurs occur here)
