blocks.text: 7.1. Projection of the heart and great vessels onto the chest

blocks.label: Figure 10.12
blocks.caption: Projection of the ventricles onto the anterior surface of the chest (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 6)

blocks.label: Figure 10.13
blocks.caption: Projection of the atria and great vessels (same source, Fig. 7)

blocks.text: The right border of the heart (1–1.5 cm lateral to the right sternal edge) is formed by the **right atrium**, the left border by the **left ventricle**, and the upper border by the **left atrial appendage and the conus of the pulmonary artery**. Most of the anterior surface is occupied by the **right ventricle**. The cardiac apex corresponds to the V intercostal space and the base to the level of the III rib.

sections.title: 8. Heart failure: pathogenesis and signs

blocks.text: **Heart failure** is a clinical syndrome in which, as a result of a disturbance of the structure or function of the heart, the heart cannot meet the oxygen demands of the tissues or does so only at the cost of raised filling pressures (ESC, 2021).

**Compensatory mechanisms:** the Frank–Starling mechanism (increased filling strengthens contraction), activation of the sympathetic nervous system (tachycardia, vasoconstriction), the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (retention of sodium and water, edema), myocardial hypertrophy and remodeling. These mechanisms help at first but later aggravate the disease — modern treatment is aimed precisely at blocking them.

This classification is used together with the NYHA functional classes.

This condition belongs to the group of **acute coronary syndromes** and requires urgent hospital admission.

blocks.text: **Causes of a nonpalpable apex beat:** the apex lying behind a rib, obesity, a thick chest wall, the breasts in women, pulmonary emphysema, left-sided exudative pleurisy, exudative pericarditis. In such cases the patient is laid on the **left side** (the impulse shifts 2–3 cm to the left and is felt better) or is examined **leaning forward**.

parts.text: Extracardiac causes of displacement of the apex beat — **“fluid and air push, adhesions and atelectasis pull”**: fluid or air in the pleura — the impulse shifts to the healthy side; pleural adhesions and atelectasis — to the affected side; a high diaphragm (ascites, pregnancy, meteorism) — upward and to the left; a low diaphragm (emphysema, ptosis) — downward and medially.

sections.title: 13. Examination of the peripheral arteries and veins

blocks.text: **Signs of atherosclerosis of the leg arteries:** intermittent claudication (calf pain after walking a certain distance that passes on stopping), pale, cold, dry skin of the legs with hair loss, thickened nails, trophic ulcers; weakened or absent pulses in the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries. **The ankle-brachial index** (the ratio of the systolic pressure at the ankle to the systolic pressure in the arm) is normally **1.0–1.4**; **below 0.9** indicates peripheral arterial disease.

**Veins:** varicose veins of the legs, signs of chronic venous insufficiency (edema, hyperpigmentation, trophic ulcers — most often in the region of the medial malleolus); signs of deep vein thrombosis — swelling and pain of the calf, a calf circumference more than 3 cm larger than that of the healthy leg.

sections.title: 14. “Red flags” and emergencies in chest pain

blocks.text: In a patient presenting with chest pain, **life-threatening** causes must be excluded first.

parts.text: **Beck’s triad** (cardiac tamponade): **arterial hypotension + distended neck veins + muffled heart sounds**. Suspicion of **aortic dissection** — a difference in systolic BP between the two arms of **more than 20 mm Hg** and sudden severe back pain.

sections.title: 18. Clinical part

blocks.text: Sample case history entry

**Cardiovascular system.** The patient is in the orthopnea position. Acrocyanosis. Firm, cyanotic, cold edema of the lower legs and ankles. The neck veins are distended and visible even in the upright position; the hepatojugular reflux is positive. On inspection, the heart region is unchanged, and the apex beat is not visible. On palpation, the apex beat is in the VI intercostal space 2 cm lateral to the left midclavicular line, with an area of 3 cm^2^, high, forceful and resistant. The cardiac impulse and epigastric pulsation are not detected. There is no “cat’s purr”.
**Conclusion:** signs of left ventricular hypertrophy and dilation; heart failure with congestion in the systemic circulation.

skills.title: Skill: palpation of the apex beat

items: Undress the patient to the waist, lying on the back (with the head raised by 30°) or standing.
Place the palm of the right hand over the region of the III–VI ribs, with the base of the palm toward the sternum and the fingers toward the axillary line.
Place the tips of 2–3 fingers (bent) perpendicularly over the place where the impulse is felt and find its exact site — the most lateral and lowest point.
Count the intercostal space (starting from the II rib — next to the sternal angle) and measure the distance from the midclavicular line.
Assess its area, height, force and resistance.
If the impulse is not detected, turn the patient onto the left side (the impulse shifts 2–3 cm to the left) and examine again; ask the patient to breathe out deeply and hold the breath.
Record the result.

skills.title: Skill: detecting the “cat’s purr”

items: Place the palm in turn over the cardiac apex, the II intercostal space to the right and left of the sternum, and the left sternal border (III–IV space).
At the same time, palpate the pulse in the carotid artery with the other hand.
Determine the presence, site and phase (systolic or diastolic) of the thrill.
To feel the thrill better in mitral stenosis, lay the patient on the left side.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 56-year-old man has complained for 2 years of squeezing retrosternal pain appearing on walking fast and climbing stairs. The pain radiates to the left arm, lasts 3–5 minutes and passes 1–2 minutes after he stops to rest or takes nitroglycerin. This morning severe pain appeared at rest; it has lasted for 40 minutes, nitroglycerin has not helped, the patient is drenched in cold sweat and has a feeling of fear.
cases.ask: Interpret the pain over the 2 years and today’s pain. What urgent investigation is needed?
cases.answer: The pain over the 2 years is characteristic of typical exertional angina (squeezing, on exertion, relieved by nitroglycerin). Today’s pain began at rest, has lasted more than 20–30 minutes, does not respond to nitroglycerin and is accompanied by cold sweat and fear — acute coronary syndrome (myocardial infarction) is suspected. An ECG (within 10 minutes) and cardiac troponins are performed immediately, and the patient is admitted to the cardiac intensive care unit.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: In a 48-year-old woman, the neck veins are distended even in the upright position, and they distend further on inspiration. There is leg edema and an enlarged liver. On inspection of the heart region, indrawing of the area of the apex beat is observed during systole.
cases.ask: What are the signs found called, and which disease are they characteristic of?
cases.answer: Increased distension of the neck veins on inspiration is Kussmaul’s sign; indrawing of the area of the apex beat during systole is a negative apex beat. Together with the signs of congestion in the systemic circulation, these are characteristic of constrictive (adhesive) pericarditis: the pericardium thickens and restricts the filling of the heart in diastole.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 25-year-old woman has dyspnea and hemoptysis. She had rheumatism in childhood. There are bluish-red patches on her cheeks. On palpation with the palm at the cardiac apex, a thrill is felt in diastole, and there is a diffuse pulsation at the left sternal border in the III–IV spaces.
cases.ask: What signs have been found? Which defect are they characteristic of? Why has the cardiac impulse appeared?
cases.answer: Facies mitralis, a diastolic “cat’s purr” at the apex and a cardiac impulse have been found. These signs are characteristic of mitral stenosis. When the mitral orifice narrows, the pressure in the left atrium rises, and congestion in the pulmonary circulation and pulmonary hypertension develop; the right ventricle hypertrophies and dilates to overcome the resistance — that is why the cardiac impulse appears.

topics.title: Percussion of the heart: the borders of relative and absolute dullness. Configuration of the heart. The pulse and its features. Analysis of radiographs

goals.text: To teach the student to determine the borders of relative and absolute cardiac dullness and the width of the vascular bundle in a healthy person and in cardiovascular diseases, to assess the configuration of the heart, to examine the arterial pulse and interpret its features, and to analyze the cardiac shadow on a chest radiograph.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the rules and sequence of cardiac percussion;
the normal borders of relative and absolute cardiac dullness and the width of the vascular bundle;
the causes of displacement of the cardiac borders (cardiac and noncardiac);
the normal, mitral, aortic and trapezoid configurations of the heart;
the features of the arterial pulse (symmetry, rhythm, rate, filling, tension, amplitude, shape) and their changes;
the structures forming the cardiac contours on a frontal radiograph and the cardiothoracic ratio.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine the borders of relative and absolute cardiac dullness and draw the configuration of the heart;
examine the pulse in the radial artery and assess all its features;
detect the pulse in other arteries (carotid, femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis);
assess the shape of the cardiac shadow on a radiograph and calculate the cardiothoracic ratio.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Normal borders of relative cardiac dullness: **right — IV intercostal space, 1–1.5 cm lateral to the right sternal edge; upper — III rib; left — V intercostal space, 1–1.5 cm medial to the midclavicular line**. The transverse diameter of the heart is **11–13 cm** (the right part 3–4 cm, the left part 8–9 cm).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Relative dullness: **“4-3-5”** — the right border in the IV space, the upper border at the III rib, the left border in the V space. Absolute dullness: **“Sternum-4”** — the right border is the left sternal edge, the upper border the IV rib.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Percussion assesses the size of the heart only approximately: the error is large in obesity, emphysema and chest deformities. **Echocardiography** and radiography are used to assess the size of the cardiac chambers precisely.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **In aortic regurgitation** the pulse is rapid, high and large (pulsus celer, altus, magnus); **in aortic stenosis** it is slow and small (pulsus tardus, parvus). **Pulse deficit** is a typical sign of atrial fibrillation; to detect it, one person counts the heartbeats on auscultation and another counts the pulse at the same time for one minute.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The normal pulse rate differs between sources: in Russian and Uzbek textbooks it is **60–80** (or 60–90), and in international cardiology guidelines (ESC) **60–100** beats. More than 100 per minute is tachycardia. The manual gives 60–80 as normal, but the range 80–100 should not be regarded as pathological.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **The cardiothoracic ratio** (CTR) is the ratio of the greatest transverse diameter of the cardiac shadow to the greatest internal transverse diameter of the chest. Normally it **does not exceed 0.5** (50 %); more than 0.5 is cardiomegaly.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **The “auscultatory gap”** is a temporary disappearance of the sounds between phases I and II (most often in hypertension and atherosclerosis). If the cuff is not first checked by the palpatory method, the lower limit of the gap is taken as the systolic pressure by mistake, and the systolic pressure is underestimated by 20–40 mm Hg. **The “infinite sound”** — the sounds are heard down to zero (aortic regurgitation, thyrotoxicosis, pregnancy, children).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The ESC 2024 guideline proposed a simplified classification: **non-elevated BP** — below 120/70; **elevated BP** — 120–139/70–89; **hypertension** — 140/90 or higher. In both classifications the threshold of hypertension is **140/90 mm Hg** when measured in the clinic and **135/85 mm Hg** when measured at home.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The pulses in the carotid arteries must not be palpated **on both sides at the same time** or with strong pressure: this may reduce cerebral blood flow and, through the carotid sinus reflex, lead to bradycardia and syncope (especially in the elderly). When the signs of clinical death are being determined, the pulse is checked **in the carotid artery** (within 10 seconds).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: By the displacement of the contrast-filled esophagus: **“small radius — Mitral stenosis, large radius — Mitral regurgitation”**. In mitral stenosis the left atrium is moderately enlarged (the esophagus is displaced along an arc of small radius), whereas in mitral regurgitation it may be very large (an arc of large radius).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **The ejection fraction** (EF) is the ratio of the blood ejected from the left ventricle with each systole to the diastolic volume. By EF, heart failure is divided into three types (ESC, 2021): **reduced EF** (40 % or less), **mildly reduced EF** (41–49 %) and **preserved EF** (50 % or more).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Physical signs characteristic of essential hypertension: a **resistant** apex beat slightly displaced to the left, a widened left cardiac border, an **aortic configuration**, an **accentuated II sound** over the aorta (sometimes with a metallic tinge), a **tense (hard)** pulse.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The cardiac borders and the chambers: **“Right — Right atrium, Upper — Left atrium, Left — Left ventricle”**. Whichever border is displaced, that chamber is enlarged.

sections.title: 1. Percussion of the heart

blocks.text: Part of the heart is covered by the lungs, and part is in direct contact with the chest wall. That is why two kinds of dullness are distinguished:

items: **Relative cardiac dullness** is the **true projection** of the heart onto the anterior surface of the chest (including the parts covered by the lungs). It is determined by percussion of moderate strength, by the change from the clear lung note to an impaired note.

**Absolute cardiac dullness** is the part of the heart not covered by the lungs and in direct contact with the chest wall (mainly the right ventricle). It is determined by **the quietest** percussion, by the change from an impaired note to a completely dull note.

blocks.text: 1.1. Rules of percussion

items: The patient stands or lies on the back (always in the same position, so that the results can be compared).
The pleximeter finger is placed **parallel** to the border being determined.
Percussion proceeds from the resonant note toward the dull note.
The border is marked along the edge of the pleximeter facing the resonant note.
Sequence: the right border is determined first, then the upper border, then the left border.

blocks.text: 1.2. Determining the borders of relative cardiac dullness

**The right border.** First the lower border of the right lung is determined along the midclavicular line (normally the VI rib). Then the pleximeter is moved one intercostal space higher — to the **IV intercostal space** — and percussion proceeds medially with the pleximeter parallel to the sternum.

blocks.label: Figure 11.1
blocks.caption: Determining the right border of relative cardiac dullness (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 18)

blocks.text: **The left border.** The apex beat is found first. Percussion is performed **in the V intercostal space**, starting from the anterior axillary line, with the pleximeter placed parallel to the border (vertically), and proceeds medially. If the apex beat cannot be found, it starts in the V space from the mid-axillary line.
**The upper border.** The pleximeter is placed 1 cm lateral to the left sternal edge (along the left parasternal line), parallel to the ribs, and moved downward from the I intercostal space.

blocks.caption: The left border in a normal person (same source, Fig. 22)

parts.text: Normal borders of relative cardiac dullness: **right — IV intercostal space, 1–1.5 cm lateral to the right sternal edge; upper — III rib; left — V intercostal space, 1–1.5 cm medial to the midclavicular line**. The transverse diameter of the heart is **11–13 cm** (the right part 3–4 cm, the left part 8–9 cm).

Relative dullness: **“4-3-5”** — the right border in the IV space, the upper border at the III rib, the left border in the V space. Absolute dullness: **“Sternum-4”** — the right border is the left sternal edge, the upper border the IV rib.

blocks.text: 1.3. Determining the width of the vascular bundle

Percussion is performed **in the II intercostal space** from the right and left midclavicular lines toward the sternum. Normally the borders of the vascular bundle coincide with the sternal edges, and its width is **5–6 cm**. It is formed on the right by the aorta and the superior vena cava and on the left by the pulmonary artery. It widens in atherosclerosis and aneurysm of the aorta, aortic regurgitation and arterial hypertension.

sections.title: 3. The arterial pulse

blocks.text: **The arterial pulse** is the rhythmic oscillation of the arterial walls resulting from the ejection of blood into the aorta during cardiac systole.
3.1. Examining the pulse in the radial artery

The pulse is palpated between the styloid process of the radius and the tendon of the inner muscle of the forearm, on both arms at the same time. The physician holds the patient’s hand from the palmar side, places the index, middle and ring fingers over the artery, with the thumb on the back of the forearm.

parts.text: **Equalization of the absolute cardiac dullness with the relative dullness** (that is, the two borders almost coincide) is seen when **fluid accumulates in the pericardium**: the fluid pushes the lung edges aside, and the whole heart region comes into direct contact with the chest wall. This sign helps to distinguish exudative pericarditis from myocardial dilation.

sections.title: 6. Arterial pressure and its measurement

blocks.text: **Arterial pressure** (BP) is the pressure exerted by the blood on the walls of the arteries. **Systolic** (upper) pressure is the highest pressure during ventricular systole; **diastolic** (lower) pressure is the lowest pressure in diastole; **pulse pressure** is the difference between them (normally 40–50 mm Hg); **mean arterial pressure** ≈ diastolic + 1/3 of the pulse pressure.

blocks.label: Figure 11.25
blocks.caption: Technique of measuring arterial blood pressure (same source, Fig. 64)

blocks.label: Figure 11.24
blocks.caption: Correct placement of the cuff (same source, Fig. 61)

blocks.label: Figure 11.23

blocks.text: 6.1. Rules for measuring BP by the Korotkoff method

items: The patient sits quietly for 5 minutes; for 30 minutes beforehand he does not smoke, drink coffee or exert himself physically; the bladder is empty.
The patient sits leaning back, legs uncrossed, arm resting on a table, the middle of the upper arm **at the level of the heart**.

The cuff is wrapped around the upper arm, its lower edge **2–3 cm above** the elbow crease, so that one finger fits between the cuff and the skin. The cuff width should cover **40 %** of the arm circumference, and the bladder length **80 %** (a large cuff for obese patients).
First, by the palpatory method, air is pumped in until the pulse in the radial artery disappears; then the pressure is raised a further **20–30 mm Hg** above this level.
The membrane of the stethoscope is placed over the brachial artery in the cubital fossa.
The air is released at a rate of **2–3 mm Hg per second**.
The reading at which **the first Korotkoff sound** appears is the systolic pressure; the reading at which the sounds **disappear completely** (phase V) is the diastolic pressure.
The measurement is repeated 2–3 times at intervals of 1–2 minutes, and the average is taken; at the first visit BP is measured on both arms (the difference should not exceed 10–15 mm Hg).

parts.text: **The “auscultatory gap”** is a temporary disappearance of the sounds between phases I and II (most often in hypertension and atherosclerosis). If the cuff is not first checked by the palpatory method, the lower limit of the gap is taken as the systolic pressure by mistake, and the systolic pressure is underestimated by 20–40 mm Hg. **The “infinite sound”** — the sounds are heard down to zero (aortic regurgitation, thyrotoxicosis, pregnancy, children).

blocks.text: 6.2. Classification of arterial pressure

parts.text: The ESC 2024 guideline proposed a simplified classification: **non-elevated BP** — below 120/70; **elevated BP** — 120–139/70–89; **hypertension** — 140/90 or higher. In both classifications the threshold of hypertension is **140/90 mm Hg** when measured in the clinic and **135/85 mm Hg** when measured at home.

blocks.text: **Arterial hypotension** — BP below 100/60 (in women 95/60) mm Hg: physiological (athletes, young asthenic people) or pathological (shock, blood loss, adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, drug effects). **Orthostatic hypotension** — a fall in systolic BP of more than 20 mm Hg or in diastolic BP of more than 10 mm Hg within 3 minutes of standing up.

parts.text: The pulses in the carotid arteries must not be palpated **on both sides at the same time** or with strong pressure: this may reduce cerebral blood flow and, through the carotid sinus reflex, lead to bradycardia and syncope (especially in the elderly). When the signs of clinical death are being determined, the pulse is checked **in the carotid artery** (within 10 seconds).

blocks.text: **State of the arterial wall:** after the pulse has been stopped by pressure, the artery is palpated distally; normally it is not felt or is felt as a soft elastic tube. In atherosclerosis the artery is hard, tortuous and “beaded” (calcified).

sections.title: 8. The venous pulse

blocks.text: **The venous pulse** visible in the neck veins reflects pressure changes in the right atrium. Normally there is a **negative venous pulse**: the vein empties during ventricular systole (the blood flows into the right atrium). Waves on the phlebogram: **a** — atrial systole; **c** — bulging of the tricuspid valve toward the atrium; **x** descent — atrial relaxation; **v** — filling of the atrium; **y** descent — opening of the tricuspid valve.

In mitral stenosis the left atrium is moderately enlarged (the esophagus is displaced along an arc of small radius), whereas in mitral regurgitation it may be very large (an arc of large radius).

blocks.text: In modern practice, the size of the cardiac chambers, the wall thickness and contractility are determined by **echocardiography** (echo).

parts.text: **The ejection fraction** (EF) is the ratio of the blood ejected from the left ventricle with each systole to the diastolic volume. By EF, heart failure is divided into three types (ESC, 2021): **reduced EF** (40 % or less), **mildly reduced EF** (41–49 %) and **preserved EF** (50 % or more).

sections.title: 11. Arterial hypertension: basics of semiotics

blocks.text: **Arterial hypertension** is a BP of 140/90 mm Hg or higher on repeated measurements in the clinic. In 90–95 % of cases it is **primary (essential) hypertension**; in 5–10 % it is **secondary (symptomatic)** hypertension.

blocks.text: **Target-organ damage in essential hypertension:** left ventricular hypertrophy (a resistant apex beat, an accentuated II sound over the aorta, ECG and echo signs), retinopathy on the fundus, the kidneys (microalbuminuria, raised creatinine), the brain (stroke, encephalopathy), the peripheral arteries.

parts.text: Physical signs characteristic of essential hypertension: a **resistant** apex beat slightly displaced to the left, a widened left cardiac border, an **aortic configuration**, an **accentuated II sound** over the aorta (sometimes with a metallic tinge), a **tense (hard)** pulse.

blocks.text: **“White-coat hypertension”** — BP is high in the clinic but normal at home and on ambulatory monitoring. **Masked hypertension** is the opposite — normal in the clinic, high at home. To detect them, **24-hour ambulatory BP monitoring** (ABPM; normal — below 135/85 during the day, below 120/70 at night, and a 24-hour average below 130/80) or home measurement is used.
**In atrial fibrillation** BP should be measured several times and the average taken; automatic devices may be inaccurate.

blocks.text: Sample case history entry

**Percussion.** Borders of relative cardiac dullness: right — in the IV intercostal space, 1 cm lateral to the right sternal edge; upper — III rib; left — in the V intercostal space, 2 cm lateral to the left midclavicular line. The cardiac waist is deepened, aortic configuration. The width of the vascular bundle is 7 cm. **The pulse** is the same on both arms, regular, 84 per minute, well filled, tense, large, rapid and high. There is no pulse deficit.
**Conclusion:** left ventricular enlargement, an aortic configuration and a rapid, high pulse — characteristic of aortic valve regurgitation.

skills.title: Skill: determining the borders of relative cardiac dullness

items: Have the patient undress to the waist, standing or lying down.

**Right border:** find the lower border of the right lung along the midclavicular line, move one intercostal space higher, place the pleximeter in the IV space parallel to the sternum and percuss medially with moderate force; mark the point where the dullness begins (along the outer edge of the pleximeter).

**Left border:** locate the apex beat; percuss in the V space from the anterior axillary line medially, with the pleximeter held vertically; mark the border and measure the distance to the midclavicular line.
**Upper border:** percuss downward from the I space along the left parasternal line, with the pleximeter parallel to the ribs.
**Vascular bundle:** percuss in the II space from the right and from the left toward the sternum and measure the width.
Draw the cardiac contour and determine the configuration.

skills.title: Skill: examining the pulse in the radial artery

items: The patient holds the arms relaxed, at the level of the heart.
Palpate both radial arteries at the same time and compare their symmetry.
Assess the rhythm on one arm; if the pulse is regular, count for 30 seconds and multiply by 2; if it is irregular, count for 1 full minute.
If the pulse is irregular, count the heart rate on auscultation and determine the pulse deficit.
Assess the filling (compress the artery completely, then release it and feel it fill), the tension (the force needed to stop the pulse), the amplitude and the shape.
Record the result: “The pulse is the same on both arms, regular, 72 per minute, full, not tense, of moderate amplitude and shape.”

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: In a 32-year-old woman, on percussion the upper border of relative cardiac dullness is at the II rib, the right border 3 cm lateral to the right sternal edge, and the left border normal. The pulse is irregular, 96 per minute, and the heart rate on auscultation is 118. The pulse on the left arm is smaller than on the right.
cases.ask: Interpret the percussion findings and determine the configuration. What do the features of the pulse indicate?
cases.answer: Upward displacement of the upper border shows enlargement of the left atrium, and displacement of the right border to the right shows dilation of the right ventricle and right atrium; the cardiac waist is smoothed out — a mitral configuration (mitral stenosis). The pulse is irregular with a pulse deficit of 22 (118 − 96) — atrial fibrillation. The smaller pulse on the left arm is pulsus differens (the enlarged left atrium compresses the left subclavian artery).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: In a 40-year-old man, the apex beat is in the VI intercostal space, 2 cm lateral to the midclavicular line. The left cardiac border is at this point, the cardiac waist is deepened, the vascular bundle is 7 cm. The pulse is rapid and high, BP 160/40 mm Hg.
cases.ask: Determine the configuration and the character of the pulse. Which defect may be suspected?
cases.answer: Aortic configuration (the left ventricle is markedly enlarged, the cardiac waist is deepened), the vascular bundle is widened; the pulse is rapid, high and large (pulsus celer et altus); the pulse pressure is very large (120 mm Hg), and the diastolic pressure is low. These signs are characteristic of aortic valve regurgitation.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: In a 55-year-old patient, on a frontal radiograph the transverse diameter of the cardiac shadow is 17 cm and the internal transverse diameter of the chest is 30 cm. The cardiac shadow is trapezoid, and pulsation of its contours is reduced. Clinically there is a paradoxical pulse and distension of the neck veins.
cases.ask: Calculate the cardiothoracic ratio. Which condition should be considered? How will you confirm the diagnosis?
cases.answer: CTR = 17 / 30 = 0.57 — cardiomegaly. A trapezoid shadow, a paradoxical pulse and distended neck veins are characteristic of exudative pericarditis with a risk of cardiac tamponade. The diagnosis is confirmed by echocardiography (fluid in the pericardium).

topics.title: Auscultation of the heart. Heart sounds in health and disease. Splitting and reduplication of the sounds. Extra sounds. Heart murmurs

goals.text: To teach the student the rules and points of cardiac auscultation, the mechanism of formation and normal features of the heart sounds, the accentuation, weakening, splitting and reduplication of the sounds in disease, the extra sounds, and also the mechanism of formation, classification and features of heart murmurs.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the projection of the heart valves onto the chest and the points and order of auscultation;
the mechanism of formation of the I and II sounds and their distinguishing features;
the causes of accentuation and weakening of the sounds, accentuation of the II sound;
physiological and pathological splitting of the II sound;
the III and IV sounds, the “quail rhythm”, the gallop rhythm, the pericardial knock;
the classification of murmurs, the differences between organic and functional murmurs;
the plan for describing a murmur (phase, epicenter, radiation, intensity, shape, timbre).

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: perform cardiac auscultation in the correct order and in different positions;
distinguish the I and II sounds and assess their features;
detect extra sounds and murmurs and describe them according to the plan.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The order of listening follows the frequency of valve involvement: **“Mitral — Aortic — Pulmonary — Tricuspid — Botkin”** — “**M**y **A**unt **P**olly **T**akes **B**uses”. By site: apex → right II → left II → xiphoid → Botkin–Erb.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: In a healthy person **the I sound is louder than the II sound at the apex** (the I sound is about 1.5–2 times stronger), and **the II sound is louder than the I sound at the base of the heart**. In young people the II sound over the pulmonary artery is slightly louder than over the aorta; after the age of 40 it is the opposite — louder over the aorta.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Physiological** splitting of the II sound appears on inspiration and disappears on expiration. **Pathological** splitting is constant and does not depend on the phases of respiration. To distinguish them, the patient is auscultated while holding the breath after inspiration and after expiration.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **“Quail rhythm” = “Snapping I sound + II sound + opening snap”** — only in mitral stenosis. Remember it by the rhythm “**SNAP — dub — click**”: “snap” is the snapping I sound, “dub” the II sound and “click” the opening snap.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: To hear a diastolic murmur well: **mitral stenosis — “lie on the left side”** (bell, at the apex); **aortic regurgitation — “lean forward and breathe out”** (diaphragm, at the Botkin–Erb point).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Any **diastolic murmur** is almost always regarded as **organic** (the Austin Flint and Graham Steell murmurs are exceptions — but they too arise against the background of an organic defect). If a diastolic murmur is found, echocardiography is always performed.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: In modern practice, in addition to the points, it is recommended to listen over the whole heart region by **“inching” auscultation** (moving the stethoscope from the apex upward along the left sternal edge, then to the right); otherwise murmurs between the points are missed.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The ability to auscultate requires regular practice. According to studies, students and young physicians correctly identify only about half of heart murmurs. It is therefore recommended to listen to every patient, compare the result with the echocardiogram and practice with recorded heart sounds.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: A short formula for remembering a murmur — **“WHERE, WHEN, WHERE TO, HOW LOUD”**: where it is heard best (epicenter), when (systole or diastole), where it radiates, and how loud it is (Levine grade).

sections.title: 1. General rules of cardiac auscultation

items: The room should be quiet and warm.
The patient is auscultated standing, sitting and lying down, and if necessary on the left side (mitral defects) and leaning forward (aortic regurgitation).
Auscultation is performed first during quiet breathing, then while the breath is held after inspiration and after expiration (so that lung sounds do not interfere).
Sometimes auscultation is performed after physical exertion (sitting down and standing up 10–15 times) — the murmur of mitral stenosis becomes louder.

**The diaphragm** is used for high-frequency sounds (the I and II sounds, the murmur of aortic regurgitation), and **the bell** for low-frequency sounds (the III and IV sounds, the diastolic murmur of mitral stenosis).
To distinguish the sounds, the carotid pulse or the apex beat is palpated at the same time: they coincide with **the I sound**.

sections.title: 2. Projection of the heart valves and auscultation points

blocks.text: Because the anatomical projections of the valves onto the chest lie close to each other, the valves are auscultated at the sites where sound is best conducted along the blood flow.

sections.title: 3. Heart sounds

blocks.text: 3.1. Mechanism of formation of the sounds
**The I sound (systolic)** arises at the beginning of ventricular systole and consists of four components:

items: **The valvular component** (the main one) — closure and vibration of the atrioventricular (mitral and tricuspid) valves;
**The muscular component** — vibration of the ventricular myocardium during isovolumetric contraction;
**The vascular component** — vibration of the initial segments of the aorta and pulmonary artery as they fill with blood;
**The atrial component** — atrial contraction (at the onset of the I sound).

blocks.text: **The II sound (diastolic)** arises at the beginning of ventricular diastole from **closure of the semilunar (aortic and pulmonary) valves** and vibration of the walls of the aorta and pulmonary artery. It consists of two components: **aortic (A~2~)** and **pulmonary (P~2~)**.

**The III sound** — vibration of the ventricular walls during rapid ventricular filling in early diastole (0.12–0.18 seconds after the II sound); it may be heard in healthy children and adolescents and in thin young people.
**The IV sound** — vibration of the ventricular walls in presystole (before the I sound), when the atria contract and drive blood into the ventricles; it is usually not heard in healthy adults.

In young people the II sound over the pulmonary artery is slightly louder than over the aorta; after the age of 40 it is the opposite — louder over the aorta.

sections.title: 4. Changes in the heart sounds

blocks.text: 4.1. Simultaneous change of both sounds

items: **Accentuation of both sounds**: extracardiac causes — thinness, a thin chest wall, shrinkage of the lung edges; cardiac causes — thyrotoxicosis, physical exertion, excitement, fever, anemia, tachycardia.

**Weakening (muffling) of both sounds**: extracardiac causes — obesity, a thick chest wall, pulmonary emphysema, left-sided exudative pleurisy, pericardial fluid; cardiac causes — myocardial damage (reduced contractility in myocarditis, myocardial infarction, cardiosclerosis), collapse, shock.

blocks.text: 4.3. Changes in the II sound. Accentuation of the II sound
**Accentuation of the II sound** is an increase in the loudness of the II sound over the aorta or the pulmonary artery compared with the symmetric point.

blocks.text: 4.4. Splitting and reduplication of the sounds

When the components of a sound do not arise at the same time but are heard at a certain interval, this is called **splitting** (an interval of 0.02–0.04 s — the sound is “cleft”) or **reduplication** (an interval of more than 0.05 s — two separate sounds).
**Reduplication of the I sound** — in bundle branch block (the ventricles do not contract at the same time) and in ventricular extrasystole.

**Physiological reduplication of the II sound** — on inspiration the negative pressure in the chest increases, the blood flow to the right ventricle rises, right ventricular systole lengthens and the pulmonary valve closes later. This reduplication is heard **only on inspiration** and disappears on expiration; it is found over the pulmonary artery in young people.

blocks.text: **Pathological reduplication of the II sound** is a constant reduplication that does not depend on the phase of respiration: pulmonary hypertension (mitral stenosis), increased right ventricular load, atrial septal defect (a strict, “fixed” reduplication), right bundle branch block.

To distinguish them, the patient is auscultated while holding the breath after inspiration and after expiration.

sections.title: 6. Heart murmurs

blocks.text: 6.1. Mechanism of formation of murmurs
Normally the blood flow in the heart and vessels is **laminar** (in layers) and silent. A murmur appears when the blood flow becomes **turbulent** (eddying).

blocks.label: Figure 12.5
blocks.caption: Mechanisms of murmur formation: A — normal laminar flow; B — turbulent flow through a narrowing; D — turbulent flow in a dilated vessel; E — irregularity of the wall (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 43)

blocks.text: Causes of turbulent flow:

items: **Narrowing of an orifice** (stenosis) — the blood passes through the narrow site at high speed.
**Valvular regurgitation** — the blood flows back in the opposite direction through a narrow slit.
**Dilation of a vessel or cavity** — eddies form as blood passes from a narrow site into a wider one.
**Reduced blood viscosity** and **increased blood flow velocity** (anemia, fever, thyrotoxicosis) — functional murmurs.
Pathological shunts (ventricular septal defect, patent ductus arteriosus).

blocks.text: 6.2. Classification of murmurs

blocks.title: Table 12.6. Classification of heart murmurs

blocks.text: By phase, **systolic** (between the I and II sounds) and **diastolic** (between the II sound and the next I sound) murmurs are distinguished. Diastolic murmurs in turn are **protodiastolic** (at the beginning of diastole), **mesodiastolic** (in the middle) and **presystolic** (at the end).

blocks.text: 6.3. Plan for describing a murmur

items: **Phase** — systolic or diastolic (determined by palpating the apex beat or the carotid pulse at the same time).
**Relation to the sounds** — whether it begins after a sound or “swallows” the sound.
**Epicenter** — the point where it is heard best (shows which valve it belongs to).
**Radiation** — in the direction of the blood flow.
**Intensity (loudness)** — grades 1–6 on the Levine scale.
**Shape** — increasing (crescendo), decreasing (decrescendo), diamond-shaped, band-shaped.
**Timbre** — harsh, saw-like, blowing, soft, musical.
**Duration** — how much of the phase it occupies.
**Dependence on position, respiration and exertion**.

Definition

Very loud, heard even when only the edge of the stethoscope touches the skin
Heard even with the stethoscope off the skin

parts.text: To hear a diastolic murmur well: **mitral stenosis — “lie on the left side”** (bell, at the apex); **aortic regurgitation — “lean forward and breathe out”** (diaphragm, at the Botkin–Erb point).

blocks.text: 6.4. Differences between organic and functional murmurs

blocks.title: Table 12.9. Organic and functional murmurs

parts.text: Any **diastolic murmur** is almost always regarded as **organic** (the Austin Flint and Graham Steell murmurs are exceptions — but they too arise against the background of an organic defect). If a diastolic murmur is found, echocardiography is always performed.

blocks.text: 6.5. Extracardiac murmurs

**The pericardial friction rub** is heard in systole and diastole, best over the area of absolute cardiac dullness (at the left sternal edge); it does not radiate anywhere, becomes louder when pressed with the stethoscope and when leaning forward, and persists when the breath is held. **The pleuropericardial murmur**, by contrast, becomes louder on inspiration and decreases or disappears when the breath is held.

sections.title: 7. Anatomical basis of the valve projections and auscultation points

blocks.label: Figure 12.7
blocks.caption: Projection of the heart valves onto the chest (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 36)

blocks.label: Figure 12.8
blocks.caption: Points of cardiac auscultation (same source, Fig. 37)

blocks.text: The valves lie very close to each other on the chest (within an area of about 3–4 cm). That is why the sounds are heard not at the valve projections but where the sound is best conducted **in the direction of the blood flow**: the sounds of the mitral valve pass through the left ventricle to the apex, those of the aortic valve through the ascending aorta to the right II intercostal space, those of the pulmonary artery to the left II space, and those of the tricuspid valve through the right ventricle to the base of the xiphoid process.

parts.text: In modern practice, in addition to the points, it is recommended to listen over the whole heart region by **“inching” auscultation** (moving the stethoscope from the apex upward along the left sternal edge, then to the right); otherwise murmurs between the points are missed.

sections.title: 8. Phonocardiography and the physical characteristics of the sounds

blocks.text: **Phonocardiography (PCG)** is the graphic recording of heart sounds with a microphone. It shows precisely the timing, duration and shape of the sounds and murmurs, but has now largely been replaced by echocardiography.

blocks.text: 10.1. Types of functional murmurs

items: **The “innocent” (physiological) murmur of young people** — in children and adolescents and in thin young people; Still’s murmur (“musical”, midway between the apex and the left sternal edge).
**Flow murmurs** — anemia (blood viscosity is reduced), fever, thyrotoxicosis, pregnancy, physical exertion.

**Murmurs of relative valvular regurgitation** — in left ventricular dilation the valve ring widens and the leaflets do not close completely (relative mitral and tricuspid regurgitation); they become softer when the dilation decreases with treatment.
**Venous hum** (a continuous murmur in the jugular veins) — in children and in anemia; it disappears when the head is turned or the vein is compressed.

parts.text: **Embryocardia** (pendulum rhythm) — the intensity of the sounds and the pauses become equal, resembling the fetal heart rhythm; it may be a sign of severe myocardial damage (myocardial infarction, myocarditis, shock).

sections.title: 12. Echocardiography — confirming the auscultatory findings

blocks.label: Figure 12.9
blocks.caption: Two-dimensional echocardiogram: RV — right ventricle, IVS — interventricular septum, LV — left ventricle, Ao — aorta (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 82)

blocks.label: Figure 12.10
blocks.caption: Diagram of the propagation of ultrasound pulses (same source, Fig. 83)

blocks.text: Echocardiography shows the structure of the valves, the movement of the leaflets, the area of the orifices, the regurgitant jet (color Doppler) and the pressure gradients. **Any diastolic murmur, a systolic murmur louder than grade 3, a murmur accompanied by symptoms, or a murmur combined with ECG and radiographic changes** is an indication for echocardiography.

parts.text: The ability to auscultate requires regular practice. According to studies, students and young physicians correctly identify only about half of heart murmurs. It is therefore recommended to listen to every patient, compare the result with the echocardiogram and practice with recorded heart sounds.

sections.title: 13. Auscultation after valve replacement and heart surgery

items: **Mechanical prosthetic valves** — distinct, loud, metallic closing (and opening) “clicks” (with a mitral prosthesis in place of the I sound, with an aortic prosthesis in place of the II sound); their disappearance or weakening may be a sign of thrombosis.
**Biological valves** — the sounds are close to normal.
With an aortic prosthesis a mild systolic murmur is normal; any new **diastolic** murmur raises the suspicion of prosthetic dysfunction or infective endocarditis.

sections.title: 14. Auscultatory signs in congenital heart defects

blocks.text: Although the propaedeutics course mainly studies acquired defects, it is necessary to know the auscultatory signs of the congenital defects seen in adults.

parts.text: To diagnose **acute pericarditis** (ESC), at least two of the following four signs are required: **pericardial chest pain** (reduced on leaning forward), **a pericardial friction rub**, **widespread ST elevation on the ECG** (or PR depression), **new or increasing pericardial fluid**.

sections.title: 16. Useful rules for recording and teaching murmurs and sounds

items: Listen **to the sounds first, then to the murmurs**: the phase of a murmur cannot be determined without placing it relative to the I and II sounds.
**Attend to one sound at a time**: listen “selectively” first only to the I sound, then only to the II sound, then to systole, then to diastole.
**In tachycardia** the duration of systole and diastole becomes equal — determine the phases by the carotid pulse.

**In atrial fibrillation** the loudness of a murmur varies with the cycle: in the cycle after a long pause the murmur of aortic stenosis becomes louder, while the murmur of mitral regurgitation does not change.
Always record the result in the same form: **phase — epicenter — radiation — intensity (Levine) — shape — timbre — relation to the sounds — dynamic maneuvers**.

parts.text: A short formula for remembering a murmur — **“WHERE, WHEN, WHERE TO, HOW LOUD”**: where it is heard best (epicenter), when (systole or diastole), where it radiates, and how loud it is (Levine grade).

sections.title: 17. Auscultatory signs of tricuspid valve defects

blocks.text: **Tricuspid regurgitation** is most often **relative** (right ventricular dilation due to mitral stenosis, pulmonary hypertension or cor pulmonale), less often organic (infective endocarditis — in injecting drug users, rheumatism, Ebstein anomaly). Signs: a **pansystolic murmur** at the base of the xiphoid process and the lower part of the left sternal edge that **becomes louder on inspiration (Rivero-Carvallo sign)**; a **positive venous pulse**, systolic pulsation of the liver, hepatomegaly, ascites, edema.

**Tricuspid stenosis** is rare and almost always rheumatic and combined with mitral stenosis; a diastolic murmur at the base of the xiphoid process that becomes louder on inspiration, large “a” waves in the neck veins, marked peripheral edema and ascites (even though pulmonary congestion is slight).

sections.title: 18. Clinical part

blocks.text: Sample case history entry

**Auscultation.** The heart sounds are regular, 78 per minute. At the apex the I sound is weakened, and a systolic murmur is heard at the apex: it merges with the I sound, occupies the whole of systole, has a blowing timbre, is grade 3 on the Levine scale, radiates to the left axillary region and becomes louder in the left lateral position. Accentuation of the II sound over the pulmonary artery. The II sound over the aorta is preserved. No extra sounds.

**Conclusion:** weakening of the I sound at the apex, a systolic murmur radiating to the left axilla and accentuation of the II sound over the pulmonary artery — characteristic of mitral valve regurgitation.

skills.title: Skill: auscultation of the heart

items: Have the patient lie down or sit, undressed to the waist; ensure quiet in the room.
Locate the apex beat by palpation (the first point).
Listen to the points in order: apex → II space to the right of the sternum → II space to the left of the sternum → base of the xiphoid process → Botkin–Erb point.

At each point: distinguish the I and II sounds (using the carotid pulse), compare the rhythm and rate and the loudness of the sounds (the I sound should be louder at the apex and the II sound louder at the base).
Compare the II sound over the aorta and over the pulmonary artery and determine any accentuation.
Look for splitting, reduplication and extra sounds (on inspiration and on expiration).
If there is a murmur, describe it according to the plan; to check its radiation, move the stethoscope from the epicenter in different directions.
Listen again at the apex with the patient lying on the left side and at the Botkin–Erb point with the patient leaning forward.
Record the result in the case history.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: In a 20-year-old student at a medical examination, reduplication of the II sound was heard over the pulmonary artery on inspiration; the reduplication disappears on expiration. At the apex a short, soft, grade 1 systolic murmur is heard at the beginning of systole; it disappears on standing and does not radiate anywhere. The cardiac borders are normal, and the sounds are unchanged.
cases.ask: Interpret the changes found. Are they pathological?
cases.answer: Reduplication of the II sound that appears on inspiration and disappears on expiration is physiological reduplication (on inspiration right ventricular filling increases and the pulmonary valve closes later). A short, soft, faint murmur that does not radiate and varies with position, with unchanged sounds and cardiac borders, is characteristic of a functional (“innocent”) murmur. Both are variants of normal in young people; if in doubt, echocardiography is performed.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: In a 30-year-old woman, a snapping I sound at the apex, an extra sound after the II sound and a low-pitched diastolic murmur increasing in presystole are heard; the murmur is heard well in the left lateral position. Accentuation and reduplication of the II sound over the pulmonary artery.
cases.ask: Interpret the auscultatory findings. What is the rhythm called? Which defect is involved?
cases.answer: Snapping I sound + II sound + mitral opening snap — the “quail rhythm”; a diastolic murmur at the apex increasing in presystole; accentuation and reduplication of the II sound over the pulmonary artery (pulmonary hypertension). All of this is characteristic of mitral stenosis.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 62-year-old man complains of fainting and retrosternal pain on exertion. A harsh, saw-like, diamond-shaped systolic murmur is heard in the II intercostal space to the right of the sternum; it radiates to the carotid arteries, and a systolic thrill is felt in this area. The II sound over the aorta is weakened.
cases.ask: Grade the murmur on the Levine scale. Which defect may be suspected?
cases.answer: A loud murmur accompanied by a thrill is at least grade 4. A harsh diamond-shaped systolic murmur over the aorta radiating to the carotid arteries, weakening of the II sound, syncope and angina are characteristic of aortic stenosis; the diagnosis is confirmed by echocardiography.

topics.title: Symptoms and initial diagnosis of rheumatism (acute rheumatic fever) and primary rheumatic carditis. Mitral defects: mitral valve regurgitation and mitral stenosis

goals.text: To teach the student the etiology, the major and minor clinical features of acute rheumatic fever, the symptoms of primary rheumatic carditis and the modern diagnostic criteria (the Jones criteria revised by the AHA in 2015), and also the hemodynamics and the clinical and physical signs of mitral valve regurgitation and mitral stenosis.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the definition, etiology and pathogenesis of acute rheumatic fever;
the major and minor manifestations of rheumatism, the Jones criteria (2015);
the signs of primary rheumatic carditis;
the laboratory parameters that determine the activity of the rheumatic process;
the hemodynamic changes in mitral regurgitation and mitral stenosis;
the findings of inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation, radiography, ECG and echocardiography in each defect;
the grades of severity of mitral stenosis (ESC/EACTS 2025).

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: take the history from and examine a patient with suspected rheumatism;
justify the diagnosis by applying the Jones criteria;
detect mitral defects by physical examination and distinguish them from each other.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The older literature used the term “rheumatism”. International and CIS classifications now use the terms **“acute rheumatic fever”** and **“chronic rheumatic heart disease”**. The term “rheumatism” in the course syllabus is understood in this sense.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Diagnosis of **initial ARF**: **2 major** or **1 major + 2 minor** criteria together with evidence of a preceding group A streptococcal infection. **Recurrent ARF** (with a history of ARF or rheumatic heart disease): 2 major, 1 major + 2 minor, or **3 minor** criteria. Evidence of streptococcal infection — a raised or rising ASO titer, a positive throat culture for streptococcus or a positive rapid antigen test. Chorea alone is also sufficient for the diagnosis.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The major Jones criteria — **“JONES”**: **J** — Joints (polyarthritis); **O** — the heart-shaped “O” (carditis); **N** — Nodules (subcutaneous nodules); **E** — Erythema marginatum; **S** — Sydenham chorea.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The textbook gives three grades of activity of the rheumatic process (maximal — III, moderate — II, minimal — I) (A.I. Nesterov classification). This classification is partly retained in CIS practice, but in international practice the diagnosis is made by the Jones criteria, and carditis is assessed by echocardiography (including subclinical carditis).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The auscultatory triad of mitral regurgitation: **weakening of the I sound at the apex + a systolic murmur merging with the I sound and radiating to the left axilla + accentuation of the II sound over the pulmonary artery**.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The auscultatory signs of mitral stenosis: **snapping I sound + mitral opening snap (“quail rhythm”) + a diastolic murmur at the apex increasing in presystole + accentuation of the II sound over the pulmonary artery**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Mitral stenosis — **“Face, Blood, Quail”**: facies mitralis, hemoptysis, the “quail rhythm”. Mitral regurgitation — **“Soft I sound, murmur to the Axilla”**.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Streptococcal **pharyngitis and tonsillitis** lead to ARF, whereas streptococcal **skin infections** (impetigo) usually do not (they are associated more with glomerulonephritis). That is why, in a child with a sore throat and fever, detecting the streptococcal infection and giving a full 10-day course of antibiotics — **primary prevention** — is extremely important.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Duration of secondary prevention (AHA): without carditis — **5 years or until the age of 21** (whichever is longer); carditis without residual valve disease — **10 years or until the age of 21**; carditis with residual valve disease — **10 years or until the age of 40**, sometimes lifelong.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: To remember the changes in the cardiac chambers in mitral defects: **“In stenosis — the left atrium and the right heart; in regurgitation — the left atrium and the left ventricle”**. The left atrium enlarges in both defects; the difference lies in the ventricles.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Every pregnant woman with a heart defect should be followed jointly by **a cardiologist and an obstetrician** and monitored by echocardiography. In pregnant women with a mechanical prosthetic valve, anticoagulant therapy is managed according to a special protocol.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: In mitral stenosis, the shorter the **“II sound — opening snap” interval**, the more severe the stenosis (the pressure in the left atrium is high, and the valve opens earlier). If this interval on the PCG is less than 0.07 s, the stenosis is severe.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Complications of mitral stenosis — **“RASH”**: **R**ight ventricular failure, **A**trial fibrillation, **S**troke and other thromboembolism, **H**emoptysis and pulmonary edema.

sections.title: 1. Acute rheumatic fever (rheumatism)

blocks.text: **Acute rheumatic fever** (ARF) is a systemic inflammatory disease that develops **2–3 weeks** after tonsillitis or pharyngitis caused by group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus in genetically predisposed individuals and mainly involves the cardiovascular system, the joints, the central nervous system and the skin. It most often occurs in children and adolescents aged **7–15 (20) years**, more often in girls.
**Rheumatic heart disease** is a chronic disease formed after ARF and characterized by permanent damage to the heart valves (a defect).

parts.text: The older literature used the term “rheumatism”. International and CIS classifications now use the terms **“acute rheumatic fever”** and **“chronic rheumatic heart disease”**. The term “rheumatism” in the course syllabus is understood in this sense.

blocks.text: 1.1. Etiology and pathogenesis

The main cause is **group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus** (GABHS). **Molecular mimicry** plays the main role in the pathogenesis: the streptococcal M protein and other antigens resemble antigens of the heart tissues (myosin, valves), the synovium of the joints and the basal ganglia of the brain.

The antibodies and T lymphocytes produced against the streptococcus damage the body’s own tissues (autoimmune inflammation). The morphological basis is disorganization of the connective tissue (mucoid swelling → fibrinoid changes → granulomatosis — **Aschoff–Talalayev granulomas** → sclerosis).
1.2. Clinical picture
The disease usually begins 2–3 weeks after tonsillitis or pharyngitis: fever (38–39 °C), weakness, sweating, joint pain.

blocks.title: Table 13.1. Main manifestations of acute rheumatic fever
head: Manifestation
Frequency
Features
rows: The most important sign, determines the outcome of the disease; endocarditis (valvulitis) predominates, most often of the mitral and aortic valves
Large joints (knee, ankle, elbow, shoulder, wrist), migratory, symmetric, severe pain, swelling, redness; resolves completely without deformity; responds rapidly to NSAIDs
More often in girls; involuntary, irregular movements of the facial and limb muscles, disturbed handwriting, emotional lability; disappears during sleep; may appear late (after 1–6 months)
Pale pink annular rashes with pale centers on the trunk and proximal parts of the limbs; not itchy, change quickly
Painless, firm nodules of 0.5–2 cm over the joints, bony prominences and the occipital region; occur together with severe carditis

parts.text: Rheumatic arthritis in adults often takes the form of **arthralgia** and is mild. A classic rule: “**Rheumatism licks the joints but bites the heart**” (Lasègue–Bouillaud) — the joint changes pass without a trace, while the heart is damaged with a permanent defect.

blocks.text: 1.3. Primary rheumatic carditis
**Rheumatic carditis** is rheumatic inflammation of all layers of the heart (endocardium, myocardium, sometimes pericardium); in primary rheumatic carditis **endomyocarditis** is most often seen.

blocks.title: Table 13.2. Signs of primary rheumatic carditis
head: Method of examination
Signs
rows: Discomfort or pain in the heart region, palpitations, skipped beats, dyspnea on exertion, weakness
Tachycardia out of proportion to the fever (sometimes bradycardia), arrhythmia, a soft and small pulse
Widening of the cardiac borders to the left (myocarditis, dilation)

Weakening of the I sound at the apex; a III sound or a protodiastolic gallop; a soft blowing systolic murmur at the apex (valvulitis or relative mitral regurgitation); sometimes a mesodiastolic murmur at the apex (Carey Coombs murmur — swelling of the mitral valve leaflets); a protodiastolic murmur over the aorta (aortic valvulitis); in pericarditis — a pericardial friction rub
Prolongation of the PQ interval (first-degree AV block), extrasystole, changes in the ST segment and T wave, reduced voltage
Swelling and thickening of the valves, pathological regurgitation (mitral, aortic), restricted leaflet mobility, pericardial fluid — subclinical carditis is also detected

blocks.text: 1.4. Laboratory findings

items: In the blood, neutrophilic leukocytosis, **raised ESR** (in severe cases 50–70 mm/h), appearance and rise of **C-reactive protein**;
dysproteinemia: decreased albumin, increased alpha2- and gamma-globulins, raised fibrinogen, raised seromucoid and sialic acids;
a rise in the titers of antistreptococcal antibodies: **antistreptolysin O (ASO)**, antistreptokinase, antihyaluronidase;
a throat swab culture for group A streptococcus or a rapid antigen test.

blocks.text: 1.5. Diagnostic criteria: the Jones criteria (AHA, 2015)

blocks.title: Table 13.3. The revised Jones criteria (2015)
head: Criterion
Low-risk populations

parts.text: Diagnosis of **initial ARF**: **2 major** or **1 major + 2 minor** criteria together with evidence of a preceding group A streptococcal infection. **Recurrent ARF** (with a history of ARF or rheumatic heart disease): 2 major, 1 major + 2 minor, or **3 minor** criteria. Evidence of streptococcal infection — a raised or rising ASO titer, a positive throat culture for streptococcus or a positive rapid antigen test. Chorea alone is also sufficient for the diagnosis.

The major Jones criteria — **“JONES”**: **J** — Joints (polyarthritis); **O** — the heart-shaped “O” (carditis); **N** — Nodules (subcutaneous nodules); **E** — Erythema marginatum; **S** — Sydenham chorea.

The textbook gives three grades of activity of the rheumatic process (maximal — III, moderate — II, minimal — I) (A.I. Nesterov classification). This classification is partly retained in CIS practice, but in international practice the diagnosis is made by the Jones criteria, and carditis is assessed by echocardiography (including subclinical carditis).

sections.title: 2. General information on acquired heart defects

blocks.text: **A heart defect** is a permanent anatomical change of the valves or orifices that disturbs the blood flow. If a valve does not close completely, it is **regurgitation** (insufficiency); if an orifice is narrowed, it is **stenosis**. If both are present on one valve, it is a **combined (complex)** defect; if several valves are involved, it is a **multivalvular** defect.

**Causes:** rheumatic heart disease (the main cause in developing countries), infective endocarditis, atherosclerosis and degenerative calcification of the valves (in the elderly), connective tissue diseases, syphilis, mitral valve prolapse, cardiac injuries.

**Stages of the course of defects:** compensation (the circulation is maintained through hypertrophy and dilation of the cardiac chambers, no complaints) → subcompensation → decompensation (heart failure).

sections.title: 3. Mitral valve regurgitation

blocks.text: **Mitral regurgitation** is incomplete closure of the mitral valve leaflets during systole with backflow of blood from the left ventricle into the left atrium (regurgitation).

**Types: organic** (wrinkling and shortening of the leaflets and chordae: rheumatism, endocarditis, prolapse, chordal rupture) and **functional (relative)** — dilation of the valve ring and the left ventricle (dilated cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, aortic defects), papillary muscle dysfunction (myocardial infarction).

blocks.label: Figure 13.1
blocks.caption: Hemodynamics in mitral valve regurgitation (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 120)

blocks.text: **Hemodynamics:** in systole part of the blood returns to the left atrium → the left atrium is overfilled with blood and dilates → in diastole excess blood also enters the left ventricle → **dilation and hypertrophy of the left ventricle** (volume overload). Compensation is maintained for a long time; in decompensation the pressure in the left atrium rises, and congestion in the pulmonary circulation, pulmonary hypertension and later right ventricular failure develop.

blocks.title: Table 13.4. Signs of mitral valve regurgitation

parts.text: The auscultatory triad of mitral regurgitation: **weakening of the I sound at the apex + a systolic murmur merging with the I sound and radiating to the left axilla + accentuation of the II sound over the pulmonary artery**.

sections.title: 4. Mitral stenosis (narrowing of the left atrioventricular orifice)

blocks.text: **Mitral stenosis** is narrowing of the left atrioventricular orifice resulting from fusion of the mitral valve leaflets along the commissures, their thickening and calcification, and shortening of the chordae. It is almost always of **rheumatic** origin and is more common in women.

blocks.label: Figure 13.2
blocks.caption: Hemodynamics in mitral stenosis (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 119)

blocks.text: **Hemodynamics:** the normal mitral orifice area is **4–6 cm^2^**. When the orifice narrows, blood cannot pass completely from the left atrium into the left ventricle in diastole → **the pressure in the left atrium rises**, and the atrium hypertrophies and dilates → the pressure is transmitted to the pulmonary veins and capillaries (**“passive” or venous pulmonary hypertension**) → reflex spasm of the pulmonary arterioles (**the Kitaev reflex** — “active”, arterial pulmonary hypertension, the “second barrier”) → **hypertrophy and dilation of the right ventricle** → right ventricular failure. The left ventricle, being underfilled, remains unchanged or becomes smaller.

Mitral stenosis — **“Face, Blood, Quail”**: facies mitralis, hemoptysis, the “quail rhythm”. Mitral regurgitation — **“Soft I sound, murmur to the Axilla”**.

blocks.text: **Complications:** pulmonary edema, pulmonary hemorrhage, atrial fibrillation, thrombus formation in the left atrium and arterial thromboembolism (brain, kidneys, spleen, leg vessels), right ventricular failure, infective endocarditis.

sections.title: 5. Acute rheumatic fever: extended information

blocks.text: 5.1. Epidemiology and risk factors

ARF and rheumatic heart disease remain the main cause of acquired heart defects among young people worldwide, especially in developing countries. According to the WHO, **more than 40 million** people in the world live with rheumatic heart disease. Risk factors: crowded and poor living conditions, delayed medical care, inadequate treatment of streptococcal pharyngitis, hereditary predisposition (familial cases, certain HLA antigens, the D8/17 marker of B lymphocytes).

parts.text: Streptococcal **pharyngitis and tonsillitis** lead to ARF, whereas streptococcal **skin infections** (impetigo) usually do not (they are associated more with glomerulonephritis). That is why, in a child with a sore throat and fever, detecting the streptococcal infection and giving a full 10-day course of antibiotics — **primary prevention** — is extremely important.

blocks.text: 5.2. Pathomorphology
Rheumatic inflammation of the connective tissue proceeds in four stages:

items: **Mucoid swelling** (1–2 weeks) — reversible changes;
**Fibrinoid changes** (2–4 weeks) — irreversible;
**Granulomatosis** — **Aschoff–Talalayev granulomas** (clusters of large basophilic cells in the heart tissue) — 1–3 months;
**Sclerosis** — scar formation; in the valves — thickening, fusion and wrinkling of the leaflets, shortening of the chordae → a defect.

blocks.text: **Rheumatic valvulitis** most often affects the mitral valve (70–75 %), then the aortic valve; the tricuspid and pulmonary valves are rarely involved (and usually together with others).
5.3. Differences between rheumatic and other arthritides

blocks.text: 5.4. Rheumatic chorea

**Minor chorea** (Sydenham chorea) is autoimmune damage to the subcortical nuclei of the brain. It most often occurs in girls aged 5–15 years, **1–6 months** after the streptococcal infection (so other signs and laboratory activity may be absent). Signs: involuntary, irregular, purposeless movements (facial expressions, limbs), muscle hypotonia, impaired coordination, emotional lability. The movements become stronger with excitement and disappear during sleep. Clinical tests: **the “choreic hand”** (when the arms are stretched forward, the wrist flexes and the fingers extend), **the “milkmaid’s grip”** (rhythmic relaxation when squeezing the physician’s fingers), inability to keep the tongue protruded.

parts.text: Duration of secondary prevention (AHA): without carditis — **5 years or until the age of 21** (whichever is longer); carditis without residual valve disease — **10 years or until the age of 21**; carditis with residual valve disease — **10 years or until the age of 40**, sometimes lifelong.

parts.text: In mitral stenosis, patients often deteriorate sharply for the first time against the background of **pregnancy**, **the onset of atrial fibrillation** or **fever**: in these situations the heart rate rises and diastole shortens — there is not enough time for the left ventricle to fill through the narrowed orifice, the pressure in the left atrium rises sharply, and pulmonary edema may develop.

blocks.text: 6.3. Mitral valve prolapse

**Mitral valve prolapse** is bulging of the mitral valve leaflets (most often the posterior leaflet) into the cavity of the left atrium by more than 2 mm during systole. It occurs in 2–3 % of the population, more often in asthenic women and in connective tissue dysplasia (Marfan syndrome). In most cases it is asymptomatic; sometimes there is stabbing pain in the heart region, palpitations, weakness. **Auscultation:** a **midsystolic “click”** at the apex followed by a **late systolic murmur**; on standing and during the Valsalva maneuver the click moves closer to the I sound and the murmur lengthens. Complications: significant mitral regurgitation, arrhythmias, infective endocarditis (if there is regurgitation).
6.4. Combined mitral defect
In rheumatic disease, mitral stenosis and regurgitation often occur together. It is important to determine which one predominates:

sections.title: 7. Principles of treatment of mitral defects (in brief)

blocks.text: Knowing the principles of treatment helps the student understand the essence of the disease:

items: **Mitral stenosis:** in severe symptomatic stenosis — **percutaneous balloon mitral commissurotomy** (if the leaflets are suitable) or surgical valve replacement; slowing the heart rate with drugs (beta-blockers), diuretics; in atrial fibrillation — **anticoagulants** (warfarin) are mandatory.

**Mitral regurgitation:** in severe primary regurgitation — valve **repair** (plasty) or replacement; in the secondary type — full treatment of heart failure, sometimes transcatheter edge-to-edge repair of the leaflets.
In all patients — secondary prevention of rheumatism, sanitation of foci of infection, dental hygiene.

parts.text: To remember the changes in the cardiac chambers in mitral defects: **“In stenosis — the left atrium and the right heart; in regurgitation — the left atrium and the left ventricle”**. The left atrium enlarges in both defects; the difference lies in the ventricles.

sections.title: 8. Chronic rheumatic heart disease and pregnancy

blocks.text: Rheumatic defects often occur in young women, so pregnancy has a great effect on their course. During pregnancy the circulating blood volume increases by **30–50 %**, and the heart rate and cardiac output rise.

items: **In mitral stenosis** pregnancy is most dangerous: the heart rate increases and diastole shortens, the pressure in the left atrium rises — **pulmonary edema** (most often in the II–III trimester and during delivery), atrial fibrillation. In severe mitral stenosis, balloon commissurotomy may be performed before or during pregnancy.
**In mitral and aortic regurgitation** pregnancy usually goes relatively well (the fall in peripheral resistance reduces the regurgitation).
**In severe aortic stenosis** the risk is high.

parts.text: Every pregnant woman with a heart defect should be followed jointly by **a cardiologist and an obstetrician** and monitored by echocardiography. In pregnant women with a mechanical prosthetic valve, anticoagulant therapy is managed according to a special protocol.

sections.title: 12. Natural course of mitral defects

blocks.text: **Mitral stenosis:** it usually takes **10–20 years** after ARF for the defect to form; symptoms often appear at the age of 30–40. Once symptoms have appeared, the 10-year survival of untreated patients is about 50–60 %. Causes of death: progressive heart failure, thromboembolism (stroke), pulmonary edema, infective endocarditis.

**Chronic mitral regurgitation** remains compensated for many years; left ventricular dilation and a fall in the ejection fraction (below 60 %) are indications for surgery, because the results of the operation are good if it is performed before irreversible myocardial dysfunction develops.

parts.text: Complications of mitral stenosis — **“RASH”**: **R**ight ventricular failure, **A**trial fibrillation, **S**troke and other thromboembolism, **H**emoptysis and pulmonary edema.

blocks.text: Sample case-history entry (mitral stenosis)

Bluish-red patches on the cheeks, the lips cyanotic. A cardiac impulse at the left sternal edge in the III–IV intercostal spaces, epigastric pulsation. The apex beat is in the V space, 1 cm medial to the midclavicular line, weak, with an area of 1 cm^2^. A diastolic thrill at the apex. Borders of relative cardiac dullness: right — 2.5 cm lateral to the sternum, upper — II rib, left — 1 cm medial to the midclavicular line; mitral configuration. At the apex a snapping I sound, a mitral opening snap (“quail rhythm”) and a diastolic murmur increasing in presystole; accentuation and reduplication of the II sound over the pulmonary artery. The pulse is irregular, 104/min, pulse deficit 18, the pulse on the left arm smaller.
**Conclusion:** chronic rheumatic heart disease: mitral stenosis; atrial fibrillation; pulmonary hypertension.

skills.title: Skill: justifying the diagnosis of ARF by the Jones criteria

items: Establish whether there was tonsillitis or pharyngitis 2–3 weeks earlier.
Look for the major criteria: carditis (complaints, auscultation, ECG, echocardiography), arthritis (location, migratory character), chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules.
Determine the minor criteria: fever, arthralgia, ESR and CRP, the PR interval.
Check for evidence of streptococcal infection: ASO titer, throat swab.
Count the criteria taking into account the risk group of the population and draw a conclusion.

skills.title: Skill: hearing the diastolic murmur in mitral stenosis

items: Have the patient lie on the left side.
Find the apex beat by palpation.
Place the bell of the stethoscope lightly over the apex (do not press).
Ask the patient to breathe out and hold the breath.
Listen for the opening snap after the II sound, the diastolic murmur and the presystolic accentuation before the I sound.
If the murmur is faint, have the patient sit down and stand up 10–15 times and listen again.
