cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 14-year-old girl had tonsillitis 3 weeks ago. For 5 days she has had a fever of 38.6 °C and swelling and pain in the knee joint; two days later the pain moved to the ankle joint and then to the elbow. There are pink annular rashes on the trunk. Pulse 118/min, the I sound at the apex is weakened, a soft systolic murmur. ESR 56 mm/h, CRP markedly raised, ASO 800 IU/ml. ECG: PQ 0.24 s.
cases.ask: Analyze according to the Jones criteria. What is the diagnosis?
cases.answer: Major criteria: carditis (tachycardia, weakening of the I sound, a systolic murmur at the apex), migratory polyarthritis, erythema marginatum — 3. Minor criteria: fever, raised ESR and CRP (the prolonged PR is not counted because carditis is a major criterion). Evidence of a preceding streptococcal infection: tonsillitis and a raised ASO. Diagnosis: acute rheumatic fever, primary rheumatic carditis (mitral valvulitis), polyarthritis, erythema marginatum. Echocardiography for confirmation.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: In a 45-year-old man, the apex beat is in the VI space, 2 cm lateral to the midclavicular line, diffuse and strong. The cardiac borders are widened upward and to the left. At the apex the I sound is inaudible; a blowing murmur merging with the I sound and occupying the whole of systole radiates to the left axillary region. Accentuation of the II sound over the pulmonary artery.
cases.ask: Which defect is this? Which cardiac chambers are enlarged, and why?
cases.answer: Mitral valve regurgitation. Because blood returns to the left atrium in systole, the left atrium dilates (displacement of the upper border); because excess blood enters the left ventricle in diastole, left ventricular dilation and hypertrophy develop (displacement of the apex beat and the left border to the left). Accentuation of the II sound shows raised pressure in the pulmonary circulation.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 32-year-old woman complains of dyspnea on exertion, hemoptysis and palpitations. Echocardiography: mitral orifice area 1.1 cm^2^, left atrium 52 mm, a thrombus in the left atrial appendage. ECG: atrial fibrillation.
cases.ask: Assess the severity of the stenosis. What is expected on auscultation? What complication is she at risk of?
cases.answer: An orifice area of less than 1.5 cm^2^ — clinically significant (severe) mitral stenosis. On auscultation: a snapping I sound, an opening snap, a diastolic murmur at the apex (without presystolic accentuation because of the fibrillation), accentuation of the II sound over the pulmonary artery; irregular sounds and a pulse deficit. The thrombus in the left atrium and the fibrillation sharply increase the risk of arterial thromboembolism (especially stroke); anticoagulant therapy and surgery (commissurotomy or valve replacement) are considered.

topics.title: Symptoms of septic (infective) endocarditis. Aortic defects: aortic valve regurgitation and narrowing of the aortic orifice

goals.text: To teach the student the etiology, predisposing factors, clinical signs and modern diagnostic criteria of infective (septic) endocarditis (Duke-ISCVID 2023, ESC 2023), and also the hemodynamics and the clinical and physical signs of aortic valve regurgitation and aortic stenosis.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the definition, causative agents and risk factors of infective endocarditis;
the general, cardiac, vascular (embolic) and immune signs of infective endocarditis;
the major and minor Duke-ISCVID (2023) criteria;
the hemodynamic changes in aortic valve regurgitation and aortic stenosis;
the peripheral signs of aortic regurgitation;
the findings of inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation, radiography, ECG and echocardiography in aortic defects;
the severity criteria of aortic stenosis (ESC/EACTS 2025).

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: examine a patient with suspected infective endocarditis and identify the main signs;
explain the rules for taking blood cultures;
detect and distinguish aortic defects by physical examination.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The term **“septic endocarditis”** in the course syllabus is outdated; the term **“infective endocarditis”** is now used (in the textbook, “infectious endocarditis”). The older literature distinguished, by course, **acute** (develops over a few days to weeks, most often staphylococcal) and **subacute** (endocarditis lenta, most often viridans streptococci) types.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The peripheral signs of IE — **“Osler — Ouch, Janeway — painless”**: Osler nodes are painful (immune vasculitis), Janeway lesions are painless (microembolism); Roth spots — on the fundus, Lukin spots — on the conjunctiva.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Definite IE**: 2 major criteria, or 1 major + 3 minor criteria, or 5 minor criteria (or pathological confirmation). **Possible IE**: 1 major + 1 minor or 3 minor criteria. If the criteria are insufficient or another diagnosis is clear, **IE is rejected**.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The main signs of aortic regurgitation: **aortic configuration + weakening of the II sound over the aorta + a protodiastolic murmur at the Botkin–Erb point + a rapid and high pulse + a wide pulse pressure (low diastolic pressure) + peripheral vascular signs**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The peripheral signs of aortic regurgitation — **“Everything pulsates”**: the head (de Musset), the carotid arteries (“carotid dance”), the nail-bed capillaries (Quincke), the pupils (Landolfi), the uvula (Müller); and the femoral artery “speaks” (Traube’s double sound, Duroziez’s double murmur).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The classic **symptom triad** of aortic stenosis: **angina, fainting (syncope) and dyspnea (heart failure)**. Once symptoms appear, the average survival without surgery shortens sharply (about 5 years with angina, 3 years with syncope and 2 years with heart failure) — that is why symptomatic severe aortic stenosis is an indication for valve replacement.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: If a vegetation is **larger than 10 mm**, especially on the mitral valve and mobile, the risk of embolism increases sharply — this is one of the indications for early surgery. Other indications: severe heart failure, uncontrolled infection (abscess, persistent bacteremia), a fungal or multidrug-resistant pathogen.

But the most important prevention is **oral hygiene** and dental check-ups 1–2 times a year, as well as proper care of intravenous catheters.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: In IE, involvement of the aortic valve and heart failure are an indication for **urgent surgery**. A patient with endocarditis should have daily cardiac auscultation and ECG monitoring: the appearance of a new murmur or block indicates a complication.

sections.title: 1. Infective (septic) endocarditis

blocks.text: **Infective endocarditis** (IE) is microbial inflammation of the heart valves or the parietal endocardium (and also of prosthetic valves, intracardiac devices and the endothelium of large vessels), accompanied by the formation of **vegetations**, destruction of the valves, emboli and immune complications.

parts.text: The term **“septic endocarditis”** in the course syllabus is outdated; the term **“infective endocarditis”** is now used (in the textbook, “infectious endocarditis”). The older literature distinguished, by course, **acute** (develops over a few days to weeks, most often staphylococcal) and **subacute** (endocarditis lenta, most often viridans streptococci) types.

blocks.text: 1.1. Etiology and risk factors

blocks.title: Table 14.1. Main causative agents of infective endocarditis
head: Pathogen
Features
rows: The most common pathogen today; acute, severe course; injecting drug users, vascular catheters, prosthetic valves
After dental procedures; subacute course (classic endocarditis lenta)
After urogenital and intestinal procedures, in the elderly
Associated with tumors of the colon — colonoscopy is needed

blocks.text: **Risk factors (cardiac):** previous IE, prosthetic valves, rheumatic and degenerative valve defects, congenital heart defects, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, mitral valve prolapse (with regurgitation), intracardiac devices (pacemaker). **Extracardiac factors:** injecting drug use (the tricuspid valve is most often involved), hemodialysis, long-term venous catheters, dental and other invasive procedures, immunodeficiency, diabetes mellitus.
1.2. Pathogenesis

Bacteremia (tooth extraction, catheter, injection) → microbes settle on the fibrin-platelet layer of the damaged endocardium → **vegetation** (microbes, fibrin, platelets) → destruction and perforation of the valve leaflets (**valvular regurgitation** — most often aortic and mitral), abscesses → detachment of fragments of the vegetation (**emboli**: brain, kidneys, spleen, coronary arteries, lungs — in tricuspid IE) → formation of immune complexes (**vasculitis, glomerulonephritis**, Osler nodes, Roth spots).
1.3. Clinical picture

blocks.title: Table 14.2. Clinical signs of infective endocarditis
head: Group
Signs
rows: Fever (the most constant sign, up to 90 %) — often with chills and profuse sweating, hectic or irregular; weakness, loss of appetite, weight loss, joint and muscle pain
Pallor, a pale yellowish “café-au-lait” skin color (anemia and hemolysis); petechiae (skin, conjunctiva — Lukin–Libman sign, oral mucosa); splinter hemorrhages under the nails

Osler nodes — painful, red, pea-sized nodules on the fingertips (immune vasculitis); Janeway lesions — painless hemorrhagic spots on the palms and soles (septic microembolism); in a prolonged course, “drumstick” fingers and “watch-glass” nails
Roth spots — hemorrhages with pale centers on the fundus

Signs of valve damage: a newly appeared regurgitant murmur (most often the diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation or the systolic murmur of mitral regurgitation) or a change in the character of an existing murmur; heart failure; conduction disturbances (perivalvular abscess)

Stroke, renal infarction (low back pain, hematuria), splenic infarction (pain under the left costal margin), embolism of the leg arteries, mycotic aneurysms; in tricuspid IE — septic infarcts and foci in the lungs

blocks.label: Figure 14.1
blocks.caption: Fingers: the “watch-glass” sign (A) — one of the signs of long-standing infective endocarditis (Gadayev A. et al., 2012, Fig. 11)

parts.text: **Fever + a newly appeared heart murmur** = infective endocarditis must be ruled out. In any patient with a valve defect, a prolonged fever (more than 1 week) of unknown cause also raises the suspicion of IE. In such a patient, blood cultures are taken **before** antibiotics are started.

The peripheral signs of IE — **“Osler — Ouch, Janeway — painless”**: Osler nodes are painful (immune vasculitis), Janeway lesions are painless (microembolism); Roth spots — on the fundus, Lukin spots — on the conjunctiva.

blocks.text: 1.4. Laboratory and instrumental investigations

items: **Blood cultures** are the main investigation: they are taken before antibiotics are started, **at least 3 times**, from different veins, at 30-minute intervals (each time into aerobic and anaerobic bottles); there is no need to wait for a temperature spike.
Complete blood count: normochromic **anemia**, leukocytosis (or leukopenia), **markedly raised ESR** (50–70 mm/h); raised CRP and procalcitonin; rheumatoid factor may be positive.
Urine: proteinuria, microhematuria (glomerulonephritis, renal infarction).
**Echocardiography** — transthoracic and, if necessary, **transesophageal** (higher sensitivity): vegetations, valve perforation, abscess, new regurgitation.
Additional: cardiac CT, 18F-FDG PET/CT (especially with prosthetic valves), brain MRI (to detect emboli).

blocks.text: 1.5. Diagnostic criteria: Duke-ISCVID (2023)

blocks.title: Table 14.3. Major Duke-ISCVID (2023) criteria
head: Group
Criterion
rows: Isolation of microorganisms typical of IE (Staphylococcus aureus, viridans streptococci, S. gallolyticus, HACEK, enterococci) from 2 or more separate blood cultures; isolation of nontypical microbes from 3 or more cultures; PCR or serological confirmation in the blood for Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella, Tropheryma whipplei

On echocardiography and/or cardiac CT: a vegetation, valve perforation or aneurysm, an abscess, a pseudoaneurysm, an intracardiac fistula; new significant valvular regurgitation; new partial dehiscence of a prosthetic valve; metabolic activity on 18F-FDG PET/CT in the region of prosthetic valves and devices
Direct visualization of IE during surgery

blocks.title: Table 14.4. Minor Duke-ISCVID (2023) criteria
head: Criterion
Content
rows: Previous IE, a prosthetic valve, valve repair, a congenital heart defect, more than moderate regurgitation or stenosis, intracardiac devices, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, injecting drug use
Arterial emboli, septic infarcts in the lungs, brain or splenic abscess, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial hemorrhage, conjunctival hemorrhages, Janeway lesions, purulent purpura
Positive rheumatoid factor, Osler nodes, Roth spots, immune-complex glomerulonephritis
A positive blood culture that does not meet the major criterion, or a microbe consistent with IE from another sterile site
Activity on 18F-FDG PET/CT within 3 months of valve or device implantation
When echocardiography is unavailable, a new regurgitant murmur on auscultation (an increase in an existing murmur does not count)

parts.text: **Definite IE**: 2 major criteria, or 1 major + 3 minor criteria, or 5 minor criteria (or pathological confirmation). **Possible IE**: 1 major + 1 minor or 3 minor criteria. If the criteria are insufficient or another diagnosis is clear, **IE is rejected**.

sections.title: 2. Aortic valve regurgitation

blocks.text: **Aortic regurgitation** is incomplete closure of the aortic valve leaflets during diastole with backflow of blood from the aorta into the left ventricle.

**Causes:** rheumatic heart disease, **infective endocarditis**, atherosclerosis and degenerative changes, a bicuspid aortic valve, dilation of the aortic root (Marfan syndrome, arterial hypertension, aortic dissection), syphilitic aortitis, ankylosing spondylitis, rheumatoid arthritis, SLE.

**Hemodynamics:** in diastole part of the blood returns from the aorta to the left ventricle → the left ventricle receives blood both from the atrium and from the aorta → **volume overload of the left ventricle, eccentric hypertrophy and marked dilation** (the largest heart — “ox heart”) → in systole a large stroke volume is ejected into the aorta (**the systolic pressure rises**), while in diastole the pressure in the aorta falls sharply because of the backflow (**the diastolic pressure falls**) → **wide pulse pressure**. After a long period of compensation, left ventricular failure develops.

blocks.title: Table 14.5. Signs of aortic valve regurgitation
head: Method of examination
Signs
rows: None for a long time; then palpitations, a sensation of pulsation in the neck vessels, dizziness, a tendency to faint (poor blood supply to the brain), angina (reduced coronary perfusion), dyspnea

The skin is pale; pulsation of the vessels: “carotid dance”, de Musset sign (nodding of the head), Quincke capillary pulse, pupillary pulsation (Landolfi), pulsation of the uvula (Müller); the apex beat is visible
The apex beat is displaced to the left and downward (VI–VII space), diffuse, high, strong, resistant (“dome-shaped”)
The left cardiac border is markedly widened to the left and downward; aortic configuration (cardiac waist deepened); the vascular bundle is widened

The II sound over the aorta is weakened or absent; a diastolic (protodiastolic) murmur — begins immediately after the II sound, soft, blowing, decreasing, heard best at the Botkin–Erb point and in the II space on the right, radiates to the apex; heard well when the patient leans forward and holds the breath after expiration; the I sound at the apex is weakened; the Austin Flint murmur at the apex (functional narrowing of the mitral orifice — presystolic); a functional systolic murmur of relative stenosis over the aorta
Traube’s double sound over the femoral artery; Duroziez’s double murmur when the femoral artery is compressed with the stethoscope
Rapid, high and large (pulsus celer, altus, magnus) — the “water-hammer” (Corrigan) pulse

The systolic pressure is raised, the diastolic pressure markedly lowered (sometimes to 0 — the “infinite sound”), wide pulse pressure (for example, 160/40 mm Hg); the systolic pressure in the legs exceeds that in the arms by more than 20 mm Hg (Hill sign)
The left ventricle is markedly enlarged, aortic configuration (“boot”), the ascending aorta is dilated, the amplitude of pulsation is increased
Left ventricular hypertrophy, left axis deviation
The diastolic regurgitant jet (color Doppler) and its severity, the size of the left ventricle, the state of the valve leaflets and the aortic root

parts.text: The main signs of aortic regurgitation: **aortic configuration + weakening of the II sound over the aorta + a protodiastolic murmur at the Botkin–Erb point + a rapid and high pulse + a wide pulse pressure (low diastolic pressure) + peripheral vascular signs**.

The peripheral signs of aortic regurgitation — **“Everything pulsates”**: the head (de Musset), the carotid arteries (“carotid dance”), the nail-bed capillaries (Quincke), the pupils (Landolfi), the uvula (Müller); and the femoral artery “speaks” (Traube’s double sound, Duroziez’s double murmur).

sections.title: 3. Narrowing of the aortic orifice (aortic stenosis)

blocks.text: **Aortic stenosis** is narrowing of the aortic orifice resulting from fusion, thickening and calcification of the aortic valve leaflets, which impedes the outflow of blood from the left ventricle in systole.

**Causes:** in the elderly, **degenerative (calcific) stenosis** — now the most common cause; a **congenital bicuspid aortic valve** (at the age of 40–60); rheumatic heart disease (often together with a mitral defect).

**Hemodynamics:** the normal aortic orifice area is **3–4 cm^2^**. When it narrows, a systolic **pressure gradient** appears between the left ventricle and the aorta → pressure overload of the left ventricle → **concentric hypertrophy** (the wall thickens without dilation of the cavity) → long compensation; then increased myocardial oxygen demand and reduced coronary perfusion (angina), limited stroke volume (syncope), and finally left ventricular dilation and failure.

parts.text: The classic **symptom triad** of aortic stenosis: **angina, fainting (syncope) and dyspnea (heart failure)**. Once symptoms appear, the average survival without surgery shortens sharply (about 5 years with angina, 3 years with syncope and 2 years with heart failure) — that is why symptomatic severe aortic stenosis is an indication for valve replacement.

blocks.title: Table 14.6. Signs of aortic stenosis
head: Method of examination
Signs
rows: None for a long time; then angina on exertion, dizziness and fainting (on exertion), dyspnea, fatigue
The skin is pale; the apex beat is barely visible
The apex beat is slightly displaced to the left, strong, resistant (concentric hypertrophy); a systolic thrill in the II space to the right of the sternum, transmitted to the carotid arteries
The left border is displaced to the left (more marked in decompensation), aortic configuration

A harsh, saw-like, loud, diamond-shaped (crescendo-decrescendo) systolic murmur in the II space on the right, radiating to the carotid arteries, the clavicles and the interscapular region; the II sound over the aorta is weakened (it may disappear in severe stenosis); the I sound at the apex is weakened; a IV sound; with a bicuspid valve — an early systolic ejection sound
Slow and small (pulsus tardus et parvus), often with a tendency to bradycardia
Systolic pressure low or normal, narrow pulse pressure
Rounding of the left ventricular contour, aortic configuration, poststenotic dilation of the ascending aorta, valve calcification
Signs of left ventricular hypertrophy and systolic overload (ST depression, negative T in V5–V6), left bundle branch block
The leaflets are thickened and calcified, their opening restricted; the orifice area, peak velocity and mean gradient — determine the severity

blocks.caption: ECG in aortic stenosis: signs of left ventricular hypertrophy and systolic overload (Kamolov N.M., Qo‘yliyev M.U., 1991, Fig. 4)

blocks.text: 4.3. Complications of IE

items: **Cardiac complications:** acute valvular regurgitation and **heart failure** (the most common complication and the main cause of death), perivalvular abscess and fistulas, AV block (when the abscess extends to the conduction system), myocarditis, pericarditis, coronary embolism — myocardial infarction.
**Emboli:** to the central nervous system (stroke — 20–40 %), spleen, kidneys, mesentery, leg arteries; in right-sided IE — multiple septic infarcts in the lungs.
**Mycotic aneurysms** — of the brain and the abdominal aorta.
**Renal complications:** immune-complex glomerulonephritis, renal infarction, renal failure.
**Sepsis and metastatic abscesses.**

parts.text: If a vegetation is **larger than 10 mm**, especially on the mitral valve and mobile, the risk of embolism increases sharply — this is one of the indications for early surgery. Other indications: severe heart failure, uncontrolled infection (abscess, persistent bacteremia), a fungal or multidrug-resistant pathogen.

blocks.text: 4.4. Prevention of IE

Antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended only for **high-risk** patients before **high-risk dental procedures** (manipulations of the gingival tissue or the periapical region of the teeth, or perforation of the oral mucosa) (ESC, 2023).

blocks.title: Table 14.10. High-risk group for IE
head: Group
Examples
rows: Prosthetic valves and prosthetic material used for valve repair
Mechanical and biological prostheses, transcatheter valves, annuloplasty rings
Untreated cyanotic defects; defects repaired with prosthetic material (within 6 months or if there is a residual shunt)

parts.text: Standard prophylaxis: **amoxicillin 2 g orally 30–60 minutes before** the procedure (children 50 mg/kg); in penicillin allergy — antibiotics of another group. But the most important prevention is **oral hygiene** and dental check-ups 1–2 times a year, as well as proper care of intravenous catheters.

blocks.text: 6.3. Natural course of aortic stenosis and principles of treatment

Aortic stenosis gradually progresses over the years: the orifice area decreases on average by **0.1 cm^2^** per year, and the gradient increases by **7 mm Hg** per year. The asymptomatic stage lasts a long time, but the prognosis worsens sharply once symptoms appear.

items: **Treatment:** there is no effective drug therapy; in severe symptomatic stenosis — **valve replacement**: surgical (open-heart) or **transcatheter (TAVI)** — in elderly patients and those at high surgical risk; according to the ESC/EACTS 2025 guideline, the choice is based on age and risk.
**Precautions:** in severe aortic stenosis, potent vasodilators (high-dose nitrates) and strenuous physical exertion are dangerous — they may cause syncope and sudden death.

parts.text: In severe aortic stenosis there is a risk of **sudden cardiac death** (mainly in symptomatic patients). That is why, if an elderly patient has syncope or angina on exertion and a harsh systolic murmur is heard over the aorta, echocardiography should be performed immediately.

sections.title: 7. Mixed and multivalvular aortic defects

blocks.text: **A mixed aortic defect** (stenosis + regurgitation) occurs in rheumatic and degenerative diseases. On auscultation, **systolic and diastolic murmurs** are heard together over the aorta (a “sawing” quality). Determining the predominant lesion: if stenosis predominates — the pulse is slow and small, the pulse pressure narrow, the thrill distinct; if regurgitation predominates — the pulse is rapid and high, the diastolic pressure low, the peripheral signs pronounced.

**Multivalvular mitral-aortic defects** (often rheumatic): for example, when mitral stenosis and aortic regurgitation coexist, the peripheral signs of aortic regurgitation are poorly expressed because the mitral stenosis limits the blood flow into the left ventricle — each defect “masks” the signs of the other. In such cases the diagnosis is established by echocardiography.

parts.text: Changes in the left ventricle in aortic defects: **“Stenosis — the wall thickens (pressure overload), regurgitation — the cavity dilates (volume overload)”**. That is why the heart is largest in aortic regurgitation (“ox heart”).

sections.title: 8. The relationship of aortic diseases to aortic valve defects

blocks.text: Aortic valve regurgitation often develops not because of the valve itself but as a result of **dilation of the aortic root and ascending aorta**.

parts.text: Signs of **an aneurysm of the ascending aorta**: retrosternal pain, pulsation in the II intercostal space to the right of the sternum, widening of the vascular bundle, hoarseness (an aneurysm of the aortic arch compresses the recurrent nerve), downward tugging of the trachea (Oliver–Cardarelli sign), difficulty swallowing. Confirmation — echocardiography and CT angiography.

sections.title: 10. Infective endocarditis and aortic valve defects: the relationship

blocks.text: Infective endocarditis often involves **the aortic valve** and causes acute or rapidly progressive **aortic regurgitation**. In a patient with IE the following are dangerous signs:

items: a **new** or rapidly increasing aortic diastolic murmur;
a sharp fall in the diastolic BP;
acute left ventricular failure (pulmonary edema);
prolongation of the PR interval and AV block — a sign of **an aortic root abscess** (the abscess lies close to the conduction system).

parts.text: In IE, involvement of the aortic valve and heart failure are an indication for **urgent surgery**. A patient with endocarditis should have daily cardiac auscultation and ECG monitoring: the appearance of a new murmur or block indicates a complication.

sections.title: 12. Principles of treatment of aortic defects (in brief)

items: **Aortic regurgitation:** in severe regurgitation, if symptoms appear or, even without symptoms, if there is left ventricular dilation (end-systolic diameter more than 50 mm) and a fall in the ejection fraction (50 % or less) — **valve replacement**; if the aortic root is dilated — together with the aorta. Drugs (vasodilators) reduce symptoms in inoperable patients.

**Aortic stenosis:** in severe symptomatic stenosis — **surgical or transcatheter (TAVI)** valve replacement; in asymptomatic severe stenosis — regular follow-up and exercise testing, and in some cases early surgery.

**Infective endocarditis:** intravenous bactericidal antibiotics for **4–6 weeks** according to the blood culture result; if indicated — early surgery. Treatment is managed by the “endocarditis team” (cardiologist, cardiac surgeon, infectious disease specialist, microbiologist).

parts.text: To remember the surgical signal in aortic defects — **“Symptoms or Damage”**: the appearance of **S**ymptoms (angina, syncope, dyspnea) or **d**amage to the left ventricle (dilation, a fall in the ejection fraction) means that it is time to operate.

blocks.text: Sample case-history entry (aortic regurgitation)

The skin is pale. Strong pulsation of the carotid arteries (“carotid dance”), nodding of the head with the pulse (de Musset sign), Quincke capillary pulse positive. The apex beat is in the VI intercostal space, 2 cm lateral to the left midclavicular line, with an area of 3 cm^2^, high, strong, resistant. The left cardiac border is in the VI space, 2 cm lateral to the midclavicular line, the cardiac waist is deepened, the vascular bundle is 7 cm. The II sound over the aorta is weakened; at the Botkin–Erb point there is a soft protodiastolic murmur beginning after the II sound and radiating to the apex, which becomes louder when the patient leans forward. Traube’s double sound over the femoral artery. Pulse 88/min, regular, rapid, high, large. BP 165/40 mm Hg.
**Conclusion:** aortic valve regurgitation; left ventricular dilation and hypertrophy.

skills.title: Skill: detecting the peripheral signs of aortic regurgitation

items: Observe the patient sitting: nodding of the head (de Musset), pulsation of the carotid arteries in the neck (“carotid dance”).
Press lightly on the tip of a nail and observe the rhythmic alternation of reddening and blanching under the nail (Quincke capillary pulse).
Palpate the radial artery; raise the patient’s arm and feel the pulse “knocking” (Corrigan pulse).
Measure the arterial pressure and calculate the pulse pressure.
Auscultate the femoral artery (Traube’s double sound); press slightly with the stethoscope and look for Duroziez’s double murmur.
With the patient leaning forward and holding the breath after expiration, listen for the diastolic murmur at the Botkin–Erb point.

skills.title: Skill: rules for taking blood cultures (when IE is suspected)

items: They are taken before antibiotics are started (or after a 2–3-day break).
At least 3 samples are taken from different peripheral veins at 30-minute intervals.
Each sample of 10 ml is inoculated into aerobic and anaerobic bottles.
The skin is treated in strict accordance with antiseptic rules; samples are not taken from a catheter.
There is no need to wait for a temperature spike (the bacteremia is continuous).

Where does the systolic murmur of aortic stenosis radiate?
According to ESC/EACTS 2025, what is the mean pressure gradient in severe aortic stenosis?
How does the left ventricle change in aortic stenosis?

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 38-year-old man who had rheumatism in childhood is being followed up for mitral regurgitation. A tooth was extracted a month ago. For two weeks his temperature has risen to 38.5–39 °C in the evenings, with chills, profuse sweating and weakness; he has lost 4 kg. On examination the skin is pale yellowish, there are petechiae on the left conjunctiva and painful red nodules on the fingertips. A diastolic murmur that was not present before has appeared at the Botkin–Erb point. The spleen is palpable. Hb 98 g/l, ESR 62 mm/h.
cases.ask: Which disease is suspected? Which signs have been found? What should be done to confirm the diagnosis?
cases.answer: Infective endocarditis (probably viridans streptococcal, after a dental procedure, on the background of a rheumatic defect). Signs: fever, weight loss, “café-au-lait” skin and anemia, the Lukin–Libman sign (conjunctival petechiae), Osler nodes, a new murmur of aortic regurgitation (destruction of the aortic valve), splenomegaly, raised ESR. To confirm: at least 3 blood cultures before antibiotics and echocardiography (transthoracic, then transesophageal) to detect vegetations; assessment according to the Duke-ISCVID criteria.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 70-year-old man reports squeezing retrosternal pain on climbing stairs over the past year and two episodes of fainting on exertion. A harsh systolic murmur is heard in the II space to the right of the sternum, radiating to the carotid arteries, with a systolic thrill at the same site. The II sound over the aorta is markedly weakened. Pulse 58/min, slow and small. BP 105/80 mm Hg.
cases.ask: Which defect is this? Calculate and interpret the pulse pressure. Which echocardiographic parameters indicate severe stenosis?
cases.answer: Aortic stenosis (in old age most often degenerative calcification) — symptomatic (angina, syncope). Pulse pressure 105 − 80 = 25 mm Hg — narrow (limited stroke volume); the pulse is slow and small (tardus et parvus). Severe stenosis: orifice area less than 1.0 cm^2^, peak velocity 4 m/s or more, mean gradient 40 mm Hg or more. Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis is an indication for valve replacement (surgical or transcatheter TAVI).

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 28-year-old man (tall, with long limbs and long thin fingers) was referred because of a BP of 150/45 mm Hg found incidentally at a medical examination. Strong pulsation of the carotid arteries, Quincke pulse positive. A diastolic murmur over the aorta.
cases.ask: Which defect is this, and what is its probable cause? Why is the diastolic pressure low?
cases.answer: Aortic valve regurgitation; the body build (arachnodactyly, tall stature) suggests Marfan syndrome — valve regurgitation resulting from dilation of the aortic root. The diastolic pressure is low because in diastole blood returns from the aorta to the left ventricle and the pressure in the aorta falls sharply; the large stroke volume raises the systolic pressure — the pulse pressure is wide. On echocardiography the size of the aortic root and the severity of the regurgitation are assessed.

cards.back: Fever + a new regurgitant murmur; emboli, splenomegaly, anemia
Before antibiotics, 3 times, from different veins
Protodiastolic murmur at the Botkin–Erb point; rapid, high pulse; BP 160/40; de Musset, Quincke, Traube
Harsh systolic murmur in the II space on the right, radiating to the carotid arteries; slow, small pulse; triad: angina, syncope, dyspnea
Orifice less than 1 cm^2^; velocity 4 m/s or more; gradient 40 mm Hg or more
In regurgitation — eccentric hypertrophy and dilation; in stenosis — concentric hypertrophy
